text: I reject that member’s assertions, but, again, I return to the fact that the science system will need to be productive, efficient, financially sustainable, and generate real value for New Zealanders.
explanation: Vague platitudes with no figures, names, or commitments.

text: The traditional five-yearly survey model is no longer financially sustainable, operationally reliable, or able to produce timely, high-quality data... I do acknowledge the concerns raised by Te Kāhui Raraunga; this Government takes these concerns seriously... Stats New Zealand is committed to working with iwi Māori, including Te Kāhui Raraunga, on the design, planning, and implementation of the new census approach.
explanation: States the rationale but commitments to iwi collaboration remain general.

text: We’ve already made those statements. That will not happen in this term of Government.
explanation: Bounds the commitment to 'this term of Government'.

text: No, I’m encouraged by the last Stats NZ report that actually showed there was more scientists than we had previously and also new opportunities for science through the new emerging technologies: the Institute for Advanced Technology, through artificial intelligence, through quantum, through magnetic materials, through Robinson, and the $42 million by Biodiscovery Platform.
explanation: Names concrete initiatives and a $42m Biodiscovery Platform figure, though no detail on the job cuts at issue.

text: we’ve taken strong steps to restore law and order, with 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime; ram raids are down 85 percent; and repeat youth offending is down 22 percent... lifting childhood immunisations to 82.6 percent... We are seeing progress in education, with phonics proficiency lifting from 36 percent to 58 percent.
explanation: Stacks numerous precise figures across crime, health, and education.

text: We’ve said that we’ll talk more about the National Fuel Plan escalation, and what triggers would enable us to move from different steps, later on.
explanation: Commits to nothing; promises detail 'later on'.

text: I think, actually, burning international, Indonesian coal is about twice as bad as using domestic gas.
explanation: A concrete comparison ('twice as bad') but no underlying numbers.

text: That's why we've been incredibly targeted for the 143,000 families—working families—who are using their cars getting to work and getting their kids to school.
explanation: Names the 143,000-family target group, though without the mechanism for those excluded.

text: That's why we agreed to increase the minimum stock holding obligations for fuel importers from 21 days to 28 days.
explanation: Names a concrete obligation change with figures (21 to 28 days).

text: We do have an economic recovery under way. That's evidenced by the GDP growth being 1.1 percent in the last quarter. It's evidenced with inflation being low at 3.1 percent... We've got consumer confidence the highest it's been since 2021... business confidence the highest since 2014... building consents up 20 percent, construction jobs up 43 percent in the last year, job ads up 10 percent in the last year.
explanation: Dense with named figures and timeframes.

text: Our Government is very clear about the fact that what is happening in the Middle East is having an impact on many New Zealanders, with the fuel-price pressure that they are facing. We are also very clear that any response needs to be targeted, timely, and temporary, otherwise every single person in New Zealand would be affected by inflation going up again.
explanation: 'Targeted, timely, and temporary' is an alliterative principle rather than detail.

text: we are seeing 83,000 New Zealanders exit benefit into jobs, which is great news, and I thought that member would celebrate with me.
explanation: Cites a concrete figure (83,000) but not tied to the net target asked about.

text: we’ve got 70,000 people in case management, some of those over the phone; we have introduced a traffic light system so more people know what their obligations are; 90 percent of those on the jobseeker benefit say that is helpful to them.
explanation: Concrete figures and a named scheme (case management numbers, traffic light system, 90%).

text: at that point there were close to 190,000 people on jobseeker support. Those numbers have been steadily rising since 2022, which is before we took office. The COVID-19 royal commission inquiry has found the previous Government’s increased spending drove up debt, inflation, and interest rates, which leads to higher unemployment... As of December, the quarterly figures show 223,500 people on jobseeker support
explanation: Names figures, dates, and a quarterly data point.

text: Superannuation for a married couple who both qualify will lift more than $50 to $1,708 a fortnight, an increase of over $180 since the 2023 election. A single person over 25 years old on jobseeker support will receive an additional $22 a fortnight.
explanation: Precise dollar figures and a comparison baseline (since the 2023 election).

text: ACC deducts the full main benefit paid by MSD from the back-pay, sends that money to MSD, and the injured person gets what’s left. MSD then treats the lump sum as income and moves to recover all payments it has made, not just the main benefits.
explanation: Lays out the ACC/MSD recovery mechanism step by step.

text: Our proposed solution going forward is that we can only continue to support this bill if it is changed so that MSD has clear discretion not to recover supplementary payments where that would be unfair and unequitable.
explanation: Names a concrete change (MSD discretion in hardship/fairness cases) as a condition, though without drafting detail.

text: We pushed for an amendment that would give the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) the discretion to wipe the debt if the enforcement would cause hardship, alongside writing it off for sensitive claims
explanation: Names a concrete mechanism: discretionary debt write-off on hardship and for sensitive claims.

text: what this Government fails to genuinely do is take into account the genuine and actually quite big risks that exist, for example, to our liability for not taking action on climate change, and the money that we would have to pay offshore in relationship to that.
explanation: Names the risk (offshore climate liability) but gives no figures or mechanism.

text: This bill only came through because Community Law Centres Aotearoa, alongside others, challenged this unlawful practice in the High Court. The High Court agreed with people who fought the system. The High Court actually ruled in favour of them and said, and I quote, “The recipient of the supplementary assistance needed, and was eligible for, that assistance at the time.
explanation: Names the litigant, the forum, and quotes the ruling.

text: it was introduced during urgency and, as a concession, was given a one-week select committee process—two days for members of the public to make submissions, two days to ask survivors of sexual violence to put their thoughts on paper and to contribute to this bill
explanation: Concrete process detail: urgency, one week, two days for submissions.

text: If the Minister genuinely believed that sexual violence survivors and abuse in care survivors or victims of crime should be excluded from this bill, she could have sought out-of-scope amendments through the Business Committee.
explanation: Names the precise mechanism (out-of-scope amendments via the Business Committee).

text: Introduce a bill in urgency, rush it through the select committee with a one-week period, refuse to hear members of the public, and only invite a handful of organisations—not even engage during the select committee process with ACC.
explanation: Lists concrete procedural failings: urgency, one-week committee, limited submitters, no ACC engagement.

text: I also want to acknowledge that, yes, there are more than 37,000 people who will be affected by this change, but it’s important that we make this change right now, before more people come into this group. We don’t want more and more people being impacted because the policy is not delivering what it intends to deliver.
explanation: Names the affected population but is general about what 'making this change right now' concretely entails.

text: And people should be receiving no more or no less; they should be receiving what they’re entitled to receive, and that is what this bill will do.
explanation: States a principle (entitlement parity) but no mechanism or figures for how the bill achieves it.

text: I had the privilege, last week, to sit in these hearings and listen to the hearings of eight oral submissions, we received over 855 submissions in total.
explanation: Concrete counts of oral and total submissions.

text: What this relates to is those 37,000-odd cases that this High Court judgment has made between 1998 and 2025 is captured.
explanation: Gives a case count and a date range.

text: but we could actually look in the committee of the whole House stage of actually widening that out so those who were already engaged in the review process—that would actually gain those people into that.
explanation: Identifies the savings-provision issue to widen, though without precise drafting.

text: I think the majority of the paybacks were something like under $2,000—what is a sum of money for anyone to pay back—but the rate of that payback will definitely depend on the individual person’s circumstances.
explanation: Offers a dollar threshold for the typical payback.

text: This coalition Government doesn’t just talk about it; we deliver on housing affordability.
explanation: Slogan-like assertion with no mechanism in this sentence.

text: As this House knows, we have been absolutely focused on enabling a number of fast-track Act projects throughout the country... nearly 25 of the 149 in Schedule 2 of that Act—are either Māori-partnered or -led.
explanation: Cites concrete figures (25 of 149 Schedule 2 projects) even while off the asked topic.

text: We’d seen the event in Levin where seven people, including two police officers, were injured.
explanation: Names the place and exact injury counts.

text: We have seen nearly 5,500 Māori come off the jobseeker benefit in the quarter ending September 2025. We continue with a serious housing programme alongside, with, and for Māori, particularly in places like Hopuhopu, alongside Waikato-Tainui and their $35 million we committed to... the hundred homes that are being built up in Kaikohekohe right now by Te Hau Ora o Ngāpuhi
explanation: Names figures, locations, partners, and dollar amounts.

text: And it will increase the fine for excessive noise from vehicles through speakers and sirens from an infringement fee of $50—rima tekau tāra—to $300. The maximum court fine will increase from $1,000 to $3,000—more than the price of a Crusaders and Chiefs game.
explanation: Exact before/after figures for both the infringement fee and the maximum court fine.

text: if someone fails to provide that information without good reason, then the outcome could be that that vehicle is impounded for a 28-day period.
explanation: States the precise consequence and duration (28-day impoundment) of the new disclosure duty.

text: I reject that member’s assertions, but, again, I return to the fact that the science system will need to be productive, efficient, financially sustainable, and generate real value for New Zealanders.
explanation: Asked where the next round of job losses will come from; gives no answer and retreats to repeated talking points.

text: I do acknowledge those concerns and have also demonstrated the actions that we’re taking to address them.
explanation: Asked how he can claim a bright future given doubled unemployment and child poverty; gives a generic acknowledgement without engaging the figures.

text: There’s an inverse relationship between hardship and warm, dry homes. I’m very proud of the Our Whare Our Fale initiative, which, in Porirua, will deliver 300 homes, of which more than a dozen I’ve already enabled.
explanation: Asked about ~10,000 more children in hardship; pivots to a housing initiative without addressing the hardship figure.

text: The traditional five-yearly survey model is no longer financially sustainable, operationally reliable, or able to produce timely, high-quality data... I do acknowledge the concerns raised by Te Kāhui Raraunga; this Government takes these concerns seriously... Stats New Zealand is committed to working with iwi Māori, including Te Kāhui Raraunga, on the design, planning, and implementation of the new census approach.
explanation: Engages the bias concern directly while defending the change.

text: We’ve already made those statements. That will not happen in this term of Government.
explanation: Gives a clear, unhedged commitment that the Ministry for Pacific Peoples will not be abolished this term.

text: I'd just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.
explanation: Directly refuses to engage a clear question about whether a 10% rise signals stabilisation.

text: I’m well aware of the plans of Channel Infrastructure to expand diesel infrastructure and storage. Again, we are in constant dialogue with them on that.
explanation: Asked if he is aware his Government cancelled the reserve in 2024; deflects to Channel Infrastructure's plans without confirming or denying.

text: Because, unlike what we observed under a previous Government, we have learnt the lessons of COVID mismanagement. We are making sure that we are doing it appropriately and with industry on board, and we will deliver that, as I said, on Friday, as we foreshadowed last week.
explanation: Asked why basic questions about a two-year-old framework can't be answered; deflects with a COVID jab and another deferral.

text: It had a Lake Onslow project at $17 billion—$8,000 for every single household in the country—that led to an $800 megawatt per hour price in wholesale electricity prices. What we are doing, as I've previously explained, is we're dealing with the dry-year risk, lowering the risk premium, and therefore wanting to lower power bills by $50 for every household.
explanation: Eventually describes his own plan but only after deflecting the asked question onto the opponent.

text: No, because we believe in farmers in this country and they need utes, and, actually, they shouldn't be subsidising people who want to buy EVs. As you've seen in the last week, EV sales have been just fine.
explanation: Answers the 'do you regret it' question with a clear No and a rationale.

text: No, I’m encouraged by the last Stats NZ report that actually showed there was more scientists than we had previously and also new opportunities for science through the new emerging technologies: the Institute for Advanced Technology, through artificial intelligence, through quantum, through magnetic materials, through Robinson, and the $42 million by Biodiscovery Platform.
explanation: Claims a Stats NZ report shows more scientists than before; plausible but not verifiable from the text and used selectively against a job-cuts question.

text: In answer to the first arm of the question, yes. In answer to the second, I would note that in the enumerated 2023 Census, administrative data significantly improved the under-count in Māori descent.
explanation: Claim that admin data improved Māori under-count in 2023 is plausible but cited without figures.

text: we’ve taken strong steps to restore law and order, with 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime; ram raids are down 85 percent; and repeat youth offending is down 22 percent... lifting childhood immunisations to 82.6 percent... We are seeing progress in education, with phonics proficiency lifting from 36 percent to 58 percent.
explanation: Figures are presented favourably and some (e.g. ram raids down 85%) depend heavily on baseline choice; broad cross-portfolio claims hard to verify as stated.

text: the just transition and supporting New Zealanders to transition to a climate resilient, sustainable, and low-emissions economy seems more relevant than ever, in a time where we're seeing fuel prices really spiral out of control and out of the cost and affordability for a lot of New Zealanders.
explanation: 'Spiral out of control' is hyperbolic; fuel price pressure is real but the framing overstates it.

text: When he cut Callaghan Innovation, ransacked the Marsden Fund, and is now cutting 134 jobs from the new science institute, where can New Zealanders expect the next round of job losses to come from?
explanation: The factual scaffolding (cuts to Callaghan, Marsden changes, 134 jobs) is broadly grounded, but 'ransacked' is hyperbolic and overstated.

text: You only have to go back to question time today to see the staggering statistics around unemployment and how negatively it's impacting our Māori and Pasifika communities, but let's not look at that in any of our Budgets going forward.
explanation: Plausible claim of disproportionate unemployment impact on Māori and Pasifika, consistent with NZ data, but unspecified and 'staggering' is loaded.

text: this very bill—removes one of the key institutional reforms that was designed to and was successfully keeping pressure on the sector. The Grocery Commissioner was created because the supermarket duopoly was failing consumers, suppliers, and competitors.
explanation: Accurate that the Grocery Commissioner was created in response to the supermarket duopoly; the 'successfully keeping pressure' claim is more contestable.

text: Pam from Aranui, who’s run a campaign to bring the bus back to Aranui. She’s taken her plea to the regional council this week, and the regional council have committed to bringing a bus back to Aranui.
explanation: A checkable, specific local claim presented plausibly.

text: It was a critical piece of national infrastructure and that was a decision of a previous Government.
explanation: Attributes the Marsden Point refinery closure to the previous Government; Hipkins (and the record) hold it was a private commercial decision by Channel Infrastructure, so this is misleading.

text: It isn’t spending $66 billion and half of it we don’t know what we’re getting for it.
explanation: The $66bn COVID figure surfaces elsewhere in the debate, but 'half of it we don't know what we're getting' is rhetorical and misleading.

text: New Zealanders returning back to New Zealand was up 12 percent on the previous year. For the last four months, I'm very pleased to say that New Zealanders leaving is less than in any month in the period that he was Prime Minister.
explanation: Specific but selectively framed (returns vs departures) and unverifiable here.

text: It's a good reminder of why this Government has taken on board the mistakes of the COVID management plan, which led to a 32-year high in inflation and a tripling of our debt.
explanation: Inflation peaked ~7.3% in 2022 (a ~32-year high) and Crown debt rose sharply over COVID — directionally accurate, though 'tripling' and sole attribution to a 'management plan' are partisan framing.

text: It was in 2022 that the New Zealand Government again reset our engagement with Iran, after Mahsa Amini died at the hands of the regime's police. She was fatally beaten for failing to wear her hijab in accordance with Government regulations.
explanation: Mahsa Amini's 2022 death in custody and the resulting protests are well documented; cause-of-death details are contested but the account is broadly accurate.

text: Does he think New Zealanders are comfortable with the 12 to 14 percent of our children—roughly the population of Tauranga—living in poverty?
explanation: The 12–14% child-poverty range and the Tauranga-population comparison are broadly accurate framings.

text: he has had to correct himself at least twice because he doesn't even know what his own ministries are doing to provide some practical support to the very people who are living under stress and fear right now.
explanation: Claim that the PM corrected himself twice is plausible but not verifiable from the text.

text: ACC deducts the full main benefit paid by MSD from the back-pay, sends that money to MSD, and the injured person gets what’s left. MSD then treats the lump sum as income and moves to recover all payments it has made, not just the main benefits.
explanation: A detailed description of the inter-agency arrangement; plausible and committee-sourced but a contested characterisation.

text: These people—they're not criminals; they're Kiwis who are forced on to welfare because ACC are taking so long in terms of processing their claims.
explanation: Consistent with the cross-bench evidence that claimants were on welfare lawfully while awaiting ACC.

text: Does the Minister accept that his track record in terms of cutting Māori and targeted funding in areas like Māori housing, Māori broadcasting, and Māori trade training has resulted in a record 10-year high of Māori unemployment, and if not, why not?
explanation: Embedded claim of a 10-year high in Māori unemployment plus funding cuts; specific but the causal link is asserted.

text: We can have GDP go up, and sometimes even GDP per capita goes up, at the same time as the country is experiencing growing household debt, increased material hardship for children, and longer delays for people to access things like basic healthcare.
explanation: Accurate in principle that GDP growth can coexist with rising hardship; the specific NZ conditions cited are plausible but not quantified.

text: Almost 40,000 people have been unlawfully burdened with debts as a result of a practice that has carried on by both National and Labour Governments through decades.
explanation: Figure and 'unlawful' characterisation align with the High Court finding; rounds up to 40,000.

text: Introduce a bill in urgency, rush it through the select committee with a one-week period, refuse to hear members of the public, and only invite a handful of organisations—not even engage during the select committee process with ACC.
explanation: Consistent with other members' accounts of the truncated process.

text: Does she agree with economist Brad Olsen that “we know that the number of jobs being advertised in the economy are still 25 percent lower than pre-pandemic”, and if so, how does she expect more beneficiaries to fill fewer jobs?
explanation: Cites a named economist and a specific figure (25 percent lower job ads).

text: This bill only came through because Community Law Centres Aotearoa, alongside others, challenged this unlawful practice in the High Court. The High Court agreed with people who fought the system. The High Court actually ruled in favour of them and said, and I quote, “The recipient of the supplementary assistance needed, and was eligible for, that assistance at the time.
explanation: Cites a specific High Court ruling and quotes from it to support the claim the practice was unlawful.

text: I see that there were more than 800 submissions. So we can’t say that, because of the select committee, it didn’t receive submissions—for submissions, that number looks quite reasonable to me, and I would say that that is reflective of what people would have otherwise said.
explanation: The 800+ submissions figure is consistent with other members' counts.

text: I also want to acknowledge that, yes, there are more than 37,000 people who will be affected by this change, but it’s important that we make this change right now, before more people come into this group. We don’t want more and more people being impacted because the policy is not delivering what it intends to deliver.
explanation: The 37,000-affected figure aligns with other speakers' numbers.

text: I had the privilege, last week, to sit in these hearings and listen to the hearings of eight oral submissions, we received over 855 submissions in total.
explanation: Specific first-hand figures (eight oral submissions, 855 total) consistent with other members' accounts.

text: What this relates to is those 37,000-odd cases that this High Court judgment has made between 1998 and 2025 is captured.
explanation: Cites the ~37,000 cases and a 1998–2025 window; broadly consistent with the debate's figures.

text: I think the majority of the paybacks were something like under $2,000—what is a sum of money for anyone to pay back—but the rate of that payback will definitely depend on the individual person’s circumstances.
explanation: Attributes a 'majority under $2,000' figure to MSD evidence; specific but hedged ('something like') and unverified here.

text: Yes, whether it’s Minister Brown leading improved Māori two-year-old immunisation rates, from the terrible 64 percent it was in October 2023 to 68 percent now... or Minister Goldsmith cracking on with law and order policies that have reduced the 12-month levels of Māori victims of crime from 43,733 to 4,650. We don’t speak from the podium of truth but from the crucible of outcomes.
explanation: Some figures plausible (immunisation 64%→68%), but the crime drop from 43,733 to 4,650 is an implausibly large fall that looks like a misstatement or misleading comparison.

text: rent-to-income ratios were 27.9 percent in quarter four 2025, according to Cotality, a reduction from 28.2 percent in quarter four 2023... under the previous Government, the measure grew from 26.1 percent to 28.2 percent in 2023... the house-price-to-income ratio was 7.2, down from above 10 in 2021. This Government doesn’t just talk about it; we deliver on housing affordability.
explanation: Cites real measures, but a 0.3-point move described as delivery while he also calls it 'relatively flat' — selective framing.

text: Yes, I stand by the Government’s track record on Māori employment, particularly given that between 5,000 and 6,000 Māori came off the jobseeker benefit and into work in the quarter ending September 2025—a fantastic result, in my view.
explanation: Repeats the corrected into-work figure; plausible but a single quarter cited selectively as the headline result.

text: Cotality says that in quarter four 2025, the house price to income ratio was 7.2, down from above 10 in 2021.
explanation: Attributes a specific figure to a named source (Cotality); checkable.

text: We’d seen the event in Levin where seven people, including two police officers, were injured.
explanation: A specific, checkable incident claim (Levin; seven injured, two officers).

text: but Judith Collins indicated that when that law was brought in, there would be more than 10 vehicles a year that would actually be crushed. Now, when we look at the reality around how many were actually crushed, you only need one hand, excluding the thumb, and you’d have one spare finger, to come up with the number of vehicles that actually went through this process.
explanation: The claim that very few vehicles were ever crushed under the earlier crusher law is broadly consistent with the historical record.

text: whether it's in barracking or in speeches they deliver in this House, not much of it is worth listening to, I can assure you of that.
explanation: A blanket dismissive put-down of opponents' speeches as worthless, rather than engaging substance.

text: the other side of the House are worried about putting Robbie Williams into a stadium. That’s all you’ve got: Robbie Williams into a stadium.
explanation: Mocking, sensationalised caricature of opponents' priorities rather than substantive critique.

text: When he cut Callaghan Innovation, ransacked the Marsden Fund, and is now cutting 134 jobs from the new science institute, where can New Zealanders expect the next round of job losses to come from?
explanation: Loaded question; 'ransacked' is sensationalising rather than engaging the substance, though aimed at policy not character.

text: As other members have pointed out there were a large number of media releases and there was a large number of budgets available to be read. It's all in the skill applied to the reading of the Budget that enables the reader to get a good understanding of exactly what that Budget is committing to.
explanation: Pointed dig at opponents' competence, though framed around the substance of reading budgets.

text: the just transition and supporting New Zealanders to transition to a climate resilient, sustainable, and low-emissions economy seems more relevant than ever, in a time where we're seeing fuel prices really spiral out of control and out of the cost and affordability for a lot of New Zealanders.
explanation: Hyperbolic phrasing but directed at policy/economic conditions, not persons.

text: I'd just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.
explanation: Dismissive, calls the question a 'waste of time' and attacks the questioner's record.

text: Well, it meant that New Zealand is the only country I know of that's making the rather unique transition from domestic gas to international coal, and, in the process, worsening emissions. But that is a function of a failed Labour-Greens energy policy.
explanation: 'Failed Labour-Greens energy policy' — policy criticism with a partisan edge.

text: No. As we’ve said from the very beginning, we want councils focused on what they can do. We don’t think light shows on public toilet blocks here in Wellington is a good use of public money. We don’t think putting bike lanes up Molesworth Street is actually a very good use of money; it would be better in three waters assets.
explanation: Mocking examples ('light shows on public toilet blocks') but aimed at spending decisions, not a person.

text: It's a good reminder of why this Government has taken on board the mistakes of the COVID management plan, which led to a 32-year high in inflation and a tripling of our debt.
explanation: Criticism of the previous government's policy rather than personal attack.

text: I want to acknowledge that there are different views on the legitimacy of the actions taken by the US and Israel. I respect those views and the vigour with which they have been offered.
explanation: Respectful recognition of disagreement, no personal attack.

text: he has had to correct himself at least twice because he doesn't even know what his own ministries are doing to provide some practical support to the very people who are living under stress and fear right now.
explanation: Criticism edges into the personal ('doesn't even know') rather than focusing purely on the policy gap.

text: Does he think it's fair that home support workers who provide an essential public service, yet had their pay equity claim cancelled by his Government, are struggling to pay their bills because Government won't fully reimburse their fuel costs?
explanation: Hard-edged accusation of unfairness but anchored to a policy decision.

text: What does he say to the woman I spoke with in Manurewa over the weekend who cannot afford to take her partner to the hospital for his lifesaving medical treatments because of rising fuel prices?
explanation: Pointed but raises a constituent's hardship rather than attacking the PM personally.

text: Does he think New Zealanders are comfortable with the 12 to 14 percent of our children—roughly the population of Tauranga—living in poverty?
explanation: Pointed but policy-focused; challenges on substance (child poverty) without personal attack.

text: I'm just sitting in here listening to insults and snaps and barbs being traded and personal insults being made; it always leaves out the actual human people's realities who are at the centre of the violence of an illegal war, and those real lives and the harm on them is quickly forgotten in a tit-for-tat political debate. I abhor that.
explanation: Explicitly deplores personal insults and refocuses on substance and human impact.

text: I respect and thank the members of the select committee, who worked diligently to ensure that we were able to improve the bill.
explanation: Respectful, cross-party acknowledgement of the committee's work.

text: So I suggest that member look in the mirror.
explanation: Dismissive personal retort rather than engaging the substance.

text: Well, as we know, the unemployment rate is where Treasury forecast it would be, and, as I accept, it is higher than anyone would like. For any individual who finds themselves without a job, it’s incredibly difficult for them and their family.
explanation: Empathetic, respectful framing toward affected individuals.

text: It's sorry to hear that members opposite don't believe this group of New Zealanders should have an increase.
explanation: Strawmans the opposition as opposing the increase based on an interjection.

text: National and this coalition Government simply want to stick and to bash those who can't fight back.
explanation: Imputes cruel motive ('bash those who can't fight back') rather than engaging the policy argument.

text: It's unacceptable to drop debt on to our sickest and our most disabled Kiwis all because ACC can't process claims fast enough
explanation: Harsh language but directed at the policy and its consequences, not a personal attack.

text: Does the Minister accept that his track record in terms of cutting Māori and targeted funding in areas like Māori housing, Māori broadcasting, and Māori trade training has resulted in a record 10-year high of Māori unemployment, and if not, why not?
explanation: Sharp accountability question aimed at the record, not the person.

text: The Minister hasn’t even addressed the question. The question was specific: does he expect the Māori unemployment rate to increase even further, given the announcement of the proposed closure of food-processing plants, including the announced closure of McCain’s in Hastings? He hasn’t addressed it even slightly.
explanation: A procedural complaint about non-answering; pointed but focused on the conduct, not a personal insult.

text: I will say there’s been some goodwill from the Minister and also goodwill in terms of the committee that worked, I think, well on this over the last week, even though we all have different philosophical positions.
explanation: Generous, respectful framing of opponents despite disagreement.

text: all I see is people who are completely out of touch, who are completely out of their depth, and who are refusing to engage with the substance of the bill.
explanation: Personal attack on competence ('out of their depth').

text: For the Minister to claim that this is some great concession is a joke, when she knows—and legal experts and survivors have told her—that this bill leaves tens of thousands of people with debts that diminish their ability to make ends meet
explanation: 'Is a joke' belittles the Minister and asserts she knowingly acts against the evidence.

text: History tells me that this is not a Minister that has previously engaged constructively in these debates.
explanation: A personalised criticism of the Minister's conduct rather than engagement with her arguments.

text: it was introduced during urgency and, as a concession, was given a one-week select committee process—two days for members of the public to make submissions, two days to ask survivors of sexual violence to put their thoughts on paper and to contribute to this bill
explanation: Sharp process critique that is largely factual rather than a personal attack.

text: Is $12 extra enough to meet the additional costs of fuel and other living expenses, or does she expect people living in poverty to get further into debt simply to survive?
explanation: Pointed and loaded, but targets the policy's adequacy rather than the Minister personally.

text: I want to start by conveying my gratitude to the Social Services and Community Committee because, I must say, they have worked really hard with the time constraint that they had. I also want to acknowledge the clerk of the committee, because I know they do a lot of work in the background.
explanation: Respectful, gracious acknowledgement of the committee and staff.

text: The member thinks that it's OK if the policy doesn't deliver on its intent.
explanation: Misrepresents the opponent's position rather than engaging it.

text: No, on this side, we are not that irresponsible. We are responsible members of Parliament here.
explanation: Implies the other side is irresponsible; mild partisan jab.

text: I also thank the committee chair and the rest of the Justice Committee for their swiftness, their pace, as they reported back two months earlier than scheduled.
explanation: Cross-party thanks to the committee, focused on their work.

text: I agree with Waikato-Tainui leader Tuku Morgan, who was effusive in his praise for this Government continuing the serious support of Te Matatini... I know many of the Opposition members have never been there; you might get there one day
explanation: Mild jab at opponents ('you might get there one day') amid otherwise substantive content.

text: Yes, my ministry is involved and responsible for advocating for the increased employment of Māori, but it wasn’t too long ago under a Labour Government that the number of Māori unemployed was around 25 percent.
explanation: Concedes responsibility then pivots to a comparative jab at the previous government.

text: Rent controls don’t work. The Greens’ housing plan, in general, would make the housing market in New Zealand much worse.
explanation: Attacks the opposing party's plan but as policy, not personally.

text: That comes from a very dark and dank place, that comment—very dingy. What we’re all about is making sure we’ve got the basics sorted, infrastructure in place, better energy prices... and all the necessary steps and phases to ensure that, actually, housing is affordable.
explanation: Characterises the questioner's comment as coming from a 'dark and dank place' rather than rebutting substance.

text: at that point there were close to 190,000 people on jobseeker support. Those numbers have been steadily rising since 2022, which is before we took office. The COVID-19 royal commission inquiry has found the previous Government’s increased spending drove up debt, inflation, and interest rates, which leads to higher unemployment... As of December, the quarterly figures show 223,500 people on jobseeker support
explanation: Largely explains rising numbers rather than demonstrating delivery on reducing them.

text: We've also introduced phone-based case management, supporting 10,000 more people in case management at any time. We've also improved the way MSD works with businesses to provide opportunities for job seekers to gain employment.
explanation: Describes a concrete delivered programme expansion.

text: When you think about more than 50 percent of the Government’s spending during the years of COVID-19, having nothing to do with COVID-19... I am really proud that despite those challenges, 83,000 New Zealanders left welfare for a job, in the last year. That’s something worth celebrating.
explanation: Claims a concrete outcome (83,000 off welfare into work) but total jobseeker numbers rose over the same period.

text: Currently, the savings provision in this bill only captures individuals who have lodged an appeal with the Social Security Appeal Authority or courts prior to the date of introduction. I am now proposing to also capture individuals who have made an application to MSD for a review of decision to the benefits review committee that has not been decided before the date of introduction.
explanation: A concrete amendment actually proposed through the select committee process, but follow-through (passage) is still in progress.

text: From 1 April, the Ministry of Social Development's annual adjustments will increase financial support for more than 1.5 million New Zealanders. This includes working age beneficiaries, superannuitants, and students, as well as non-beneficiaries receiving supplementary assistance.
explanation: Describes an adjustment taking effect on a set date — delivery in train, though it is the routine annual indexation.

text: Our proposed solution going forward is that we can only continue to support this bill if it is changed so that MSD has clear discretion not to recover supplementary payments where that would be unfair and unequitable.
explanation: A conditional commitment tabled in committee; delivery depends on whether the amendment is adopted.

text: We pushed for an amendment that would give the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) the discretion to wipe the debt if the enforcement would cause hardship, alongside writing it off for sensitive claims
explanation: Describes a genuine attempt to amend the bill, but the amendment was rejected — intent without delivery.

text: The Government has announced proposals to develop new legislation to establish a light-touch regulatory regime to address issues with property managers... The proposed regime will introduce minimal standards for conduct and competence, provide effective complaints and disciplinary processes, and support better dispute resolution but not be over the top.
explanation: An announced proposal/intent to introduce a bill, not yet legislated or delivered.

text: Yes, I stand by the Government’s track record on Māori employment, particularly given that between 5,000 and 6,000 Māori came off the jobseeker benefit and into work in the quarter ending September 2025—a fantastic result, in my view.
explanation: Claims credit for an employment outcome, but attributes a labour-market quarter to government track record without mechanism.

text: Yes, whether it’s Minister Brown leading improved Māori two-year-old immunisation rates, from the terrible 64 percent it was in October 2023 to 68 percent now... or Minister Goldsmith cracking on with law and order policies that have reduced the 12-month levels of Māori victims of crime from 43,733 to 4,650. We don’t speak from the podium of truth but from the crucible of outcomes.
explanation: Claims a range of delivered outcomes across portfolios, though attribution to his own ministry is thin.

text: rent-to-income ratios were 27.9 percent in quarter four 2025, according to Cotality, a reduction from 28.2 percent in quarter four 2023... under the previous Government, the measure grew from 26.1 percent to 28.2 percent in 2023... the house-price-to-income ratio was 7.2, down from above 10 in 2021. This Government doesn’t just talk about it; we deliver on housing affordability.
explanation: Claims credit for housing affordability gains, though the rent change cited is marginal.

text: We have seen nearly 5,500 Māori come off the jobseeker benefit in the quarter ending September 2025. We continue with a serious housing programme alongside, with, and for Māori, particularly in places like Hopuhopu, alongside Waikato-Tainui and their $35 million we committed to... the hundred homes that are being built up in Kaikohekohe right now by Te Hau Ora o Ngāpuhi
explanation: Points to concrete housing commitments and a benefit-exit figure as delivery.

text: I respect and thank the members of the select committee, who worked diligently to ensure that we were able to improve the bill.
explanation: Gracious tone that credits others, mildly bridge-building.

text: the policy that the member refers to is about lowering energy prices, but let me say this: our Government fully accepts that there are too many New Zealanders today who are finding it challenging... We will not resile from our single focus on the cost of living and growing the economy.
explanation: Acknowledges hardship empathetically but ultimately restates the party line.

text: So Labour’s prepared to work with National on this, but it has to be with the wellbeing of people at the centre.
explanation: Explicit cross-party offer to cooperate while stating a condition; consensus-seeking.

text: I will say there’s been some goodwill from the Minister and also goodwill in terms of the committee that worked, I think, well on this over the last week, even though we all have different philosophical positions.
explanation: Acknowledges goodwill from opponents and shared work across philosophical divides; consensus-building.

text: National and this coalition Government simply want to stick and to bash those who can't fight back.
explanation: Pure us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side rather than persuading opponents.

text: National stands for a welfare system that punches down and makes people too fearful to ask for help in the first place; our Labour Party does not.
explanation: Divisive contrast drawn purely along party lines.

text: Labour agrees, though, that the closing of a double-dipping loophole in welfare is important, because we, like everyone, know that Kiwis must feel confident in our welfare system
explanation: Acknowledges the public concern behind the bill, seeking some common ground before disagreeing.

text: I urge my Labour colleagues to stop supporting this bill, and to stand on the right side of history and vote it down at this second reading.
explanation: A rallying appeal to allies framed in moralising 'right side of history' terms; persuasive to one's own side rather than bridge-building.

text: all I see is people who are completely out of touch, who are completely out of their depth, and who are refusing to engage with the substance of the bill.
explanation: Combative dismissal that alienates rather than persuades.

text: This Government may be making it legal, but it does not make it right.
explanation: Rhetorically effective but framed against the Government.

text: it is not too late for members and parties in the Government who know that the current bill, as it is, is unfair and it harms people who need our support.
explanation: Direct appeal to Government members to cross the floor — an attempt to persuade the other side.

text: I will be the first one to admit that some of these wellbeing objectives could have been implemented and reflected better in Government policies
explanation: Acknowledging a valid criticism softens partisanship and builds credibility.

text: I want to start by conveying my gratitude to the Social Services and Community Committee because, I must say, they have worked really hard with the time constraint that they had. I also want to acknowledge the clerk of the committee, because I know they do a lot of work in the background.
explanation: Warm, inclusive opening that credits others' work.

text: No, on this side, we are not that irresponsible. We are responsible members of Parliament here.
explanation: Self-congratulatory contrast that appeals only to her own side.

text: but we could actually look in the committee of the whole House stage of actually widening that out so those who were already engaged in the review process—that would actually gain those people into that.
explanation: Signals openness to amend the bill to address submitters' concerns at the next stage; constructive.

text: I want to be clear that this bill does not target legitimate car enthusiasts and legal car meets, like that big—
explanation: Reassures a group worried about the bill, addressing civil-liberties concerns rather than dismissing them.

text: Yes, whether it’s Minister Brown leading improved Māori two-year-old immunisation rates, from the terrible 64 percent it was in October 2023 to 68 percent now... or Minister Goldsmith cracking on with law and order policies that have reduced the 12-month levels of Māori victims of crime from 43,733 to 4,650. We don’t speak from the podium of truth but from the crucible of outcomes.
explanation: Rhetorically polished ('crucible of outcomes') but rallies his own side.

text: that’s the challenge that the member opposite has on a range of matters: he thinks that the Government is the solution to everything. On this side of the House, we don’t. We think that it is to enable interest rates and inflation rates to come down, to stop the wasteful spending that was curated under previous Governments, and to ensure that the business and enterprise regulatory framework is available to create jobs and not just handouts.
explanation: Us-vs-them 'this side of the House' framing rallies his side rather than building consensus.

text: Rent controls don’t work. The Greens’ housing plan, in general, would make the housing market in New Zealand much worse.
explanation: Dismissive of the Greens rather than seeking common ground.

text: We don’t want MSD sending—and this is how bad it could get—in debt collectors to hound that woman and to hound that whānau who are just in struggle street—just in struggle street. So we need to be supportive of that whānau. We need to show some humanity here.
explanation: Persuades chiefly through an emotive worst-case anecdote ('hound that woman') rather than data.

text: ACC deducts the full main benefit paid by MSD from the back-pay, sends that money to MSD, and the injured person gets what’s left. MSD then treats the lump sum as income and moves to recover all payments it has made, not just the main benefits.
explanation: Builds a clear causal chain to its conclusion that injured people pay for their own rehab.

text: It's unacceptable to drop debt on to our sickest and our most disabled Kiwis all because ACC can't process claims fast enough
explanation: Identifies a causal chain (ACC delays → welfare → debt) but leans on emotive framing.

text: These people—they're not criminals; they're Kiwis who are forced on to welfare because ACC are taking so long in terms of processing their claims.
explanation: Counters the 'double-dipping' framing by pointing to ACC processing delays as the real cause.

text: This is such a perfect example of the Government not wanting the public to know that they have been trampling over tens of thousands of people who are living, often, in deep poverty, waiting for their ACC claims to come through, and who have been unlawfully put in debt for decades.
explanation: Asserts hidden intent rather than evidencing it, though the underlying 'unlawful debt' claim is grounded later.

text: what this Government fails to genuinely do is take into account the genuine and actually quite big risks that exist, for example, to our liability for not taking action on climate change, and the money that we would have to pay offshore in relationship to that.
explanation: Identifies a real fiscal-risk category (offshore climate liabilities) the reporting omits; reasonable though the magnitude is asserted not quantified.

text: We can have GDP go up, and sometimes even GDP per capita goes up, at the same time as the country is experiencing growing household debt, increased material hardship for children, and longer delays for people to access things like basic healthcare.
explanation: Sound critique that aggregate GDP can mask distributional and wellbeing decline; logically valid.

text: This Government may be making it legal, but it does not make it right.
explanation: Cleanly distinguishes legality from morality, the core of his argument.

text: This bill only came through because Community Law Centres Aotearoa, alongside others, challenged this unlawful practice in the High Court. The High Court agreed with people who fought the system. The High Court actually ruled in favour of them and said, and I quote, “The recipient of the supplementary assistance needed, and was eligible for, that assistance at the time.
explanation: Grounds the argument in a court finding rather than assertion; evidence-based.

text: I see that there were more than 800 submissions. So we can’t say that, because of the select committee, it didn’t receive submissions—for submissions, that number looks quite reasonable to me, and I would say that that is reflective of what people would have otherwise said.
explanation: Counters the rushed-process objection, but 'reflective of what people would have otherwise said' is an unsupported assumption that more time would not have changed input.

text: I also want to acknowledge that, yes, there are more than 37,000 people who will be affected by this change, but it’s important that we make this change right now, before more people come into this group. We don’t want more and more people being impacted because the policy is not delivering what it intends to deliver.
explanation: Reasonable urgency argument, but asserts the policy 'is not delivering its intent' without supporting detail.

text: And people should be receiving no more or no less; they should be receiving what they’re entitled to receive, and that is what this bill will do.
explanation: A fairness-to-entitlement framing that assumes, rather than demonstrates, the bill produces that outcome.

text: Yes, it's a very important issue. We have to, otherwise we will not be doing justice to those who are going to be affected, because, as days go by, there will be more and more people—those who will be affected.
explanation: Argues urgency serves the affected, but the reasoning is thin and somewhat circular.

text: The member thinks that it's OK if the policy doesn't deliver on its intent.
explanation: Strawman: recasts Menéndez March's call to exclude vulnerable groups as indifference to policy delivery.

text: but Judith Collins indicated that when that law was brought in, there would be more than 10 vehicles a year that would actually be crushed. Now, when we look at the reality around how many were actually crushed, you only need one hand, excluding the thumb, and you’d have one spare finger, to come up with the number of vehicles that actually went through this process.
explanation: Tests a prior prediction against the actual outcome (10+/year predicted vs roughly four delivered) to argue this bill may be similarly unworkable.

text: the real risk is that the community will think that there is going to be this mass level of crushing going on and the forfeiture of vehicles, but it’s going to be very easy for people to plead hardship and get out of it.
explanation: Predicts hardship exemptions will blunt the forfeiture regime in practice; plausible given the cited record of the earlier crusher law, but the bill's outcome is unverified.

text: there would be more than 10 vehicles a year that would actually be crushed
explanation: A past prediction (quoted by Utikere) about the earlier crusher law that, per the account, was not borne out — far fewer vehicles were crushed.

text: On the definition that Shane Jones is now creating, the McCain Foods factory, the Wattie's factory, the Kinleith factory, the Winstone factory have all been closed— —by this Government.
explanation: Knowingly applies the same misleading 'closed by this Government' standard it is criticising.

text: Does he regret cutting the clean car discount, given estimates suggest that had New Zealanders continued to buy electric vehicles at the rate they were under the discount, there'd be 50,000 more electric vehicles on the road today than there are now under his Government?
explanation: The 50,000-EV figure is presented as an estimate, plausible but contestable.

text: The Labour Government did not approve the winding down of Marsden Point; it was a private business.
explanation: Accurate that the refinery's conversion was a commercial decision by a private company.

text: The Prime Minister has now asserted that the previous Government made that decision; it was a private business.
explanation: Corrects the record that Marsden Point's closure was a private commercial decision, not a Government one; consistent with the known history of Channel Infrastructure's conversion.

text: I'll quote directly from paragraph 495 of the royal commission's report: “We consider the failure to ensure that this specific advice reached Ministers and the public was significant.”
explanation: Presents a verbatim quotation of the commission's finding; accurate insofar as the text is quoted faithfully.

text: In the last day, we've heard the Pentagon telling Congress there was no sign that Iran was going to attack the US first, and no evidence to support the claim that the US attacked Iran in defence. We've heard the Senate Intelligence Committee vice chair say he had seen no intelligence that Iran was on the verge of launching any kind of pre-emptive strike against the United States of America.
explanation: Reports attributed testimony; accuracy depends on those sources, which cannot be confirmed here.

text: In October 2025, there was a paper produced that, essentially, looked at how well the administrative data does against the census data. It was a bit of an experimental test to see how well it compares, and the results were not too bad. However, they did point to second-layer data as being a potential issue. When people respond to the higher-level categories, that was fairly accurate, but those second-level categories are quite difficult to get right.
explanation: Describes the cited paper's findings in measured terms ('not too bad', second-layer data an issue) consistent with how such evaluations report.

text: it can result in an overhung Parliament, as it did in 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and, of course, this one as well.
explanation: NZ did have overhang Parliaments in those listed years; the historical claim is broadly accurate.

text: while the Edward VII and then King George VI were both born in November and December, respectively, their birthdays were celebrated in the middle of the year to allow for that.
explanation: Edward VII (Nov) and George VI (Dec) birth months are accurate, and the official mid-year birthday tradition is broadly attributed to weather, though the precise origin is contestable.

text: The Prime Minister himself said yesterday that this was a decision made without discussion nor debate. It was also made without briefings to the Opposition, and it appears to have been made without advice about international law nor overreaching security and cost considerations.
explanation: Mixes a sourced claim (PM's own statement) with hedged inferences ('it appears') about missing advice; partly verifiable, partly speculative.

text: the Opposition have opposed every single savings measure that the Government has put forward.
explanation: Sweeping ‘every single’ absolute is the kind of universal claim that is almost certainly overstated.

text: No, but 15,000 more people in work compared to three months ago does.
explanation: Cites a 15,000 quarterly jobs gain against a 32,000 two-year fall the question raised—true but selectively timed.

text: the operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses (OBEGALx) deficit was $1.9 billion lower at the end of January than was previously forecast.
explanation: Specific fiscal claim consistent with a Crown accounts release; directionally checkable but not independently confirmable here.

text: annual CPI inflation is almost never negative, which is to say that, overall, prices don't reduce across the economy on average... Inflation did turn mildly negative in 1999 when the Asian financial crisis reduced the price of imports. Before that, you have to go back to 1946 to find another example of negative inflation.
explanation: Consistent with NZ inflation history; deflation is indeed rare, with a late-1990s episode.

text: Fuel excise in New Zealand is a fixed number of cents per litre, not a percentage of the price, so when fuel prices rise, the Government does not receive additional revenue from that source.
explanation: Accurate: NZ fuel excise duty is a fixed per-litre charge, so it does not rise with pump prices.

text: There’s a reason why Florida is not covered by reinsurance but New Zealand continues to be, despite us being the second-highest amount of spending for natural disaster risks throughout the world.
explanation: The reinsurance contrast and 'second-highest' ranking are striking claims presented without sourcing and likely simplified.

text: We know that the cost of living is up, and we know that the economy has shrunk—it’s actually smaller than what it was two years ago when the Government took office.
explanation: Cost-of-living rises are well established; the claim the economy is smaller than two years prior depends on the measure and is somewhat overstated.

text: I was actually quoting from a transcript of the Hon Nicola Willis' press conference on 27 August 2025, where she said, "The purpose of this briefing is to update you on the Government's next steps to increase grocery competition and reduce food prices for Kiwis."
explanation: Presents a dated, verbatim quote to correct the record; accuracy depends on the transcript but is precise and checkable.

text: We set up the national resilience plan, which then the National Party scrapped as one of their first decisions coming into Government in 2023.
explanation: Plausible account of the plan being established and later cancelled; consistent with the policy record though stated one-sidedly.

text: We had KiwiSaver set up by a Labour Government and the New Zealand Super Fund set up by a Labour Government.
explanation: Both were established under Labour-led governments; accurate.

text: the latest figure is that there are 136,000 victims of crime, a reduction of 49,000. That's 49,000 families that don't have to go through the pain and suffering of dealing with the victims of violent crime and being the victims and being the families of those victims. That is great progress.
explanation: Figures plausible but the loose 'victims of crime' phrasing risks slight overstatement.

text: What we grumbled about was the fact that on the day that we had announced that there were 49,000 fewer victims of crime in this country, there was a story that ignored that entirely and talked about something else. We weren't happy about it—that's life.
explanation: The '49,000 fewer victims of crime' figure derives from victimisation survey comparisons; broadly grounded but a contestable headline statistic stated without caveat.

text: Great progress. Restoring law and order is a core focus of our plan to fix the basics. We banned gang patches, reintroduced tougher sentences for serious offending, and made stalking an illegal and imprisonable offence... in two years, we’ve made great progress with 49,000 fewer victims of crime.
explanation: Reforms are real; the '49,000 fewer victims' headline is a self-cited survey-based figure presented favourably.

text: When we came into Government in October 2023, there were 185,000 victims of violent crime, and the Government set a target of reducing that figure to 165,000, a reduction of 20,000 victims, by 2029.
explanation: Specific, internally consistent figures attributed to the target-setting; not independently confirmable here.

text: The Government’s initiative to clamp and seize cars of people not paying court fines has been highly successful, returning more than $700,000 and seizing 236 vehicles... Between July 2025 and February 2026, bailiffs scanned 147,000 number plates and identified 2,866 people with overdue court fines and reparations. Six hundred of those paid on the spot. Eighty vehicles have been sold at auction
explanation: Detailed, checkable figures presented as administrative data; framed as success.

text: When you think about more than 50 percent of the Government’s spending during the years of COVID-19, having nothing to do with COVID-19... I am really proud that despite those challenges, 83,000 New Zealanders left welfare for a job, in the last year. That’s something worth celebrating.
explanation: 'More than 50 percent of spending had nothing to do with COVID' is a contestable framing; 83,000 figure presented favourably without the offsetting inflow.

text: MSD also found that nearly 99 percent of clients are fulfilling their obligations, and the number of sanctions has dropped by 10.6 percent between September 2024 and September 2025 quarters. The changes we have made have increased client activity and engagement with MSD.
explanation: Attributed to MSD data; plausible but unverifiable here.

text: we’ve got 70,000 people in case management, some of those over the phone; we have introduced a traffic light system so more people know what their obligations are; 90 percent of those on the jobseeker benefit say that is helpful to them.
explanation: Operational figures plausible; the '90 percent say helpful' is an unverifiable self-cited stat.

text: This data shows international tourism contributed $12.5 billion to New Zealand's economy for the year ending December 2025, up 3 percent on the previous year.
explanation: Cited from the international visitor survey; plausible and internally consistent.

text: Around 960,000 Kiwis receiving superannuation and the veteran's pension will get increased payments. There will be over 435,000 working age beneficiaries who will get increased support, around 52,000 students receiving student allowance and loans will get a boost, and approximately 67,000 non-beneficiaries will get an increase in their supplementary assistance.
explanation: Detailed, checkable population figures, consistent with administrative data.

text: Why have we not considered a capital gains tax? Well, we don't want to tax capital, because of the surprising fact that capital assists us to grow our economy. If you tax capital, you do not grow your economy.
explanation: Overstated to the point of being misleading; taxing capital does not categorically prevent growth, and the empirical record is contested.

text: in the last 18 months, under this Government, we have had the most amount of renewable generation in the entirety of the last decade
explanation: Specific superlative claim about renewable generation built in 18 months; plausible given recent build-out but not verifiable from the text and superlatives invite overstatement.

text: this Government isn't intending to import LNG to replace natural gas, or for it to be imported regularly enough to see it set the gas price overall. LNG is simply a backup option to be imported during dry years. The alternative is we have no fuel to make electricity, and that was the policy that we inherited and which drove power prices in 2024 to over $800 per megawatt hour and put New Zealand businesses and New Zealanders out of business.
explanation: Wholesale prices did spike in 2024; the >$800/MWh figure is plausible but not confirmable here.

text: we face an acute problem, because in 2024, we had prices exceeding $800 because we did not have the fuel.
explanation: Wholesale electricity spot prices did spike sharply in 2024; the $800 figure is plausible, though the sole causal attribution to fuel shortage is partial.

text: the member will be aware that New Zealand has a brightline test that is for individuals that, in effect, have residential property, that look to build and sell that within a two-year period. They are subject to tax. That is already in the law.
explanation: Accurate: the brightline test taxes residential property gains within the two-year window then in force.

text: This is the third consecutive drop from the previous quarters, and shows a consistent downward trend in serious and persistent youth offending by children and young people. The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
explanation: Specific, internally consistent claims attributed to data; not confirmable here.

text: I have asked Oranga Tamariki about the serious allegation in the member's question of kids being housed in motels with untrained staff, and they've been unable to identify what the member is referring to. If the member has evidence of this occurring, I would strongly encourage her to provide this information so it can be addressed... yes, I am aware that motels are being used as an emergency option, as a last resort where no other safe option is available. This practice even pre-dates Oranga Tamariki as an organisation.
explanation: Claims OT could not identify the untrained-staff allegation and that motel use predates OT; plausible but unverifiable from the text.

text: The most common length of stay in a motel is one night, and most children and young people stay fewer than three nights. Sometimes, it is a case of not wanting to remove them from their community or from their family supports while we make sure we can find a safe place for them to stay.
explanation: Specific statistical claim about typical stay lengths; plausible from monitoring data but not independently confirmable here, and it omits the long-stay outliers.

text: I have read the ICM report very closely, and there is no mention in that report of untrained staff being used to look after children in motels.
explanation: Factual claim about the contents of the ICM report; checkable against the report but not verifiable from the text here.

text: New Zealand is a small country, but we can be a country that leads the world on international matters, not because we are the biggest, not because we are the loudest, not because we have the largest military or the biggest economy, but because as a country we know who we are, we know what our values are, and we have the courage to stick up for the things that we think are important around the world.
explanation: Stirring but offers no concrete mechanism or policy.

text: Speaking in the House recently, I alluded to a Facebook post of Nicola Willis where she was unpacking some groceries. I said in that Facebook post that she had committed to lowering grocery prices—I was mistaken. I should have referred to her press statements of 14 June 2023, 13 July 2023, 12 October 2023, her press conference on 27 August 2025, her Facebook video in September 2025—all of which committed her to lowering grocery prices.
explanation: Lists precise dates of the statements he relies on.

text: Does he stand by his claim that giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut would lower rents; if so, why have rents gone up almost 10 percent in the past year?
explanation: Cites a precise figure ($2.9b) and a quantified outcome (rents up ~10%).

text: Did his Government, cancelling the planned 70 million litre strategic diesel reserve, increase or decrease New Zealand's exposure to a diesel supply shock?
explanation: Cites a specific cancelled policy and volume to frame the question.

text: Does he regret cutting the clean car discount, given estimates suggest that had New Zealanders continued to buy electric vehicles at the rate they were under the discount, there'd be 50,000 more electric vehicles on the road today than there are now under his Government?
explanation: Anchors the question to a named policy and a quantified counterfactual.

text: We support the addition to the motion made by Chris Hipkins and we absolutely—absolutely—call for peace on this particular issue. We want to ensure that our people understand the impacts that it will have on our people living here in Aotearoa.
explanation: General call for peace with no concrete proposal or detail.

text: In October 2025, there was a paper produced that, essentially, looked at how well the administrative data does against the census data. It was a bit of an experimental test to see how well it compares, and the results were not too bad. However, they did point to second-layer data as being a potential issue. When people respond to the higher-level categories, that was fairly accurate, but those second-level categories are quite difficult to get right.
explanation: Dates the paper and identifies the precise data layer (second-level categories) at issue.

text: The Prime Minister himself said yesterday that this was a decision made without discussion nor debate. It was also made without briefings to the Opposition, and it appears to have been made without advice about international law nor overreaching security and cost considerations.
explanation: Itemises specific alleged process failures: no debate, no Opposition briefing, no legal/security/cost advice.

text: In the last day, we've heard the Pentagon telling Congress there was no sign that Iran was going to attack the US first, and no evidence to support the claim that the US attacked Iran in defence. We've heard the Senate Intelligence Committee vice chair say he had seen no intelligence that Iran was on the verge of launching any kind of pre-emptive strike against the United States of America.
explanation: Names specific bodies and timeframe ('in the last day').

text: it can result in an overhung Parliament, as it did in 2005, 2008, 2011, 2014, and, of course, this one as well.
explanation: Lists the precise election years to support the point about overhang.

text: if you are able to download secondary legislation, then you may well have the tools to be able to apply a voice system or to increase the size of the print, etc., and so that could be quite an effective way of addressing the accessibility issue by simply changing the word “or” in that paragraph, to the word “and”.
explanation: Precise textual amendment ('or' to 'and') tied to replacement section 75(2)(a).

text: This Government’s fiscal strategy is about returning to surplus and bending the debt curve over, from going up to going down.
explanation: States a direction (surplus, falling debt) but no figures, mechanism, or timeframe.

text: Fuel excise in New Zealand is a fixed number of cents per litre, not a percentage of the price, so when fuel prices rise, the Government does not receive additional revenue from that source.
explanation: Explains the precise mechanism distinguishing per-litre excise from ad valorem GST.

text: In total, we have made $43 billion worth of savings across the last two Budgets, with further savings planned in Budget 2026. Any slippage in our fiscal targets has occurred because of forecast revisions outside the Government's immediate control, not because of discretionary spending or revenue decisions. Unlike the last finance Minister, I stick to my operating allowances.
explanation: Quantifies savings ($43b) and attributes slippage to a named cause.

text: Recently introduced regulations require fuel importers to maintain at least 28 days of petrol and 21 days of diesel reserves, with the Government having acted to increase that requirement.
explanation: Names exact reserve-day requirements for each fuel.

text: the $50 a week increase in the in-work tax credit will last for one year—that is, until 31 March 2027—or until the prices of 91 octane petrol drops below $3 a litre for four consecutive weeks, whichever comes first.
explanation: Concrete date (31 March 2027), price threshold ($3/litre 91 octane), and duration condition (four consecutive weeks).

text: Labour’s plan is built on long-term investment, shared prosperity, and good jobs that keep young people building their futures here in New Zealand.
explanation: Slogan-level framing—‘long-term investment, shared prosperity, good jobs’—with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

text: The scope of this bill was to do some specific changes to clean up the Public Finance Act.
explanation: Names the Act and the general aim ('clean up'), but no concrete provisions, figures, or mechanisms.

text: There’s a reason why Florida is not covered by reinsurance but New Zealand continues to be, despite us being the second-highest amount of spending for natural disaster risks throughout the world.
explanation: Names a concrete comparator (Florida) and a ranking.

text: The fiscal cost of this is so small. Therefore, it points to the fact that this is not a significant change. We're not going to get much more. It's not going to incentivise those really highly skilled, capable new immigrants to New Zealand or expatriates back to New Zealand.
explanation: Detailed, technical engagement with the foreign investment fund rules and the revenue account method.

text: the New Zealand Law Society suggested there should be proportionality or necessity tests as part of this... there is no mandatory privacy impact assessments, there's short review cycles for these agreements, there's no requirement for independent audits, and stronger transparency was needed.
explanation: Concrete, itemised list of missing safeguards drawn from named submitters.

text: Very shortly, we'll be introducing legislation to strengthen trespass laws in New Zealand, followed by legislation to provide police with the power to deal with antisocial disorderly behaviour in our CBDs, and our Crime Amendment Bill is making its way through the House.
explanation: Names specific bills and areas, though 'very shortly' is vague on timing.

text: On Sunday 1 March, I received a text message from the chair of TVNZ asking for a call. We spoke about a range of matters including TVNZ financials and board appointments, and he observed, as I recall, that TVNZ had been in the news that week over a law and order story and that he was taking an interest in it... I didn't engage further in the discussion on that matter.
explanation: Names the date, the medium (text message), the topics, and his response.

text: The reform of the Crimes Act includes a raft of changes, including new specific offences for assaulting first responders or prison officers, two new specific coward-punch offences, and a new shoplifting infringement regime, as committed to in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement, that gives effect to the Government’s expansion of the citizen’s arrest powers
explanation: Enumerates the precise provisions of the bill and ties them to a coalition commitment.

text: We've seen a significant drop in the number of victims of violent crime since this Government was elected, with the latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey showing there were 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime in the year to October 2025 than two years previously.
explanation: Names the survey, the figure (49,000), and the period.

text: The Government’s initiative to clamp and seize cars of people not paying court fines has been highly successful, returning more than $700,000 and seizing 236 vehicles... Between July 2025 and February 2026, bailiffs scanned 147,000 number plates and identified 2,866 people with overdue court fines and reparations. Six hundred of those paid on the spot. Eighty vehicles have been sold at auction
explanation: Dense, precise operational figures with a defined date range.

text: We are a party and a Government of fiscal discipline. We think about where we spend taxpayer money—because it's not our money; it's taxpayer money
explanation: Slogan-level claim of fiscal discipline with no concrete measure.

text: We are a broad based – low rate party. We are not looking to increase tax. We are looking to increase economic growth, and that is the priority on this side of the Chamber.
explanation: Repeated positioning slogan with no concrete content.

text: In regard to the corporate tax rate, yes, we did consider, as part of the assessment when we put in place Investment Boost, whether we would be better to reduce the corporate tax rate or do another alternative. We selected to do Investment Boost, because Investment Boost is a targeted mechanism in order to ensure that the benefit goes to those who most need it.
explanation: Names the actual policy choice (Investment Boost vs rate cut) but gives no figures or detail on the assessment.

text: The modelling showed that the key benefit of LNG is to provide the market with certainty to access fuel during a dry year. That will reduce the risk premium and provide downward pressure on electricity prices... that is why we expect to see a reduction in consumer bills by at least $50 per household.
