explanation: Gives a concrete claimed saving ($50 per household) and a mechanism (risk premium, dry-year certainty), but no price path or amounts behind the modelling.

text: Forward prices for electricity have declined about 13 percent, or $20 a megawatt hour since the Government’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) announcement. This clearly shows that despite international events, the market is confident that LNG will work as an insurance for the sector during a dry year.
explanation: Exact percentage and dollar-per-MWh change.

text: This is the third consecutive drop from the previous quarters, and shows a consistent downward trend in serious and persistent youth offending by children and young people. The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
explanation: Quantifies the trend (third drop, 20%+ in 8 of 12 districts).

text: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
explanation: Names the funding ($30.6m), the budget year, age range, and cities.

text: The most common length of stay in a motel is one night, and most children and young people stay fewer than three nights. Sometimes, it is a case of not wanting to remove them from their community or from their family supports while we make sure we can find a safe place for them to stay.
explanation: Gives concrete stay-length figures (one night, fewer than three nights) and reasons.

text: My understanding is that the current website won't require retrospectivity... They're expensive to create and they're expensive to maintain, and I'd be surprised if we go for a whole new one again.
explanation: Gives a clear answer plus practical rationale (cost), but no concrete figures.

text: The term "official versions" means that a printout of the website is taken to state the law. That makes it easier to use in court proceedings. If you are presenting the court with a printout of the website, that will be accepted as what is the law.
explanation: Concrete explanation of the practical effect in court proceedings.

text: I have recently confirmed the Government's move to make RNZAF Base Ōhakea available 24/7 as an alternative runway for wide-body aircraft, resolving a longstanding constraint for airlines... To fix this, we have approved funding for Airways New Zealand to provide round-the-clock air traffic control services. Opening up Ōhakea 24/7 was one of the key actions within the aviation action plan. I am proud to see it delivered.
explanation: Names the base, the 24/7 change, the funded provider, and the underlying constraint.

text: Regulations made under the bill will set out what forms and formats legislation must be published in. We anticipate that this will require publication of secondary legislation in machine-readable formats, and so that means that people who are supported by screen readers will be able to use them to read published legislation. The new website will also aim to comply with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Level AA
explanation: Names concrete mechanisms: machine-readable formats, screen-reader support, and the WCAG 2.2 Level AA standard.

text: we’ve made a significant investment into new container-handling equipment that has just arrived at Gisborne’s Eastland Port... This $5 million investment will unlock fresh economic opportunities... In Whanganui on Monday... I announced an $8 million co-investment into the procurement of a new crane dredging barge... The equipment’s total cost is $12.9 million, with the remainder being co-funded by Northland-based marine construction company Johnson Bros Ltd.
explanation: Multiple precise figures, locations, partners, and timelines.

text: we’ve got a renewables boom going on in this country, and that’s because of the great energy policy that we’re building.
explanation: Claims credit for a 'renewables boom' but with no concrete delivered output named.

text: Well, I'm sorry, but we are going to secure fuel for New Zealanders. That is our number one priority. We are a Government that has delivered a renewables boom because we have action and investment, not just words. We are a Government that has created a strategic coal reserve for a dry-year risk.
explanation: Claims credit for a 'renewables boom' and a strategic coal reserve; delivery asserted but not substantiated.

text: Well, as I've said to the member before, I'm very proud that we've made house purchasing more affordable. Rents have come down, I think 6,000 or 7,000 people have come off the social housing wait-list, and, when I last looked, 2,100 children have been moved out of emergency housing into proper, dry homes, and there's big investment going in and support happening in homeless situations as well.
explanation: Claims concrete delivered outcomes on housing, but figures are approximate and unverified here.

text: Our Government is doing everything we can to increase storage across the fuel network across New Zealand. That is why when we came to power, we lifted the minimum stock holdings across diesel, across petrol, and across jet fuel as well. That’s what we did back in early 2025. We also updated the National Fuel Plan in the middle of 2024.
explanation: Claims concrete delivered actions (raised minimum stock holdings, updated National Fuel Plan), but partly offered to deflect a separate decision.

text: Yes, and, as I can say, that has stood New Zealand in very good stead. We do not have a fuel shortage in New Zealand at this point in time, and if you compare our stock holdings even to other countries, we have more days’ cover—which is a good thing—because of that decision we took.
explanation: Confirms a delivered policy (importers holding seven extra days' supply from April 2025) and credits it with a concrete outcome.

text: Recently introduced regulations require fuel importers to maintain at least 28 days of petrol and 21 days of diesel reserves, with the Government having acted to increase that requirement.
explanation: Points to a concrete delivered regulatory change increasing reserves.

text: I note that in July 2024, the Government did provide promised cost of living relief through tax changes that benefited around 1.9 million New Zealand households by an average of $60 extra a fortnight in their hand—$60 a fortnight I take the member would want to take back.
explanation: Points to a delivered tax change as a fulfilled commitment, though the 'average' framing softens it.

text: This Government’s fiscal strategy is about returning to surplus and bending the debt curve over, from going up to going down.
explanation: Stated fiscal intent rather than demonstrated delivery.

text: Very shortly, we'll be introducing legislation to strengthen trespass laws in New Zealand, followed by legislation to provide police with the power to deal with antisocial disorderly behaviour in our CBDs, and our Crime Amendment Bill is making its way through the House.
explanation: Mix of announced-but-not-yet-introduced legislation and one bill in progress — intent more than delivery.

text: The reform of the Crimes Act includes a raft of changes, including new specific offences for assaulting first responders or prison officers, two new specific coward-punch offences, and a new shoplifting infringement regime, as committed to in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement, that gives effect to the Government’s expansion of the citizen’s arrest powers
explanation: Bill is being introduced/at select committee—committed and progressing rather than fully enacted.

text: We've seen a significant drop in the number of victims of violent crime since this Government was elected, with the latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey showing there were 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime in the year to October 2025 than two years previously.
explanation: Claims measurable progress toward a stated target attributed to government action.

text: Great progress. Restoring law and order is a core focus of our plan to fix the basics. We banned gang patches, reintroduced tougher sentences for serious offending, and made stalking an illegal and imprisonable offence... in two years, we’ve made great progress with 49,000 fewer victims of crime.
explanation: Lists enacted measures (gang patch ban, stalking offence) as delivered, not merely promised.

text: The Government’s initiative to clamp and seize cars of people not paying court fines has been highly successful, returning more than $700,000 and seizing 236 vehicles... Between July 2025 and February 2026, bailiffs scanned 147,000 number plates and identified 2,866 people with overdue court fines and reparations. Six hundred of those paid on the spot. Eighty vehicles have been sold at auction
explanation: Reports concrete results of an implemented initiative.

text: Yes, I have received advice on the impacts of high levels of rooftop solar and household batteries on wholesale markets and distribution costs. It identified potential benefits to household bills, while also requiring significant investment in the grid. That is why the Government is making a number of regulatory changes to make it easier to install rooftop solar and batteries—this includes removing building consent requirements for installing rooftop solar and batteries, mandating retailers to pay a fair price for electricity sold back into the grid from 1 July, along with a number of other regulatory changes.
explanation: Describes regulatory changes underway rather than fully implemented outcomes.

text: This is the third consecutive drop from the previous quarters, and shows a consistent downward trend in serious and persistent youth offending by children and young people. The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
explanation: Points to measured progress against a target.

text: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
explanation: Describes a concretely funded and expanded programme.

text: I have recently confirmed the Government's move to make RNZAF Base Ōhakea available 24/7 as an alternative runway for wide-body aircraft, resolving a longstanding constraint for airlines... To fix this, we have approved funding for Airways New Zealand to provide round-the-clock air traffic control services. Opening up Ōhakea 24/7 was one of the key actions within the aviation action plan. I am proud to see it delivered.
explanation: Describes a concrete, funded, delivered action against a stated plan item.

text: In addition to our Ōhakea investment, we are also investing $1.1 million from the regional connectivity package to the first concessionary loan to Golden Bay Air. This loan will ensure that the regional airline can refinance existing aircraft debt and fund essential ongoing major maintenance checks.
explanation: A concrete funded measure, though described as ensuring future outcomes.

text: last year we announced a $3.35 million investment for Whanganui Airport to complete construction of the new sealed parallel taxiway. This will address longstanding safety issues by reducing the need for aircraft to backtrack on the active runway before take-off and after landing.
explanation: An announced/funded investment; delivery framed as future completion.

text: the Rangitata vessel will receive $3 million from the fund to improve its ability to carry different types of cargo across a wider range of ports nationwide... This investment will fund a deck-mounted crane capable of loading and unloading bulk cargo to be operating by the year’s end.
explanation: A committed, funded investment with a delivery date by year's end.

text: we’ve made a significant investment into new container-handling equipment that has just arrived at Gisborne’s Eastland Port... This $5 million investment will unlock fresh economic opportunities... In Whanganui on Monday... I announced an $8 million co-investment into the procurement of a new crane dredging barge... The equipment’s total cost is $12.9 million, with the remainder being co-funded by Northland-based marine construction company Johnson Bros Ltd.
explanation: Some delivered (Gisborne equipment arrived) and some future-dated (barge operational late 2027).

text: I want to acknowledge that there are different views on the legitimacy of the actions taken by the US and Israel. I respect those views and the vigour with which they have been offered.
explanation: Acknowledges opposing views respectfully, an attempt to bring others along.

text: I'd just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.
explanation: Combative and dismissive rather than persuasive.

text: we're in the process of approving a project in Southland that will deliver renewable energy to 100,000 homes, which the Labour-Greens Government didn't approve.
explanation: Frames an achievement against the opposition rather than building common ground.

text: Well, actually, we believe in an adult-to-adult relationship with the New Zealand people, not a parent-to-child relationship. It's one of the learnings coming out of the COVID experience that that member led.
explanation: A tidy 'adult-to-adult' line aimed at his own side rather than persuading the questioner.

text: New Zealand is a small country, but we can be a country that leads the world on international matters, not because we are the biggest, not because we are the loudest, not because we have the largest military or the biggest economy, but because as a country we know who we are, we know what our values are, and we have the courage to stick up for the things that we think are important around the world.
explanation: Inclusive, aspirational national framing intended to unite rather than divide.

text: The Iranian Government is a brutal, oppressive, and barbaric regime. It is possible to condemn their repression, to condemn the repression of their regime, and still to be clear that unilateral military escalation is not the answer.
explanation: Nuanced framing that seeks to bridge those who detest the regime and those who oppose the strikes.

text: International law applies to everyone, including our friends and allies. No country should place itself above international law.
explanation: Principled, universal framing, though appeals mainly to those already sympathetic.

text: I'd like to welcome the second royal commission into the COVID-19 response report that is being presented to the House today and thank the royal commission for the work that they have done.
explanation: Opens magnanimously, welcoming a report whose findings are contested; inclusive framing.

text: I would like to thank all of the front-line workers who were involved in New Zealand's COVID-19 response: our doctors, our nurses, all those in the health system, those who worked at the border, those who managed our quarantine and isolation facilities—all of the essential workers who went to work at a time when there was huge fear and huge uncertainty.
explanation: Warm, inclusive recognition of a broad range of workers; unifying rather than partisan.

text: We support the addition to the motion made by Chris Hipkins and we absolutely—absolutely—call for peace on this particular issue. We want to ensure that our people understand the impacts that it will have on our people living here in Aotearoa.
explanation: Conciliatory, peace-focused and supportive of a cross-party amendment.

text: We respect international law because the alternative is worse. The alternative is a world where only force dictates outcomes.
explanation: Values-based appeal for upholding law over force.

text: we are absolutely going into this, examining the questions, being open to supporting the bill, and we’d gently encourage Government members to be open to, at some stage, exploring other reserved provisions
explanation: Constructive, cross-party tone — signals openness to support and invites the Government to collaborate on further reserved provisions.

text: New section 76(b)—I think this is a brilliant new section of the bill—requires the administering agency to publish details as to the availability of anything that has been exempt.
explanation: Opposition member openly praising a provision of the Government's bill — collegial, bridge-building tone.

text: Absolutely not. Just because we have achieved the target well ahead of expectations doesn't mean we stop now. Every young person deserves the opportunity to be the best version of themselves.
explanation: Aspirational, inclusive note about young people.

text: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
explanation: Cross-party acknowledgement builds goodwill rather than partisan point-scoring.

text: Does he stand by his claim that giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut would lower rents; if so, why have rents gone up almost 10 percent in the past year?
explanation: Pointed but engages the policy substance.

text: Did his Government, cancelling the planned 70 million litre strategic diesel reserve, increase or decrease New Zealand's exposure to a diesel supply shock?
explanation: Pointed but targets a policy decision, not the person.

text: The Prime Minister has now asserted that the previous Government made that decision; it was a private business.
explanation: Procedural correction focused on the facts of who decided, not a personal attack.

text: the fact that the Government of the day considered a report on the implications of Marsden Point being closed by its private sector owners does not mean the Government approved of it... But lack of intervention to prop up a business that was closing anyway does not mean the Government approved of that business closing.
explanation: Engages the substance of the dispute without personal attack.

text: I would like to thank all of the front-line workers who were involved in New Zealand's COVID-19 response: our doctors, our nurses, all those in the health system, those who worked at the border, those who managed our quarantine and isolation facilities—all of the essential workers who went to work at a time when there was huge fear and huge uncertainty.
explanation: Respectful and gracious.

text: The Government’s actions have been irresponsible, unprincipled, and do a disservice to New Zealand’s independent approach to foreign affairs.
explanation: Strong condemnatory language but directed at the Government's conduct and foreign-policy stance, not personal insult.

text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I would first say, then, that we do condemn Iran’s attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf, but the Government have made a clear promise in this statement that puts New Zealand at risk in expressing New Zealand’s readiness to assist in opening the Strait of Hormuz.
explanation: Criticises the Government's foreign-policy decision while explicitly condemning Iran's attacks; engages substance, not persons.

text: we are absolutely going into this, examining the questions, being open to supporting the bill, and we’d gently encourage Government members to be open to, at some stage, exploring other reserved provisions
explanation: Respectful and collegial ('gently encourage'), focused on the substance of the legislation.

text: my concern would be that if you had secondary legislation that was published that subsequently fell off the portal and the website, it would continue to have effect in law, however would not be accessible to individuals who are trying to assess what the law is. Of course, that is entirely what this piece of legislation is trying to address. ... the amendments that I would propose to the Minister’s amendment are that we allow a window of time to rectify that error. I’ve proposed 20 days or 40 days
explanation: Constructive, policy-focused engagement with the Minister's amendment.

text: New section 76(b)—I think this is a brilliant new section of the bill—requires the administering agency to publish details as to the availability of anything that has been exempt.
explanation: Respectful, substance-focused, generous to the drafters.

text: I'd suggest the person doing the most damage to themselves today is Mr Hipkins, who seems to be in a state of fervent denial.
explanation: Personal characterisation of an opponent rather than engagement with substance.

text: What I do know is that this conflict won't result in a windfall gain of hundreds of millions of dollars in extra GST, as some have alleged; that is simply economic illiteracy.
explanation: 'Economic illiteracy' dismisses opponents' argument with a belittling label.

text: In total, we have made $43 billion worth of savings across the last two Budgets, with further savings planned in Budget 2026. Any slippage in our fiscal targets has occurred because of forecast revisions outside the Government's immediate control, not because of discretionary spending or revenue decisions. Unlike the last finance Minister, I stick to my operating allowances.
explanation: 'Unlike the last finance Minister' is a comparative dig but policy-focused.

text: Unlike that member, I say good on all of those people who went to that job fair; I say good on them for going out and looking for work... To every New Zealander who is taking the effort to go out and find more work: we’re on your side. Go for it.
explanation: Mild 'unlike that member' contrast but otherwise constructive.

text: what that clause is essentially doing is legislative repair, updating a reference to a definition in another piece of legislation that’s since been repealed and replaced. It replaces the reference to the term defined by reference to the now out of date Securities Market Act 1988, i.e. “registered market”, to the relevant term in the New Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013, which is “licensed market” and that replaced the Securities Market Act in 1988.
explanation: Patient, substantive explanation engaging directly with the member's question.

text: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
explanation: Generously credits the previous Government for starting a programme that is working.

text: Because what New Zealanders understand is that the poor spending during COVID under the last Government caused huge amounts of pain and suffering. They know that they have a Government that is balancing good economic management so we don’t run up debt and actually mortgage the future of our kids and our grandkids, while also making sure we have targeted, temporary, timely support for New Zealanders in need.
explanation: Asserts COVID spending 'caused' present pain without evidence and reframes the question rather than reasoning to it.

text: No, because we believe in farmers in this country and they need utes, and, actually, they shouldn't be subsidising people who want to buy EVs. As you've seen in the last week, EV sales have been just fine.
explanation: Leans on a farmers-vs-EV-buyers false dichotomy rather than addressing the 50,000-EV estimate.

text: Well, what I was about to say was: that was the member who banned oil and gas; that drove up electricity prices to $800 a megawatt hour; and ended up making the rather unique transition, thanks to a Labour-Greens Government, of domestic gas to imported Indonesian coal.
explanation: Chains several claims into a causal story without establishing the links.

text: It had a Lake Onslow project at $17 billion—$8,000 for every single household in the country—that led to an $800 megawatt per hour price in wholesale electricity prices. What we are doing, as I've previously explained, is we're dealing with the dry-year risk, lowering the risk premium, and therefore wanting to lower power bills by $50 for every household.
explanation: Marshals figures and a mechanism (dry-year risk premium) but blends in contestable causal claims.

text: New Zealand is far from the Middle East, and I do not overestimate our influence over events there. We are not central to this region or this conflict.
explanation: Measured, realistic appraisal of NZ's limited influence rather than overclaiming.

text: It didn't work in Iraq, it didn't work in Afghanistan, and it won't work in Iran.
explanation: Leans on historical analogy rather than evidence specific to Iran.

text: Did his Government, cancelling the planned 70 million litre strategic diesel reserve, increase or decrease New Zealand's exposure to a diesel supply shock?
explanation: Frames a causal claim with a concrete policy referent, though stated as a leading binary.

text: Does he stand by his claim that giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut would lower rents; if so, why have rents gone up almost 10 percent in the past year?
explanation: Tests a prior claim against an outcome — evidence-based challenge.

text: the fact that the Government of the day considered a report on the implications of Marsden Point being closed by its private sector owners does not mean the Government approved of it... But lack of intervention to prop up a business that was closing anyway does not mean the Government approved of that business closing.
explanation: Clean logical distinction between considering a report and approving an outcome.

text: I'll quote directly from paragraph 495 of the royal commission's report: “We consider the failure to ensure that this specific advice reached Ministers and the public was significant.”
explanation: Cites the report by paragraph and quotes it directly to rebut the Minister's characterisation — evidence-anchored argument.

text: We respect international law because the alternative is worse. The alternative is a world where only force dictates outcomes.
explanation: Coherent but rests on a somewhat binary framing of the alternatives.

text: We have two obligations in respect of the rules-based order. The first is to follow the rules. The second is to hold others accountable to them. New Zealand has, throughout our history, upheld both these obligations, but this week we have seen a Government shrugging its shoulders at the second of those obligations.
explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion structure identifying which obligation she says is being neglected.

text: In the last day, we've heard the Pentagon telling Congress there was no sign that Iran was going to attack the US first, and no evidence to support the claim that the US attacked Iran in defence. We've heard the Senate Intelligence Committee vice chair say he had seen no intelligence that Iran was on the verge of launching any kind of pre-emptive strike against the United States of America.
explanation: Marshals specific evidentiary sources to rebut the self-defence justification.

text: In October 2025, there was a paper produced that, essentially, looked at how well the administrative data does against the census data. It was a bit of an experimental test to see how well it compares, and the results were not too bad. However, they did point to second-layer data as being a potential issue. When people respond to the higher-level categories, that was fairly accurate, but those second-level categories are quite difficult to get right.
explanation: Grounds her caution in a specific October 2025 comparison study and draws a nuanced distinction between accurate high-level and unreliable second-layer data.

text: my concern would be that if you had secondary legislation that was published that subsequently fell off the portal and the website, it would continue to have effect in law, however would not be accessible to individuals who are trying to assess what the law is. Of course, that is entirely what this piece of legislation is trying to address. ... the amendments that I would propose to the Minister’s amendment are that we allow a window of time to rectify that error. I’ve proposed 20 days or 40 days
explanation: Identifies a concrete failure mode (law in force but inaccessible) and proposes a targeted fix; conclusion follows from premise.

text: to say that there is no plan for energy security other than hoping that it rains
explanation: Strawman framing rather than engagement with the actual policy.

text: The loudest false promise I have heard in recent times has been from those who out of one side of their mouth say that they care deeply about the cost of living and out the other side of their mouth say that they would change the inflation targeting regime, would introduce new taxes on tenants, and at the same time would remove the Investment Boost tax policy that is the very thing that Treasury says will drive future wage growth. I care deeply about the cost of living, but it is not enough to care; that member needs to come up with serious policies on the cost of living if she wants to be taken seriously.
explanation: Cites Treasury on Investment Boost but largely an attack listing opponent positions.

text: this clause is simply clarifying an ambiguity in the interpretation of the Act, specifying essentially that an appropriation does not create an obligation to spend; it creates a permission to spend, but not an obligation to spend, which is a good thing because when public agencies feel that spending is no longer necessary, it’s appropriate that those dollars paid for by hard working taxpayers can be put to purposes that are necessary rather than simply spent because of a technical requirement of the Act.
explanation: Sound conceptual distinction (permission vs obligation), but the justification leans partly on a rhetorical appeal to 'hard working taxpayers' rather than evidence.

text: We’re not sure that Brad Olsen has calculated his figures correctly... in New Zealand, we legally require every company that is importing fuel into the country to have a minimum stockholding obligation (MSO) of at least 21 days’ worth of diesel... we would expect to be notified if there was any risk of those MSOs being breached, and we have not had any such notification.
explanation: Marshals evidence: diesel's inelastic demand, Middle East disruption, and the 21-day MSO buffer to rebut the warning.

text: The latest update shows that around 59 days of petrol, 54 days of diesel, and 50 days of jet fuel are in country, within our exclusive economic zone, or on the water heading here. That data is updated twice weekly. Importantly, we use maritime tracking, including the Starboard software system, to cross-check against the shipping information that fuel companies share with us.
explanation: Describes cross-checking shipping data against independent maritime tracking — evidence-based.

text: We don't have a policy to tax people's homes. We don't have a policy to tax people's farms or their baches—which I appreciate the member is keen to do all that, or a 66 percent tax rate, which seems to be on the agenda; we're not doing any of that.
explanation: Relies on a strawman of the opponent's position rather than engaging her actual argument.

text: Kiwis can be confident because LNG makes New Zealand more resilient. Surprisingly enough, having more options than less options gives you greater resilience, and greater resilience means less volatility... if you have less volatility, you see less power prices and downward pressure on power prices.
explanation: A chained-assertion argument (more options → resilience → less volatility → lower prices) asserted rather than evidenced, and it sidesteps the analytical gaps raised.

text: What I think is irresponsible is to pursue energy policy which incurs blackouts for New Zealanders because we do not have fuel to make electricity in a dry year. That is a situation which we inherited as a Government. We have taken decisive action to import fuel for those dry years as an insurance policy, and as a result we've seen future energy prices in this country—subsequent to our announcements—have a downward trajectory, which is positive.
explanation: Reasoned defence, but attributes the downward price trajectory to its announcements as if causally established.

text: The challenge is that the last Government stopped gas exploration and, as a result, we have no gas. So we are looking to import that.
explanation: Causal claim is plausible but compressed and overstated.

text: Forward prices for electricity have declined about 13 percent, or $20 a megawatt hour since the Government’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) announcement. This clearly shows that despite international events, the market is confident that LNG will work as an insurance for the sector during a dry year.
explanation: Uses price data, but infers market 'confidence' in LNG from a price fall — a correlation-as-proof gap.

text: The Bioeconomy Science Institute performs an important role in supporting the growth and development of New Zealand's biological sector, but it will only be effective if it's operating on a financially sustainable footing... The Bioeconomy Science Institute brought together four Crown Research Institutes with subsequently identified areas of overlap and duplication. I note this has been a voluntary redundancy round and operational decisions about staffing sit with the Bioeconomy Science Institute Board.
explanation: Offers an overlap/duplication rationale, though doesn't address the growth question directly.

text: I think he’s probably on a few things, actually!
explanation: Ad hominem insinuation with no relevance to the argument.

text: Even today, there are people, sadly—and I see one of them is in this House—who think that Mr Putin's really quite a nice bloke, if only he wasn't provoked by that nasty NATO, aka our allies.
explanation: Strawmans the opponent's view ('Putin's really quite a nice bloke') to dismiss it.

text: A former Prime Minister said that we were removing interest deductibility from residential property to tilt the market towards first-home buyers. You know what happened? Rents went through the roof and first-home buyers had less to save a deposit. We actually have helped first-home buyers, who are now buying homes at record levels—I think at 28 percent of new purchases
explanation: Constructs a cause-and-effect story (policy → rents up → reversal → record first-home buying) but asserts the causal links rather than isolating them from other market factors.

text: When the Opposition say, “Oh, we already had ferries arriving.”, maybe you did, but you didn’t know how to fit them through the channel that they had to pass through, you didn’t have the ports that they needed to load and unload, so you are pointing to a fantasy rather than a solution.
explanation: Makes a concrete point about channel/port constraints undermining the prior ferries, though stated as assertion.

text: a natural monopoly is a service that has constantly increasing returns to scale, so one provider is the most efficient way to provide. And, as it happens, roads and sewer networks and water pipes and public transport networks and a whole lot of things that cities rely on are natural monopolies. That's why you can't have a competitive market, and that is the public policy case for zoning
explanation: A clearly structured argument from a definition to a conclusion (the case for zoning), with the steps spelled out.

text: Multiple statements in that question were wrong.
explanation: Dismisses the question wholesale without engaging any of its claims.

text: It is worth remembering that 2.9 million New Zealanders are working in jobs across the country, and that this rose by 15,000 in the last quarter. While the last few years have been challenging for many manufacturers, the Performance of Manufacturing Index has shown the manufacturing sector, as a whole, expanding each month since the middle of last year.
explanation: Asked whether the closures contribute to growth; answers obliquely via aggregate framing.

text: Well, the Deputy Prime Minister asks a very good question because, yes, I can confirm that our Government is committed to achieving fiscal consolidation through better spending. I note that the Fitch report said that the Opposition would achieve fiscal consolidation through increased taxation. It seems that the Opposition is telling the Fitch Ratings agency more—than it’s prepared to tell New Zealanders.
explanation: Answers Seymour's friendly question directly (consolidation via spending restraint), then adds a partisan jab.

text: the Public Finance Act and Public Service Act clearly work together. Ventures and boards are set up under the Public Service Act and those provisions remain, whereas the Public Finance Act deals with their financial accountability. Hence the cross references are the simplest way to address that.
explanation: Directly answers Edmonds' repeated 'why keep this in' question, explaining the rationale rather than deflecting.

text: Because it starts from 1 April—that is, from next Wednesday. Families already receiving the in-work tax credit won’t have to do anything. Inland Revenue will automatically deliver the increase. Families paid weekly will see the increase from 7 April 2026, and those paid fortnightly will see it from 14 April 2026.
explanation: Answers Brewer's 'How is this support timely?' directly with start dates and delivery mechanism.

text: We have a range of advice regarding solar and batteries that is under active consideration, and when it is no longer under active consideration, then that will be released.
explanation: Asked plainly whether advice was shared with the National Party, he gives a non-answer about release timing.

text: Yeah, a lot of consideration in regards to revenue methods. The primary method that we're focused on is growing our economy so that we can grow the revenue of every business and every household in this country. That's been a major focus of this Government, and one of the ways we achieve that is through a broad based - low rate tax system. I receive a wide range of advice from Treasury as part of my role.
explanation: Woods asked specifically what consideration he gave to broadening the base / taxing things other than income; he pivots to economic growth and offers no substance on base-broadening.

text: What I think is irresponsible is to pursue energy policy which incurs blackouts for New Zealanders because we do not have fuel to make electricity in a dry year. That is a situation which we inherited as a Government. We have taken decisive action to import fuel for those dry years as an insurance policy, and as a result we've seen future energy prices in this country—subsequent to our announcements—have a downward trajectory, which is positive.
explanation: Rebuts the 'volatile gas market' premise but does not engage the specific LNG price-spike figures put to him.

text: Has the Government considered a land value tax? No. Has the Government considered a capital gains tax? No. Has the Government considered a death tax? No. Has the Government considered a whole lot of taxes that one wants to make up off the cuff? No.
explanation: Gives clear, unambiguous 'No' answers to Russell's questions about whether specific taxes were considered, though he avoids the corporate-rate/2022-briefing question.

text: The answer in regards to asset sales is no. The Government has not considered that and is not considering that at this point.
explanation: Direct, complete answer to Woods' specific question about whether asset-sale revenue was considered.

text: Absolutely not. Just because we have achieved the target well ahead of expectations doesn't mean we stop now. Every young person deserves the opportunity to be the best version of themselves.
explanation: Gives a clear, direct answer ('Absolutely not') to whether she is satisfied.

text: I have asked Oranga Tamariki about the serious allegation in the member's question of kids being housed in motels with untrained staff, and they've been unable to identify what the member is referring to. If the member has evidence of this occurring, I would strongly encourage her to provide this information so it can be addressed... yes, I am aware that motels are being used as an emergency option, as a last resort where no other safe option is available. This practice even pre-dates Oranga Tamariki as an organisation.
explanation: Directly engages the 'were you aware' question: challenges the untrained-staff premise as unverified, then answers yes on motel use as a last resort.

text: The most common length of stay in a motel is one night, and most children and young people stay fewer than three nights. Sometimes, it is a case of not wanting to remove them from their community or from their family supports while we make sure we can find a safe place for them to stay.
explanation: Carter asked her to justify a 25%-plus increase under her watch; she offers context on stay lengths and reasons but does not directly address or justify the increase.

text: I think that, because the first question was incorrect, I would have to take away and verify what that member is saying before I can answer it.
explanation: Asked what she would say to a quoted caregiver, she declines to answer and defers to verification, citing an alleged earlier inaccuracy.

text: I have read the ICM report very closely, and there is no mention in that report of untrained staff being used to look after children in motels.
explanation: Asked how placing complex-needs children with untrained caregivers fits her priorities, she rebuts the premise (the report doesn't mention untrained staff) rather than addressing the priorities question.

text: Despite my intense passion and love of that particular piece of legislation, I haven't yet committed them all to memory, so I'll take a chance to look it up.
explanation: Honestly admits he cannot answer the Civil Aviation Act point now and defers to looking it up.

text: I have done a bit of work in the past on the Incorporated Societies Act when that came into force. From memory, that's the Incorporated Societies Act 2020, and I think there was sort of a fallback provision of being five years or six years after Royal assent for some of those provisions.
explanation: Engages Xu-Nan's question about the five-year fallback with a relevant example, but qualified as recollection rather than a confirmed answer.

text: It is the case that if a piece of secondary legislation is needing to be published, which provides a consolidation of all secondary legislation that incorporates all of the amendments made by every amending instrument—if it doesn't meet the requirements of publication, it is all repealed. So I have to correct that: it is all repealed.
explanation: Gives the corrected substantive answer rather than glossing over the change.

text: If it was "must include", then, therefore, the report would be legally required to include recommendations on something that it might not have a recommendation on. A report has the option of including a recommendation, but it doesn't have to do it
explanation: Directly answers Walters' question about why the annual report's repeal recommendations are 'may' not 'must'.

text: the transitional provisions require all existing agencies' secondary legislation to be republished. So everything needs to be republished. If an agency fails to republish, regulations can be made under the Legislation Act, which can provide the possibility that the legislation is revoked.
explanation: Directly answers Xu-Nan's question about what happens to secondary legislation not updated by the deadline.

text: In answer to the first part, absolutely, but as I have just explained to the member, we don't have the information or intelligence by which these independent actions by the US and Israel were launched, and the member doesn't, either.
explanation: Affirms standing by his pledge to 'call out' threats to the rules-based order, yet refuses to apply that standard to the US/Israel strikes — tension between stated value and conduct.

text: New Zealand opposed the US invasion of Iraq and history proved that was the correct decision.
explanation: Invokes a consistent NZ tradition of independent foreign policy to back his current stance.

text: When Russia invaded Ukraine, we called that out as a breach of the international rules-based order, and we were right to do that. When Vladimir Putin invades his next country of choice, what moral authority will we have as a country to call on him to obey the international rules-based order if we are not willing to ask the same standard of countries that we have a closer relationship with?
explanation: Demands consistency between NZ's Ukraine stance and its response to allies' actions.

text: Speaking in the House recently, I alluded to a Facebook post of Nicola Willis where she was unpacking some groceries. I said in that Facebook post that she had committed to lowering grocery prices—I was mistaken. I should have referred to her press statements of 14 June 2023, 13 July 2023, 12 October 2023, her press conference on 27 August 2025, her Facebook video in September 2025—all of which committed her to lowering grocery prices.
explanation: Openly corrects his own earlier error on the record, consistent with owning mistakes.

text: The loudest false promise I have heard in recent times has been from those who out of one side of their mouth say that they care deeply about the cost of living and out the other side of their mouth say that they would change the inflation targeting regime, would introduce new taxes on tenants, and at the same time would remove the Investment Boost tax policy that is the very thing that Treasury says will drive future wage growth. I care deeply about the cost of living, but it is not enough to care; that member needs to come up with serious policies on the cost of living if she wants to be taken seriously.
explanation: Charge of opponent hypocrisy (caring vs their policies) — a low-authenticity signal about Labour, not about Willis.

text: the FamilyBoost tax credit, we made changes to that last year, which I note the member's party supported—having earlier opposed—which mean that many families have now got more than $150 a fortnight in relief from that policy
explanation: Attacks the opponent's position reversal — a signal about Labour, not primarily about Willis's own consistency.

text: Once again in answering a question from this member, I would wish to quote my full statement, which was from a recent speech to the New Zealand Economics Forum, and which said, “Others may argue for higher taxes and more spending. But every one of those choices comes with a price - and that price is paid by hard working Kiwis.” Since the member asked a primary question about a quote, I think I should make it very clear that I was talking about the policies of the Opposition.
explanation: Stands by the statement and explains its original context rather than disowning it.

text: I can confirm that unemployment is higher now than we would both wish it to be and than it has been in the past. That is why our Government is so focused on growing the economy, creating the conditions in which businesses and firms can hire more people.
explanation: Acknowledging an unfavourable fact about her own Government's record is consistent and non-evasive.

text: Yes, I stand by my statement of 6 March, and I also stand by this Government's decision to unwind proposed petrol tax increases by the previous Government which would have added 12c extra to fuel as well as 10c in a regional fuel tax.
explanation: Asserts her words match her government's action (unwinding the fuel tax), consistent with her stated cost-of-living stance.

text: It didn't work in Iraq, it didn't work in Afghanistan, and it won't work in Iran.
explanation: Prediction that the intervention will fail; directionally plausible by historical analogy but uncertain and unfalsifiable in the near term.

text: When Russia invaded Ukraine, we called that out as a breach of the international rules-based order, and we were right to do that. When Vladimir Putin invades his next country of choice, what moral authority will we have as a country to call on him to obey the international rules-based order if we are not willing to ask the same standard of countries that we have a closer relationship with?
explanation: Presumes Putin 'invades his next country of choice'; plausible concern but speculative and undated.

text: What I think is irresponsible is to pursue energy policy which incurs blackouts for New Zealanders because we do not have fuel to make electricity in a dry year. That is a situation which we inherited as a Government. We have taken decisive action to import fuel for those dry years as an insurance policy, and as a result we've seen future energy prices in this country—subsequent to our announcements—have a downward trajectory, which is positive.
explanation: Implies forward prices will keep trending down; plausible but contingent and unverified.

text: The modelling showed that the key benefit of LNG is to provide the market with certainty to access fuel during a dry year. That will reduce the risk premium and provide downward pressure on electricity prices... that is why we expect to see a reduction in consumer bills by at least $50 per household.
explanation: Prediction that bills will fall by at least $50 per household; optimistic and dependent on volatile global LNG prices, so uncertain.

text: Yes. Independent modelling shows that a liquefied natural gas (LNG) importation facility will reduce forward prices by at least $10 per megawatt hour, reducing the average Kiwi's power bill by $50.
explanation: Forecast price reduction dependent on volatile global LNG markets; plausible but uncertain.

text: I reject the premise in that question because that is factually not correct. Kiwi power bills for both households and businesses will reduce as a result of the LNG importation terminal because the simple reality is that when you don't have fuel to make electricity, our prices spike.
explanation: Predicts household and business bills will fall as a result of the terminal; uncertain and contested.

text: currently, our tax base does not cover certain revenue-generation methods when it comes to things like capital gains and additional assets like private jets, superyachts, etc.
explanation: Identifies the gap (capital gains, certain assets) with concrete examples, though without figures or a defined mechanism.

text: will there be ways for us to be accessible from a disability lens, particularly when we’re looking at the ability for the new legislation website to have better ways for, I guess, speech transcription for those who are blind, in particular?
explanation: Names a concrete feature (speech transcription / screen-reader access for blind users).

text: I have never seen this second paragraph, "(b) is not to be drafted by the PCO under section 67(1)(d)(i) of that Act." Is there a reason? I'm genuinely curious. How prevalent is something like that, and is there a reason why it is specified explicitly that it cannot be drafted by the Parliamentary Counsel Office?
explanation: Pinpoints the exact provision (Civil Aviation Act 2023, Schedule 4, the PCO-drafting carve-out) he is querying.

text: I think in cross referencing with Part 3 of Schedule 2 of the Public Service Act, the specificity of a singular servicing department is understandable.
explanation: Cites a precise legislative reference (Part 3 of Schedule 2 of the Public Service Act) to ground the point.

text: if you’re looking at the subheading, am I correct to assume that it can’t incur expenses that’re not within the appropriation, but in clause 6(1A) it seems to imply that it can’t occur expenses that it already has authorised.
explanation: Cites the exact clause (6(1A)) and articulates the precise interpretive discrepancy.

text: it still doesn’t make sense as to why you would keep this in there, because it’s superfluous legislation given that it’s quite clear there’s no intention for there to be an interdepartmental venture, unless, Minister, there is going to be a new interdepartmental venture.
explanation: Pointed challenge to the Minister but focused entirely on the substance of the clause, no personal attack.

text: Yeah, I’m not surprised to hear that sort of speech coming from Ryan Hamilton, the MP up in Hamilton, given his personal views in 2021, which are well reported in the media, in relation to COVID. I’m going to leave it there lest I embarrass that member with a number of quotes that he has in relation to vaccinations and mandates.
explanation: An insinuating personal attack on a member's past views with a threat to 'embarrass' him, rather than engaging his argument.

text: When National’s answer to every fiscal challenge has been the same—and that’s been to sell off or to hand stuff overseas or to keep cutting public services, while at the same time investing in other parts of the economy like property speculation, those are the types of choices as to why they’re so unpopular and so out of touch with everyday New Zealanders.
explanation: Caricatures the opponent's position ('answer to every fiscal challenge has been the same') and impugns motives ('property speculation').

text: I do want to acknowledge the Finance and Expenditure Committee's work on this. We had very constructive discussions around whether some of the measures went far enough... I do want to also acknowledge the 275 individuals and groups who submitted on this bill.
explanation: Constructive, acknowledges cross-party committee work and public submitters with respect.

text: When we have a higher tax rate, and also particularly when we’re punishing those who cannot already afford it in a cost of living crisis, plus not expanding the scope of the tax base, we wonder why we are in this fiscal black hole that we are seeing right now.
explanation: Critique aimed at policy settings rather than individuals, though 'punishing those who cannot afford it' is emotive.

text: I think in cross referencing with Part 3 of Schedule 2 of the Public Service Act, the specificity of a singular servicing department is understandable.
explanation: Acknowledges and accepts the Minister's reasoning, constructive and respectful.

text: can I just check, as a starting question, that replacing “registered market” with “licensed market” which has two separate meanings, is something that is quid pro quo, as in it’s a one-to-one transition from “registered market” into “licensed market” and as in those two are essentially referring to the same thing and it is simply an update to the primary Act?
explanation: A clarifying, good-faith question seeking to understand the change; entirely substance-focused.

text: I always find the committee of the whole House stage with the particular Minister in the chair to be extremely enjoyable and engaging.
explanation: Warm, respectful tone toward the Minister.

text: I have never seen this second paragraph, "(b) is not to be drafted by the PCO under section 67(1)(d)(i) of that Act." Is there a reason? I'm genuinely curious. How prevalent is something like that, and is there a reason why it is specified explicitly that it cannot be drafted by the Parliamentary Counsel Office?
explanation: Genuinely inquisitive, non-adversarial questioning.

text: When National’s answer to every fiscal challenge has been the same—and that’s been to sell off or to hand stuff overseas or to keep cutting public services, while at the same time investing in other parts of the economy like property speculation, those are the types of choices as to why they’re so unpopular and so out of touch with everyday New Zealanders.
explanation: Relies on a strawman generalisation rather than evidenced analysis.

text: Until you give our young people a reason to stay here, they will be on the next plane, even with the fuel charge, off to Australia, where they can feel they can get their first home, where they can get a job that pays them well, and where they can access the healthcare that they need.
explanation: Leans on emotional/rhetorical appeal about young people fleeing; a plausible point but no data offered, framed as a near-certainty.

text: it still doesn’t make sense as to why you would keep this in there, because it’s superfluous legislation given that it’s quite clear there’s no intention for there to be an interdepartmental venture, unless, Minister, there is going to be a new interdepartmental venture.
explanation: Reasoned argument that the provision is redundant given no interdepartmental venture is intended, with a conditional caveat; logical but rests on an assumption about intent rather than cited evidence.

text: The fiscal cost of this is so small. Therefore, it points to the fact that this is not a significant change. We're not going to get much more. It's not going to incentivise those really highly skilled, capable new immigrants to New Zealand or expatriates back to New Zealand.
explanation: Reasons from the low fiscal cost to the conclusion that the measure is marginal — a sound evidence-to-conclusion chain.

text: the New Zealand Law Society suggested there should be proportionality or necessity tests as part of this... there is no mandatory privacy impact assessments, there's short review cycles for these agreements, there's no requirement for independent audits, and stronger transparency was needed.
explanation: Grounds the objection in authoritative submissions (Law Society, Privacy Commissioner) with specific deficiencies.

text: When we have a higher tax rate, and also particularly when we’re punishing those who cannot already afford it in a cost of living crisis, plus not expanding the scope of the tax base, we wonder why we are in this fiscal black hole that we are seeing right now.
explanation: Rhetorically implies the bill's approach causes the 'fiscal black hole' but asserts the causal link rather than demonstrating it; loaded framing ('punishing').

text: those who are uber-wealthy in Aotearoa New Zealand pay half the effective tax rate of a nurse.
explanation: Uses a comparative statistic to support the case for broadening the tax base; the conclusion follows, though the figure is presented without its source or caveats.

text: while this has been in place since the 1990s, that was at a time when PCO may not have had the capacity to do some of the drafting, which is not necessarily the case nowadays.
explanation: Argues the historical rationale for IRD self-drafting no longer holds given PCO capacity — evidence-based reasoning.

text: can I just check, as a starting question, that replacing “registered market” with “licensed market” which has two separate meanings, is something that is quid pro quo, as in it’s a one-to-one transition from “registered market” into “licensed market” and as in those two are essentially referring to the same thing and it is simply an update to the primary Act?
explanation: Carefully distinguishes whether the change is a like-for-like definitional update versus a substantive shift, testing the premise before accepting it.

text: if you’re looking at the subheading, am I correct to assume that it can’t incur expenses that’re not within the appropriation, but in clause 6(1A) it seems to imply that it can’t occur expenses that it already has authorised.
explanation: Closely parses the apparent tension between the cross-heading and clause 6(1A), laying out the two readings to identify an ambiguity; disciplined textual reasoning.

text: Get a hearing aid!
explanation: A dismissive personal jab at another member during debate, not engagement with substance.

text: That is to make sure you suppress Māori voters, and that is to make sure that Māori are not deciding who the next Prime Minister is come 7 November
explanation: Accuses the government of deliberately suppressing voters — an attack on motive rather than the policy merits.

text: How can Aotearoa trust that this Government will stick to their word and keep Aotearoa out of this invasion when it was the National Party who advocated for New Zealand to support the invasion of Iraq in 2003?
explanation: Challenging but directed at the party's record and policy, not a personal attack.

text: This is hypocrisy. I didn't call anybody a hypocrite, Mr Speaker, but this is hypocrisy.
explanation: Charges the government with hypocrisy while pointedly avoiding naming an individual — accusatory but procedurally careful.

text: This bill enacts changes with prospective and retrospective effect. This is not standard, and we acknowledge that.
explanation: Openly acknowledges an unusual aspect rather than glossing over it — straightforward and respectful of the House.

text: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
explanation: Disagrees respectfully and defers a broader discussion to 'another day'.

text: I would like to thank Labour and Willie Jackson for his collegiality on this bill.
explanation: Gracious, respectful recognition of an opponent's constructive role.

text: I'll have to think about the interaction between the powerful Regulations Review Committee and the Parliamentary Counsel Office's editorial ability—editorial change ability... I can't exactly comment on that at the moment, but I will get some advice from officials.
explanation: Respectful, no attacks; acknowledges others' expertise.

text: Look, I think the member raises a couple of really good points.
explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the substance of Xu-Nan's questions.

text: That is to make sure you suppress Māori voters, and that is to make sure that Māori are not deciding who the next Prime Minister is come 7 November
explanation: Asserts the boundary/census changes are intended to suppress Māori voters; this imputed intent is contested and unsupported by the bill's stated purpose.

text: We can't even send anybody over there; we've got a naval frigate underneath the ocean at the moment in the Pacific that needs to be dealt with.
explanation: Refers to the NZ navy vessel lost in the Pacific (HMNZS Manawanui) — substantially accurate.

text: Those of you that would have read The Lancet scientific journal would know that it reported that USA sanctions on other countries between 1971 and 2021 have murdered over 38 million people.
explanation: Misrepresents the source; the 38-million figure is a loose, heavily-derived estimate, and 'murdered' overstates the causal claim.

text: Over 1,500 people have been killed by the USA in Israel's illegal bombing campaign on Iran and almost 20,000 have been injured.
explanation: Precise casualty figures cited as fact in an active conflict; not independently verifiable and contestable.

text: We all know that this illegal invasion has directly led to fuel prices reaching over $4 in some parts of Aotearoa, yet the Prime Minister has refused to condemn the aggressors in this conflict.
explanation: Fuel price spikes are plausible given the Strait disruption, but 'directly led' is a simplified single-cause attribution.

text: National’s answers are property speculation. They are to sell off our assets; to look at overseas investments; and also mentioned is to promise roads that aren’t funded and don’t have a source of income; and offer things like $2.9 billion of tax cuts and additional millions of dollars for tobacco companies.
explanation: Mix of contestable framing; ‘millions for tobacco companies’ references the smokefree repeal but is presented in a misleading light.

text: Is it a sign of growth when 17,000 people attend a jobs fair in Auckland, when only 100 employers were looking for workers?
explanation: Embedded figures (17,000 attendees vs 100 employers) used to dramatise the imbalance; the ratio framing may strip context.

text: It also extends the deadline for the commission to report and publish the names and boundaries of electoral districts by four months for the first periodic division after commencement—from the 12 months to eight months before the parliamentary term expires.
explanation: A detailed, falsifiable description of the bill's deadline change.

text: The New Zealand Superannuation Fund is another excellent investment that we see. Sadly, it was paused under a previous National Government—they paused those Government contributions—and they were restarted again by the previous Labour Government.
explanation: Accurate: National suspended Super Fund contributions (2009) and Labour resumed them (2017).

text: Both of those are reserved for provisions that require a 75 percent majority of all members in this House to pass.
explanation: Accurate statement of the entrenched-provision threshold in the Electoral Act.

text: to welcome the 4,100 constituents that are moving from the Upper Harbour electorate to the great electorate of Northcote: welcome. I have doorknocked every street in that new part, and I can confirm it’s very diverse and very supportive of the current coalition Government.
explanation: The self-serving claim that the new area is 'very supportive of the current coalition Government' is an unverifiable partisan assertion.

text: the inflation expectations in this document are wildly different to the inflation expectations that New Zealand faces today because of external events—nothing to do with this Government.
explanation: Largely fair that external events shifted expectations, though the categorical disclaimer of any government role is overstated.

text: I certainly wish to acknowledge the $373 million package that the finance Minister announced this week to reach those really struggling low and middle income New Zealanders—about 140,000
explanation: Figures consistent with other speakers' references to the same package, though his '140,000' differs slightly from '143,000'.

text: It is second highest, as a net proportion of the economy, in New Zealand’s history. The first highest was in the 1990s under the previous National Government of that time. It grew 2.5 times under the previous Labour Government—2.5 times that debt increase.
explanation: Acknowledges the 1990s National peak and gives a quantified Labour-era increase; broadly consistent with the COVID debt surge, though ‘2.5x’ needs the baseline specified.

text: Don’t believe we’re going to get there? Well, Japan’s debt is 230 percent of gross domestic product.
explanation: Japan’s gross government debt-to-GDP is indeed around 230–250 percent.

text: I have done a bit of work in the past on the Incorporated Societies Act when that came into force. From memory, that's the Incorporated Societies Act 2020, and I think there was sort of a fallback provision of being five years or six years after Royal assent for some of those provisions.
explanation: Offers a precedent from memory with explicit hedging; the cited statute's year and detail are uncertain (the Incorporated Societies Act was 2022), but he flags he has to check.

text: This bill enacts changes with prospective and retrospective effect. This is not standard, and we acknowledge that.
explanation: Candidly and accurately states that the bill has retrospective effect, a real and unusual feature.

text: in October 2025, the High Court found that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) was operating outside of existing legislative authority when reassessing a person’s entitlement to supplementary assistance after they receive a backdated ACC payment for a past period.
explanation: A specific, checkable account of a High Court finding presented to justify the bill.

text: my instinct would be that the legal status of any secondary legislation or, in fact, legislation, would be that the Order in Council or the regulation which is signed off by the Minister or the Governor-General is the one that is the final version and has legal force
explanation: Accurate description of how Orders in Council and Royal assent confer legal force.

text: It is the case that if a piece of secondary legislation is needing to be published, which provides a consolidation of all secondary legislation that incorporates all of the amendments made by every amending instrument—if it doesn't meet the requirements of publication, it is all repealed. So I have to correct that: it is all repealed.
explanation: Openly corrects his own earlier explanation rather than letting the error stand.

text: That is to make sure you suppress Māori voters, and that is to make sure that Māori are not deciding who the next Prime Minister is come 7 November
explanation: Claims a hidden coordinated 'agenda' across bills with no evidence offered — bare assertion of motive.

text: How can Aotearoa trust that this Government will stick to their word and keep Aotearoa out of this invasion when it was the National Party who advocated for New Zealand to support the invasion of Iraq in 2003?
explanation: Argues distrust by reference to a 2003 position; a guilt-by-history inference rather than evidence about current intentions.

text: Those of you that would have read The Lancet scientific journal would know that it reported that USA sanctions on other countries between 1971 and 2021 have murdered over 38 million people.
explanation: Appeals to the authority of a journal but the cited statistic is contested and the causal link asserted, not shown.

text: This particular letter reminds me of a rugby game. You get punched in the face, and then you retaliate. Who gets the yellow card? The guy who retaliated.
explanation: Relies on a rugby analogy that simplifies the conflict's causation rather than arguing from evidence.

text: Where is the consistency from this Government? You cannot condemn one without the other.
explanation: A coherent consistency argument: condemning one set of attacks but not the other is logically inconsistent.

text: When we think about new people moving boundaries, moving electorates, needing to understand what electorate they are part of, and connecting with it, having two terms in an electorate before there’s another boundary change and anything there happens makes sense.
explanation: Gives a reasoned rationale (voters need time to understand and connect with a new electorate) that supports the two-term interval, though no evidence is cited.

text: it couldn’t get any more vivid as a picture to be cancelling a national resilience fund and handing out buckets of KFC. I mean, how short term can you get it?
explanation: Rhetorical ridicule and juxtaposition stand in for an argument; no evidence linking the two.

text: The reality is that National has no plan, and that’s why they’re just yelling a lot, because they think that if they yell a lot, New Zealanders won’t notice that they absolutely have no plan at all.
explanation: Strawman/assertion—the government had just laid out a debt-reduction approach, so ‘no plan at all’ ignores the substance.

text: National’s answers are property speculation. They are to sell off our assets; to look at overseas investments; and also mentioned is to promise roads that aren’t funded and don’t have a source of income; and offer things like $2.9 billion of tax cuts and additional millions of dollars for tobacco companies.
explanation: Cites a specific figure ($2.9b) but strings claims together as a caricature of National’s plan without substantiation.

text: Are wages keeping up, when Radio New Zealand reported that 70 percent of workers received a pay rise that failed to keep up with inflation last year?
explanation: Grounds the challenge in a reported figure.

text: it means that representation reviews, when they occur, and various dates associated with them will be set at regular and predictable interval periods—and that’s really important—rather than depending on where a five-year census is and where the three-year electoral cycle is.
explanation: Clear logical case for aligning the cycles: predictable intervals beat dates that float on the mismatch between a five-year census and three-year electoral cycle.

text: The purpose of this bill is to align the policy setting in the Electoral Act with the Government’s work to modernise the census... It makes the logical link between the boundary reviews and the electoral cycle.
explanation: States a coherent purpose and the logical link being made, but the reasoning is brief and assertive rather than evidenced.

text: despite escalating costs, we have been getting data that is getting poorer and poorer.
explanation: States a plausible problem (rising cost, falling quality) as the rationale for change, but offers it as assertion without supporting data.

text: to welcome the 4,100 constituents that are moving from the Upper Harbour electorate to the great electorate of Northcote: welcome. I have doorknocked every street in that new part, and I can confirm it’s very diverse and very supportive of the current coalition Government.
explanation: Infers broad constituent support from his own doorknocking — an appeal to personal anecdote rather than data.

text: the inflation expectations in this document are wildly different to the inflation expectations that New Zealand faces today because of external events—nothing to do with this Government.
explanation: Reasonable point that the BPS predates the shock, but 'nothing to do with this Government' is an absolute that overclaims.

text: The current situation, as interpreted by the courts, is those who receive lump-sum payments are treated more generously than the former, which are those on ACC and welfare. So the Government has a duty to fix this.
explanation: States a fairness-between-cohorts argument, but doesn't engage the rebuttal that the comparison is itself disputed.

text: The quality of the debt is also important: about infrastructure, economic growth, things that power our economy out, not pet projects like the other side did when they were in Government.
explanation: Sound point on debt quality, but the contrast rests on the unsupported ‘pet projects’ label.

text: It is second highest, as a net proportion of the economy, in New Zealand’s history. The first highest was in the 1990s under the previous National Government of that time. It grew 2.5 times under the previous Labour Government—2.5 times that debt increase.
explanation: Notably balanced—names his own party’s 1990s record as the historic peak—supporting the claim with proportion-of-GDP framing rather than nominal alone.

text: all Māori will start to migrate on to that Māori roll and they will be making the decisions come 7 November
explanation: Prediction tied to the 7 November election that ALL Māori will move to the Māori roll and prove decisive; the sweeping magnitude makes it implausible.

text: I’d like to take the opportunity to welcome the 5,200-odd voters that will be joining the wonderful Whanganui electorate at this year’s election.
explanation: Warm, inclusive welcome to incoming constituents, non-partisan in tone.

text: I just want to take the opportunity to acknowledge the trainers, the industry players, and, particularly, those from Whanganui who are affected by the closure of this industry.
explanation: Empathetic acknowledgement of those harmed by the policy, including his own constituents—inclusive in tone.

text: to welcome the 4,100 constituents that are moving from the Upper Harbour electorate to the great electorate of Northcote: welcome. I have doorknocked every street in that new part, and I can confirm it’s very diverse and very supportive of the current coalition Government.
explanation: Warm welcome to constituents, but blends into a partisan boast that appeals to his own side.

text: the better way to look at what the intention of Parliament is when it passes a statute is to look at the words in the purpose in the context of the statute.
explanation: Engaging, candid framing ('lengthy ramblings of a junior Minister') that brings the committee along.

text: I'll have to think about the interaction between the powerful Regulations Review Committee and the Parliamentary Counsel Office's editorial ability—editorial change ability... I can't exactly comment on that at the moment, but I will get some advice from officials.
explanation: Self-deprecating ('more experienced and cleverer people than I'), disarming and humble.

text: Despite my intense passion and love of that particular piece of legislation, I haven't yet committed them all to memory, so I'll take a chance to look it up.
explanation: Self-deprecating humour that keeps the technical debate light and collegial.

text: Look, I think the member raises a couple of really good points.
explanation: Generously credits an opposition member's argument, fostering cross-party goodwill.

text: I would like to thank Labour and Willie Jackson for his collegiality on this bill.
explanation: Reaches across the aisle to acknowledge an opposition member's cooperation, building goodwill.

text: I’d like to take the opportunity to welcome the 5,200-odd voters that will be joining the wonderful Whanganui electorate at this year’s election.
explanation: Names a concrete figure (5,200 voters) and the affected electorate.

text: I want to acknowledge those that were involved in building the straight track at the Wanganui Racecourse for its positive impact on the health of greyhounds since that has been opened.
explanation: Names a concrete facility (the straight track at the Wanganui Racecourse) and its claimed effect, though without measures.

text: Under this Government, debt is higher than Treasury has predicted, prices are rising, and productivity has stalled.
explanation: Names three concrete metrics but gives no figures or magnitudes.

text: it means that representation reviews, when they occur, and various dates associated with them will be set at regular and predictable interval periods—and that’s really important—rather than depending on where a five-year census is and where the three-year electoral cycle is.
