explanation: References the concrete five-year census and three-year electoral cycles and the mechanism of alignment.

text: Are wages keeping up, when Radio New Zealand reported that 70 percent of workers received a pay rise that failed to keep up with inflation last year?
explanation: Cites a sourced statistic (70%, RNZ) to frame the question.

text: This bill also replaces the definition of “counting day” with “reference date”, which defaults to 30 June of each year.
explanation: Names the exact definitional change and a precise default date (30 June).

text: It also extends the deadline for the commission to report and publish the names and boundaries of electoral districts by four months for the first periodic division after commencement—from the 12 months to eight months before the parliamentary term expires.
explanation: Precise figures and mechanism: a four-month extension, from 12 to 8 months before term expiry, for the first division.

text: The purpose of this bill is to align the policy setting in the Electoral Act with the Government’s work to modernise the census... It makes the logical link between the boundary reviews and the electoral cycle.
explanation: Identifies the alignment goal but stays at a high level with little concrete detail.

text: despite escalating costs, we have been getting data that is getting poorer and poorer.
explanation: Asserts a cost/quality trend for the census but gives no figures or evidence.

text: We're mandating health targets that ensure focus remains on what matters: reducing emergency wait times, improving cancer management, increasing childhood immunisations—that all went backwards under their Government.
explanation: Names the three target areas but gives no figures or mechanism.

text: This is a good bill. I commend it to the House.
explanation: A routine endorsement that commits to no detail, figure, or reasoning.

text: This bill benefits non-residents that seek to work in New Zealand; it has huge benefits for Kiwis that have foreign investment income—Kiwis returning from America or other countries, but, also, many American Kiwis, as well, that are here; and it makes a whole range of other changes designed to improve tax administration.
explanation: Identifies who benefits but in general terms ('huge benefits', 'a whole range of other changes') with no figures or mechanisms.

text: I say this because New Zealand has near on $200 billion of nominal debt and that has an interest attachment to that... Over the last few weeks that risk premium has gone up and we should expect it is going to make a difference to the Budget that is going to be announced in May.
explanation: Gives a debt figure and a concrete near-term consequence for the May Budget.

text: I certainly wish to acknowledge the $373 million package that the finance Minister announced this week to reach those really struggling low and middle income New Zealanders—about 140,000
explanation: Names the package amount and approximate number of recipients.

text: Let’s turn to the interest on that debt. It is currently about $8.4 billion in this financial year. That goes up to $13 billion by the forecast period.
explanation: Specific current and forecast dollar figures.

text: we have seen a more than doubling of compliance infringement notices, and any non-compliance will be addressed
explanation: Specific claim of more than doubling infringement notices; plausible but unverifiable from the text and no baseline given.

text: We have been asking Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon every week for two years to show us the numbers of people who have received $250. Do they answer? No, because the answer is zero. It is yet another broken promise.
explanation: Asserts zero recipients of a promised $250; the rhetorical 'zero' is likely an overstatement of a contested delivery record.

text: They don’t want to talk about the fact that the minimum wage has not kept up with the cost of living.
explanation: Plausible claim about minimum wage lagging cost of living, directionally supportable but unquantified.

text: How can he expect to house the growing number of homeless when the pipeline of houses contracted or under construction has dropped from 8,863 in 2023 to just 1,513 today, a drop of 83 percent in just two years?
explanation: Specific figures asserted in a question; plausible and checkable but not confirmed in the text.

text: The numbers tell the story: 235 education workers, 240 police, 850 defence staff.
explanation: Specific official-sounding figures, plausible but not independently verified here.

text: In 2024, a Federated Farmers survey said that about 73 percent of dairy farmers, 66 percent of sheep and beef, and 51 percent of arable had farm workers who lived on their farm.
explanation: Attributed survey statistics; plausible and sourced, though unverified in text.

text: the promise of this Government to help the squeezed middle has been an absolute lie
explanation: Characterises an opponent's promise as an 'absolute lie' — hyperbolic framing of a contested outcome.

text: At a time when we know the number one issue in Aotearoa is the cost of living, this Government is choosing to retrospectively burden people.
explanation: Cost of living being a top public concern is broadly supportable; 'number one' is an assertion.

text: Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori Health Authority, gone; cuts to Māori housing; cuts to Māori trade training budgets; cuts to Māori education programmes; cuts to Māori economic development programmes; removal of references to Te Tiriti o Waitangi; Progressive Procurement, which contributed $900 million to Māori business and the Māori economy, and therefore New Zealand, gone.
explanation: The disestablishments are accurate; the $900 million attributed to Progressive Procurement is a specific claim that is harder to verify.

text: The Māori economy grew from $69 billion in 2018 to $126 billion in 2023.
explanation: Specific figures broadly consistent with published Māori economy asset-base estimates.

text: We've seen the U-turn on size limits; that's excellent, but there's still work to go.
explanation: Factually accurate — the Government did reverse course on minimum size limits (the PM asked the amendments removing them be dropped), as confirmed elsewhere in the debate.

text: there are actually, prospectively, 3,300 people who are going to be losing their jobs because of the trajectory of oil and gas demise in our province
explanation: A forward projection presented as near-fact; magnitude is contestable.

text: when that policy was announced in 2018, no officials and no industry knew anything about it
explanation: Claim that no officials or industry were consulted on the 2018 oil/gas decision — directionally argued but an absolute that's hard to confirm.

text: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it's got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
explanation: 'Fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding' is a contested characterisation; Labour argues out-years were transparently unfunded by design, so the claim is partial.

text: Take the Green Steel project... they expect it will create about 200 skilled jobs in the region. Arataki, the new housing development in Hawke's Bay—200 new residential allotments—estimates it will create over 630 jobs over the five-year development period during construction.
explanation: Presented as applicant estimates, appropriately hedged but unverified.

text: the capacity that will be unlocked as a result of this will be, roughly, around 1.6 million homes. That is a substantial advance on the status quo, which is in the Auckland Unitary Plan—which hasn't been updated for years—which is around 1.2 million homes.
explanation: The 1.6m figure (once CRL upzoning and NPS-UD are counted) is defensible and matches the RIS headline, but it sits beside the bill's binding minimum dropping to 1.4m, which critics show on the same day.

text: New Zealand currently has over 1,800 public charge points. Combined with the investment we announced yesterday, the national total will be around 4,500. We’re well on our way to the target of 10,000 by 2030.
explanation: Charger-count figures are specific and plausible; presented as current data.

text: It is true, almost objectively, that rents in Auckland are lower now than they would otherwise have been as a result of the upzoning—Auckland rents are lower than they otherwise would be.
explanation: Peer-reviewed studies of the Auckland Unitary Plan do find upzoning lowered rents relative to the counterfactual; broadly supported, though 'almost objectively' overstates certainty.

text: Parliament, last year, passed time of use pricing legislation unanimously, and I was really pleased by that, and I was really pleased to engage with the Opposition around finding a framework that we can all accept.
explanation: Concrete, checkable claim about unanimous passage of time-of-use legislation.

text: I wish to correct a statement that I made during the second reading of the Anzac commemoration bill.
explanation: Proactively fixing an inaccurate earlier claim improves the truthfulness of the record.

text: you could see in the 1990s and late early 2000s there was actually a measurable impact and dip in life expectancy because of those [benefit cuts].
explanation: Attributes a life-expectancy dip directly to 1990s welfare reform; NZ life expectancy actually rose steadily through the period, so a causal dip is overstated/unsupported.

text: When we came into Government, it was clear that the culture that had been inculcated through the Government Public Service was profligate, it was irresponsible, and it wasn’t even putting in basic, fundamental, profit-and-loss, balance-sheet sort of stuff that I’d expect as a governor.
explanation: Broad unsupported claim that the whole Public Service lacked basic financial management; overgeneralised and not evidenced.

text: It’s a project that nobody asked for and nobody wants in Wellington.
explanation: Absolute 'nobody' is hyperbole — some support exists for the project.

text: I’ve fought against those same powerbrokers—those same old powerbrokers that live in the leafy suburbs—and guess what! I won my seat, over and over again, actually, with historic margins on that
explanation: She won Wellington Central, but “over and over again… with historic margins” overstates a relatively short electoral history.

text: Wellington Hospital goes into code red on average twice a day. That means there is not enough staff to look after the people coming to the waiting room.
explanation: Specific frequency claim about code-red status; plausible but unverified here.

text: There is no consensus in the planning world as to what character actually refers to, but there is a whole lot of literature that argues that character is a way of protecting the status quo and making sure that people of the same economic class, the same race, and the same background remain
explanation: Broadly reflects critiques in urban-planning scholarship of 'character' protections, stated without specifics.

text: Auckland is a city where 8,000 families are waiting for a public home.
explanation: A concrete, checkable figure consistent with public-housing waitlist data for Auckland.

text: We spend a greater share of our GDP on infrastructure than many compatible countries, but we achieve less.
explanation: Aligns with the report's finding on spend-vs-outcomes; broadly supportable.

text: This is why we decided to make a change in this bill to reduce the minimum housing capacity in plan change 120 from 2 million homes to 1.4 million. This is a more realistic approach, focusing growth in the city centre, around town centres, and along major transport routes.
explanation: Accurately states the bill's change; 'more realistic' is the contested editorial framing.

text: Nicola Willis tells people it’s bad luck, basically, if they lose their job—“Oh, well.”
explanation: Presented as a factual characterisation of Willis's view but is an unsupported, hostile paraphrase likely to mislead.

text: When you actually drill down to what the Treasury projections were, it's 1 percent growth. That is what is meant to be feeding New Zealanders' hope.
explanation: Attributes a specific magnitude to Treasury projections — credible but unverifiable from the text.

text: The regulatory impact statement shows that the only consultation undertaken in respect of this measure was with the Privacy Commissioner, and one of the concerns that we had that was that there needed to be a broader look taken at this.
explanation: Specific, checkable claim citing the regulatory impact statement about the scope of consultation; plausible and concrete.

text: the wellbeing approach to budgeting, for us looking at something broader than just the simple traditional economic measures, was work that had begun when Bill English was the Minister of Finance. This is the work that Treasury had begun as far back as 2011
explanation: Accurate that Treasury's Living Standards Framework originated under Bill English's tenure around 2011.

text: In the 2024 International Monetary Fund (IMF) report on the New Zealand economy, one of the things they talk about is that to achieve objectives, reform could combine comprehensive capital gains, land value tax, and changes to corporate income tax.
explanation: Accurately paraphrases the IMF's 2024 Article IV recommendations, which Russell later quotes verbatim.

text: there’s nothing to show for it but just unprecedented Government debt and a huge $8.9 billion interest bill, and growing. No bridges, no roads, no busways, no new hospitals—nothing.
explanation: 'No bridges, no roads, no busways, no new hospitals—nothing' is hyperbole that ignores any infrastructure delivered in the period.

text: Thirty billion dollars of the $60 billion-plus was spent on non-core COVID spending—that is what these reports reveal... and it’s absolutely disgusting.
explanation: The 'non-core' split is a contested characterisation of categorised pandemic spending.

text: this comes on top of yesterday's announcement of another 2,500 electric vehicle chargers up and down the country. It comes on top of our liquefied natural gas facility in New Plymouth to ensure electricity security into the future.
explanation: Cites a specific charger figure and an LNG facility; the charger figure is verifiable, though 'announcement' status is doing work.

text: what they’ve outlaid is nearly 12,000 projects that are at a value of $275 billion, with most of those projects unfunded.
explanation: Concrete figures attributed to the report; checkable and presented straightforwardly.

text: This bill, of course, locks in the Government's decision this week to reduce the minimum housing capacity required by Plan Change 120 from 2 million to 1.4 million.
explanation: Accurate description of what the bill does, consistent with the bill text and other speakers.

text: If you lose the Waikare Gorge, which we did, the time it takes to get to Wairoa from Napier is 10 hours, as opposed to one and a half.
explanation: Concrete travel-time contrast; plausible given Cyclone Gabrielle disruption, presented as fact.

text: I was very much there in 2017, when we talked about, as the last National Government, the Hawke’s Bay Expressway. It was almost all but there. Then what happened? We didn’t get in to Government that time. It got cancelled, and there goes another six years of that project.
explanation: Account of the Expressway being shelved after 2017; broadly plausible but a partisan framing of the project's history.

text: we have seen a more than doubling of compliance infringement notices, and any non-compliance will be addressed
explanation: Gives a direction ('more than doubling') but no absolute figures or timeframe.

text: We have been asking Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon every week for two years to show us the numbers of people who have received $250. Do they answer? No, because the answer is zero. It is yet another broken promise.
explanation: Names the figure ($250), the people, and a two-year timeframe.

text: They don’t want to talk about the fact that the minimum wage has not kept up with the cost of living.
explanation: General assertion with no figures or period.

text: How can he expect to house the growing number of homeless when the pipeline of houses contracted or under construction has dropped from 8,863 in 2023 to just 1,513 today, a drop of 83 percent in just two years?
explanation: Precise figures: pipeline from 8,863 to 1,513, an 83% drop over two years.

text: The numbers tell the story: 235 education workers, 240 police, 850 defence staff.
explanation: Precise counts for each affected group.

text: In 2024, a Federated Farmers survey said that about 73 percent of dairy farmers, 66 percent of sheep and beef, and 51 percent of arable had farm workers who lived on their farm.
explanation: Named source, year, and three percentage figures.

text: So I talked about this when I was campaigning in 2023. I put a member’s bill in the ballot in 2024: the KiwiSaver (First Home for Farmland and Service Tenancy Tenants) Amendment Bill.
explanation: Names dates and the exact bill title.

text: the bill will pass its first reading, but be assured that our position is crystal clear; we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits.
explanation: Names the concrete action — removing the minimum-size-limit sections — though not the mechanism or timing.

text: National backs recreational fishers, and I'm proud to say I'm one of them.
explanation: Slogan-like affirmation with no policy detail, mechanism, or measure.

text: Labour is ready with a plan and ready to work with hapū, iwi, and whānau Māori.
explanation: States readiness and a 'plan' but gives no content of it.

text: No matter how simple the compliance—“simple” the compliance—is, it still falls on volunteer labour—someone who’s simply the person in the whānau who’s good at numbers or good at words, and all the compliance falls on them, while also trying to manage their full-time job.
explanation: Concrete scenario of who does the work, but no figures, counts, or named policy detail.

text: In Wairoa, we know it was hammered by Cyclone Gabrielle... Since then, there has been zero aged-care in Te Wairoa.
explanation: Names the place and a concrete deficit (aged care).

text: One billion dollars of targeted Māori funding was cut—that is what responsible budgeting looks like under this National-led Government.
explanation: Gives a total figure, though the build-up of the number is not itemised to it.

text: The Māori economy grew from $69 billion in 2018 to $126 billion in 2023.
explanation: Exact dollar figures with years.

text: there are actually, prospectively, 3,300 people who are going to be losing their jobs because of the trajectory of oil and gas demise in our province
explanation: Names a precise number of jobs.

text: If you think about a truck that’s on the road with an “H” on it, they can carry about 35 tonnes on it, so one shipment is 1,000 trucks to get it there—down to Huntly—for it.
explanation: Concrete tonnages and counts.

text: These amendments here, there are a lot of technical amendments, but there are a lot of improvements in gaining greater transparency, improving the fiscal responsibility, and improving the practical outcomes of the Act itself.
explanation: Lists aims (transparency, fiscal responsibility, outcomes) but no concrete detail of what the amendments do.

text: We’re very proud of the changes we’ve made with Pharmac and actually changing that organisation to make sure it’s delivering for New Zealanders who need important medicines.
explanation: References changes generally without naming the specific reforms or drugs in this line.

text: New Zealanders deserve treatments not based on identity or politics or what box they have to tick.
explanation: Values statement with no mechanism or measure.

text: The second harbour crossing in Auckland is going to be a project that’s required at some point in the future... That will be the biggest infrastructure project ever built in New Zealand history by any order of magnitude.
explanation: Deliberately avoids a cost/date ('I'm not going to put a number on it').

text: the capacity that will be unlocked as a result of this will be, roughly, around 1.6 million homes. That is a substantial advance on the status quo, which is in the Auckland Unitary Plan—which hasn't been updated for years—which is around 1.2 million homes.
explanation: Gives concrete capacity figures and the comparison baseline.

text: Take the Green Steel project... they expect it will create about 200 skilled jobs in the region. Arataki, the new housing development in Hawke's Bay—200 new residential allotments—estimates it will create over 630 jobs over the five-year development period during construction.
explanation: Names projects with quantified jobs and allotments.

text: Yesterday, the Minister of Finance and the Minister for Energy and I announced the number of electric vehicle public chargers will more than double thanks to $52.7 million in zero-interest loans from ChargeNet and Meridian. Half the chargers will be spread across Auckland, Hamilton, Tauranga, Wellington, Christchurch, and Dunedin—
explanation: Names the exact funding ($52.7m zero-interest loans), the providers (ChargeNet, Meridian), and the cities.

text: On average, it's taking 128 working days for decisions on substantive applications from when officials determine an application is complete and in scope... Green Steel... said it would have taken a minimum of six years to take the project through the Resource Management Act (RMA) consenting process; under fast track, just seven months. Kings Quarry said that using fast track instead of the RMA saved them three years in consenting time. Their project was approved in just over six months.
explanation: Concrete timeframes (128 days, six years vs seven months, three years saved).

text: Auckland is a city where hundreds of Kāinga Ora public homes have been delayed or cancelled as a result of this Government.
explanation: Rough magnitude only (“hundreds”), no exact figure or location.

text: zoning is actually about sending a signal to the market that this is the kind of growth that we are planning for.
explanation: Explains a mechanism but in general terms without figures or named instruments.

text: Auckland is a city where 8,000 families are waiting for a public home.
explanation: Names a specific number and location.

text: Wellington Hospital goes into code red on average twice a day. That means there is not enough staff to look after the people coming to the waiting room.
explanation: Gives a concrete rate ('twice a day') and explains the term.

text: bus fares in the Wellington region are set to go up by 3.1 percent from May this year. If you live in the west of Wellington, in Karori, or the east of Wellington, in Miramar, it’s going to cost you $5 per trip to get into the city centre.
explanation: Exact percentage, month, named suburbs, and per-trip cost.

text: The National Infrastructure Plan provides a 30-year road map to address these challenges, and it has four basic principles. One, plan what we can afford; second, look after what we’ve got; third, prioritise the right projects; and fourth, make it easier to build better.
explanation: Enumerates four named principles but they remain high-level directions without mechanisms or figures.

text: The Labour Party is completely out of touch.
explanation: Vague slogan; commits to nothing.

text: I've been working closely with the Balmoral Residents Association, and the residents are particularly concerned that enabling large-scale development, often without confirming the infrastructure capacity, could lead to isolated and out-of-scale development.
explanation: Names the residents' group and the concrete concern (development outpacing confirmed infrastructure).

text: This is why we decided to make a change in this bill to reduce the minimum housing capacity in plan change 120 from 2 million homes to 1.4 million. This is a more realistic approach, focusing growth in the city centre, around town centres, and along major transport routes.
explanation: Gives the figures and where growth is to be focused (city centre, town centres, transport routes).

text: For us, it is imperative that we do have a long-term plan, we do invest in our future, and we set up a reason for our young people to stay—not something we have seen from this Government.
explanation: Pure aspiration — 'long-term plan' and 'invest in our future' with no policy, figure, or mechanism.

text: In the 2024 International Monetary Fund (IMF) report on the New Zealand economy, one of the things they talk about is that to achieve objectives, reform could combine comprehensive capital gains, land value tax, and changes to corporate income tax.
explanation: Names the source and the three specific reform components, though without figures.

text: the wellbeing approach to budgeting, for us looking at something broader than just the simple traditional economic measures, was work that had begun when Bill English was the Minister of Finance. This is the work that Treasury had begun as far back as 2011
explanation: Names the originator (Bill English), the body (Treasury), and a date (2011).

text: the foreign investment funds rules are being changed so that, in some circumstances, New Zealand tax residents who own foreign shares will no longer be taxed on unrealised gains.
explanation: Precise description of a specific rule change and its effect (no tax on unrealised gains in some circumstances).

text: section 59BA of the Tax Administration Act is being repealed in its entirety through this bill. This means that trusts that earn income will be required to file income tax and to pay tax, but the extra information obtained by the application of section 59BA will no longer be collected.
explanation: Cites the exact statutory provision (s 59BA) and precisely states the consequence of its repeal.

text: It’s a great day in the reform of Auckland Transport. I commend the bill.
explanation: Celebratory endorsement with no substantive content.

text: We are legislating to make it harder to hide unfunded fiscal cliffs, and we remember them well... we remember having to find money for Pharmac, and we remember having to find money for the school lunch programme.
explanation: Names concrete examples (Pharmac, school lunch programme) of the time-limited funding the bill targets.

text: Thirty billion dollars of the $60 billion-plus was spent on non-core COVID spending—that is what these reports reveal... and it’s absolutely disgusting.
explanation: Attaches dollar figures ($30bn of $60bn+) to a claim about non-core spending.

text: as the cost of universal superannuation goes from about $25 billion to over $70 billion in the middle of this century.
explanation: Names concrete dollar figures and a timeframe (mid-century).

text: In 2007, a management company signed a 40-year deal, a leasehold with Ngāti Whātua. Council chipped in some money, the build was $94 million, and they’ve got it for 40 years. In 2047, that’ll be handed back to the ratepayers of Auckland for zero.
explanation: Dates, parties, build cost, term, and handback all specified.

text: If you lose the Waikare Gorge, which we did, the time it takes to get to Wairoa from Napier is 10 hours, as opposed to one and a half.
explanation: Gives exact before/after travel times.

text: we have seen a more than doubling of compliance infringement notices, and any non-compliance will be addressed
explanation: Points to concrete enforcement results (rising notices) rather than mere intent, though detail is thin.

text: So I talked about this when I was campaigning in 2023. I put a member’s bill in the ballot in 2024: the KiwiSaver (First Home for Farmland and Service Tenancy Tenants) Amendment Bill.
explanation: Carried the issue from campaign promise to a member's bill picked up as a Government bill — demonstrated follow-through.

text: the bill will pass its first reading, but be assured that our position is crystal clear; we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits.
explanation: Clear commitment to remove specific clauses, but delivery depends on the select committee process and is not yet enacted.

text: We’re very proud of the changes we’ve made with Pharmac and actually changing that organisation to make sure it’s delivering for New Zealanders who need important medicines.
explanation: Claims credit for delivered Pharmac changes/new fundings referenced earlier; partly substantiated but framed broadly.

text: Parliament, last year, passed time of use pricing legislation unanimously, and I was really pleased by that, and I was really pleased to engage with the Opposition around finding a framework that we can all accept.
explanation: Points to enacted legislation, not just intent.

text: On average, it's taking 128 working days for decisions on substantive applications from when officials determine an application is complete and in scope... Green Steel... said it would have taken a minimum of six years to take the project through the Resource Management Act (RMA) consenting process; under fast track, just seven months. Kings Quarry said that using fast track instead of the RMA saved them three years in consenting time. Their project was approved in just over six months.
explanation: Points to actual approvals delivered under the fast-track regime.

text: which Government has given the green light to the Waikare Gorge realignment? It’s ours.
explanation: Claims credit for greenlighting a concrete project; approval is action, though delivery is still pending.

text: the escalating tensions involving Iran place real pressure on global shipping lanes, on energy markets, on fuel prices, and on the trade routes that our exporters rely on
explanation: Forecasts pressure on shipping/energy/fuel from Iran tensions; directionally plausible but uncertain in scale and timeframe.

text: It notes that New Zealand faces ongoing risks from natural hazards, including a 75 percent chance that the Alpine Fault in the South Island will rupture in the next 50 years
explanation: A falsifiable prediction with a clear timeframe, backed by expert/scientific consensus.

text: Our goal is to avoid ever getting to response phase 3 or 4. These are envisaged in the National Fuel Plan as the point at which prioritisation of fuel would be required... But in direct answer to the member’s question, I would not expect us to be skipping through the response phases.
explanation: Predicts NZ will avoid phases 3/4 and not skip levels; plausible but contingent on fuel supply, provisional.

text: New Zealanders will go, “No, you’ve had your chance”, and they’ll give them the flick.
explanation: Predicts the Government loses the coming election; partisan and uncertain.

text: there are actually, prospectively, 3,300 people who are going to be losing their jobs because of the trajectory of oil and gas demise in our province
explanation: Forecasts 3,300 job losses; specific but an optimistic-of-doom projection with uncertain timing.

text: The second harbour crossing in Auckland is going to be a project that’s required at some point in the future... That will be the biggest infrastructure project ever built in New Zealand history by any order of magnitude.
explanation: Predicts the crossing will be required and will be the largest project ever; plausible but timing and superlative are uncertain.

text: New Zealand currently has over 1,800 public charge points. Combined with the investment we announced yesterday, the national total will be around 4,500. We’re well on our way to the target of 10,000 by 2030.
explanation: Predicts reaching 10,000 chargers by 2030; directionally plausible given the doubling but the trajectory to 10,000 is uncertain.

text: Take the Green Steel project... they expect it will create about 200 skilled jobs in the region. Arataki, the new housing development in Hawke's Bay—200 new residential allotments—estimates it will create over 630 jobs over the five-year development period during construction.
explanation: Forecasts of job creation ('expect ~200', 'over 630') over multi-year horizons — plausible but unproven.

text: bus fares in the Wellington region are set to go up by 3.1 percent from May this year. If you live in the west of Wellington, in Karori, or the east of Wellington, in Miramar, it’s going to cost you $5 per trip to get into the city centre.
explanation: Near-term scheduled fare rise; high confidence as it is an announced change.

text: long-term transport planning for our biggest city, Auckland, which of course will be 2 million people by 2033.
explanation: Population forecast (2 million by 2033); consistent with projections but inherently uncertain.

text: The Prime Minister is a dud, the finance Minister has no credibility, and they are lashing around for relevance.
explanation: Direct personal attacks on competence and character ('a dud', 'no credibility').

text: We have been asking Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon every week for two years to show us the numbers of people who have received $250. Do they answer? No, because the answer is zero. It is yet another broken promise.
explanation: Accountability attack on a policy promise rather than a personal insult.

text: She’s just shitty because she’s got nothing to complain about.
explanation: Crude personal jibe (the language Seymour later flagged as unparliamentary).

text: You’ve sat there and listened to Shane Jones lie to this House on repeated occasions. All I’m doing is pointing that out.
explanation: Direct accusation that a member is lying (unparliamentary); aimed at conduct on a contested factual matter rather than personal traits.

text: when you have just agreed with the point of order made by Chris Hipkins that the assertion that the previous Government closed Marsden Point is incorrect, and he then turns around and ignores that and says it anyway, we are going to express concern about that.
explanation: A measured procedural objection focused on accuracy, distinguishing legitimate political answers from false assertions.

text: If this guy opened a funeral parlour, nobody would die. He can screw up anything—
explanation: Pure personal mockery, no policy content.

text: Some people are so blinded by their hatred of Israel, and perhaps the type of people that live there, and their hatred of America that they can't see the moral dimension of this conflict.
explanation: Imputes bigotry and hatred to opponents — a strawman of their position rather than addressing it.

text: It’d be good if people took public policy more seriously, unlike this member behind me.
explanation: A personal jab at a colleague's seriousness rather than engagement with substance.

text: When the Opposition say, “Oh, we already had ferries arriving.”, maybe you did, but you didn’t know how to fit them through the channel that they had to pass through, you didn’t have the ports that they needed to load and unload, so you are pointing to a fantasy rather than a solution.
explanation: Dismissive 'fantasy' framing of opponents' position.

text: It’s not about Labour or National or ACT or the Greens; whoever’s in power is going to have to grapple with this for all New Zealand.
explanation: Lowers the temperature by removing partisan blame.

text: the promise of this Government to help the squeezed middle has been an absolute lie
explanation: 'Absolute lie' is an accusation of bad faith rather than substantive policy critique.

text: One billion dollars of targeted Māori funding was cut—that is what responsible budgeting looks like under this National-led Government.
explanation: Sarcastic framing of 'responsible budgeting' but tied to a substantive claim about cuts.

text: It appears that no real thought has gone into how a revised tax system can actually have material impact on Māori businesses, Māori-owned corporations, and Māori land trusts.
explanation: Criticises the design of the bill rather than any person, though 'no real thought' is a fairly sweeping dismissal of the work done.

text: We've seen the U-turn on size limits; that's excellent, but there's still work to go.
explanation: Credits opponents for the change ('that's excellent') while noting more remains; constructive.

text: It's almost unsettling to hear the speeches opposite; I feel like they should be sitting on this side. I'm all for it—ka pai koutou; I'm really glad to hear that you are listening to the public of New Zealand.
explanation: Gracious and respectful toward the governing-side speakers; credits them rather than disparaging.

text: when that policy was announced in 2018, no officials and no industry knew anything about it
explanation: Criticises the process of a past Government's policy rather than attacking individuals.

text: I respect the fact that Governments of the day have the right to be able to create policy, but I do not respect policies that have been derived with no quality process to back it up.
explanation: Concedes the opponent's legitimacy before criticising the process — measured tone.

text: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it's got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
explanation: Critical of the previous government's budgeting practices, not of individuals.

text: I can’t help but admire the passion that Cushla Tangaere-Manuel has for her province.
explanation: Generous acknowledgement of a political opponent across the aisle.

text: I see that there have been a couple of amendments made by the Finance and Expenditure Committee. That tells me that the committee has done a great job of returning the bill in a stronger position than it was actually received in. I'm happy to commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Respectful, credits the select committee process, no personal attacks.

text: I'll put this Government's record on social housing up against the lunatics opposite any day of the week.
explanation: Labels opposition members 'the lunatics opposite' — a personal/collective insult rather than policy criticism.

text: Tamatha Paul’s telling New Zealanders that they’re too stupid to work out that electricity being cheaper than petrol means that electric vehicles are a good option. If Tamatha Paul wants to say that taxpayers should subsidise wealthy people to buy Teslas, that’s fine. We won’t support that.
explanation: Puts words in a named MP's mouth ('too stupid') and caricatures her position rather than engaging it.

text: homelessness went up between 2018 and 2023, at a time when you spent tens of billions of dollars on Kāinga Ora... between 2018 and 2023, people living in severe housing deprivation increased, at a time that tens of billions of dollars were spent... The social housing wait-list between 2017 and 2023 quintupled
explanation: Sharp partisan framing ('you spent') directed at the previous Government's record rather than a personal attack — but adversarial in tone.

text: there is now actually a consensus across the sensible parties in the Parliament that this is a supply issue and that urban planning rules need to reflect that.
explanation: The 'sensible parties' framing is a mild dig but not a personal attack.

text: politicians have got to stop making announcements about things they’re going to build without knowing how much they cost.
explanation: Addresses a shared failing rather than blaming one side.

text: there are more of us in this generation that deserve to live close to the places where we work our asses off than the people who sit there, have no job, own multiple properties, and do nothing to earn their wealth.
explanation: A sweeping class-based attack characterising property owners as idle and undeserving.

text: it’s about rich, wealthy people in Epsom who don’t want the poor people coming and living next door to them.
explanation: Imputes selfish, class-based motives to residents rather than engaging their stated concerns.

text: That’s the thing about zoning: it’s free. It costs nothing to change zoning—literally. You couldn’t even get that right.
explanation: “You couldn’t even get that right” is mocking rather than substantive.

text: the ACT Party are hypocrites. They say, “All hail property rights.”, but I wonder whether they know that property rights don’t only apply to oneself; they apply to your neighbour, as well.
explanation: Labels opponents “hypocrites,” but the criticism is tied to a substantive point about their stated principles.

text: It’s a project that nobody asked for and nobody wants in Wellington.
explanation: Dismissive overstatement, though aimed at the project not a person.

text: If you think about a truck that’s on the road with an “H” on it, they can carry about 35 tonnes on it, so one shipment is 1,000 trucks to get it there—down to Huntly—for it.
explanation: Quantitative reasoning to convey scale (35,000t ship / 35t truck = ~1,000 trucks); arithmetic broadly holds though rounded.

text: I respect the fact that Governments of the day have the right to be able to create policy, but I do not respect policies that have been derived with no quality process to back it up.
explanation: Argues from process quality rather than mere partisanship; a principled criterion, though the premise is asserted.

text: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it's got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
explanation: Identifies a real budgeting issue but offers no figures or examples, and 'left, right, and centre' is rhetorical.

text: Tamatha Paul’s telling New Zealanders that they’re too stupid to work out that electricity being cheaper than petrol means that electric vehicles are a good option. If Tamatha Paul wants to say that taxpayers should subsidise wealthy people to buy Teslas, that’s fine. We won’t support that.
explanation: Strawman: recasts support for EV subsidies as subsidising 'wealthy people to buy Teslas' to knock it down.

text: homelessness went up between 2018 and 2023, at a time when you spent tens of billions of dollars on Kāinga Ora... between 2018 and 2023, people living in severe housing deprivation increased, at a time that tens of billions of dollars were spent... The social housing wait-list between 2017 and 2023 quintupled
explanation: Pairs spending with rising need to imply the previous approach failed, but treats correlation as proof and ignores confounders.

text: It is true, almost objectively, that rents in Auckland are lower now than they would otherwise have been as a result of the upzoning—Auckland rents are lower than they otherwise would be.
explanation: Appeals to the academic evidence on the Unitary Plan, a legitimate basis, but asserts it as near-certain.

text: On average, it's taking 128 working days for decisions on substantive applications from when officials determine an application is complete and in scope... Green Steel... said it would have taken a minimum of six years to take the project through the Resource Management Act (RMA) consenting process; under fast track, just seven months. Kings Quarry said that using fast track instead of the RMA saved them three years in consenting time. Their project was approved in just over six months.
explanation: Uses named project examples to support the time-saving claim.

text: Public-private partnerships (PPPs) are not magic. PPPs are a procurement tool; they are not a funding tool.
explanation: Clear conceptual distinction that corrects a common misconception; reasoning is tight.

text: It’s a project that nobody asked for and nobody wants in Wellington.
explanation: Sweeping appeal-to-popularity assertion without evidence.

text: it’s about rich, wealthy people in Epsom who don’t want the poor people coming and living next door to them.
explanation: Asserts motive without evidence.

text: the ACT Party are hypocrites. They say, “All hail property rights.”, but I wonder whether they know that property rights don’t only apply to oneself; they apply to your neighbour, as well.
explanation: Contains a genuine consistency argument—property rights of neighbours to develop—though the “hypocrites” label is asserted, not argued.

text: There is no consensus in the planning world as to what character actually refers to, but there is a whole lot of literature that argues that character is a way of protecting the status quo and making sure that people of the same economic class, the same race, and the same background remain
explanation: Appeals to a body of planning literature to support the claim, though the literature is not specifically cited.

text: zoning is actually about sending a signal to the market that this is the kind of growth that we are planning for.
explanation: Clear, reasoned explanation of zoning's function that follows logically.

text: We spend a greater share of our GDP on infrastructure than many compatible countries, but we achieve less.
explanation: Frames the problem as efficiency not just spend; reasonable, though the comparator is unspecified.

text: I've been working closely with the Balmoral Residents Association, and the residents are particularly concerned that enabling large-scale development, often without confirming the infrastructure capacity, could lead to isolated and out-of-scale development.
explanation: Grounds the position in stated constituent engagement and a coherent infrastructure-sequencing concern.

text: Nicola Willis tells people it’s bad luck, basically, if they lose their job—“Oh, well.”
explanation: Strawman: attributes a flippant position to an opponent without evidence and reasons from it.

text: the changes in the Public Finance Act are what allow the invention of the operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses (OBEGALx)... what Nicola Willis didn’t do was fix the books; she simply went and crossed out ACC.
explanation: Specific, technical argument that OBEGALx flatters the surplus by excluding ACC; logically articulated, though 'creative accounting' is a contestable characterisation of a defined new measure.

text: Well, by Shane Jones' logic, Oji Fibre Solutions, Smithfield meatworks, Winstone Pulp, Carter Holt Harvey, Heinz Wattie's, and McCain Foods have all been allowed to be shut down by this Government.
explanation: A reductio that exposes the inconsistency in applying 'allowed to close' as government approval.

text: How can New Zealanders have confidence in his claims when the regulatory impact statement and cost recovery analysis record a constrained analysis of options, constrained time frames, no completed business case, and no independent stage gate review?
explanation: Marshals specific documented process deficiencies from the RIS and cost-recovery analysis to question the basis of the policy; evidence-anchored.

text: We have GDP that is lower than it was two years ago. That will be a context for the delivery of this year's Budget. We have unemployment that is higher now than it was two years ago. We have business liquidations higher now than they were two years ago. We have the number of children in poverty higher now than it was two years ago. And our economic outlook from our credit agency, Fitch, has been downgraded under this Government.
explanation: Marshals multiple indicators to frame the fiscal context coherently.

text: In 2007, a management company signed a 40-year deal, a leasehold with Ngāti Whātua. Council chipped in some money, the build was $94 million, and they’ve got it for 40 years. In 2047, that’ll be handed back to the ratepayers of Auckland for zero.
explanation: Uses a concrete worked example to support the PPP/BOOT argument.

text: Thirty billion dollars of the $60 billion-plus was spent on non-core COVID spending—that is what these reports reveal... and it’s absolutely disgusting.
explanation: Cites report figures but layers a partisan 'non-core/wastage' interpretation onto them.

text: there’s nothing to show for it but just unprecedented Government debt and a huge $8.9 billion interest bill, and growing. No bridges, no roads, no busways, no new hospitals—nothing.
explanation: Absolute 'nothing' claim is rhetorical exaggeration unsupported by the nuance in the reports.

text: In contrast, over the last two Budgets, the Government has made cumulative ongoing savings of over $11 billion a year... $60 billion was borrowed and spent during COVID-19, and $30 billion of that was on non-direct COVID expenditure—half of it not directly related to COVID.
explanation: References Treasury and a royal commission report to support the figures, but the 'non-direct' framing is interpretive.

text: That was a provision within this bill that encourages residential solar uptake, ensuring residents up and down this country who export excess power back to the grid... won't face income tax, recognising that the compliance burden would outweigh any benefit and it will encourage solar and battery uptake.
explanation: Gives a coherent compliance-cost justification linking the measure to its intended effect.

text: to say that there is no plan for energy security other than hoping that it rains
explanation: Mocking, us-vs-them rallying line, not consensus-building.

text: Denial is not an option. Mistakes were made in the economic response, and these mistakes were costly. Those who choose to minimise these errors are not well placed to learn from them.
explanation: Rhetorically firm but addressed to its own side, not consensus-building.

text: challenges no one has got up on this House to say aren’t real. No one in this House has got up to say they can somehow solve... challenges that are real and that are coming for us.
explanation: Briefly acknowledges shared recognition of the problem across the House before pivoting to attack; partial common-ground gesture.

text: I also want to note that it is a very difficult time for anyone affected by these proposals—workers, growers, and contractors alike—and my thoughts are with those involved. Support is available from the Ministry of Social Development, including help with finding new employment and income support for those who are eligible.
explanation: Empathetic and inclusive in tone before the political argument.

text: Unlike that member, I say good on all of those people who went to that job fair; I say good on them for going out and looking for work... To every New Zealander who is taking the effort to go out and find more work: we’re on your side. Go for it.
explanation: Warm, encouraging direct address to job seekers; reframes positively.

text: The Prime Minister is a dud, the finance Minister has no credibility, and they are lashing around for relevance.
explanation: Purely combative, alienating, no attempt to persuade the undecided.

text: Some people are so blinded by their hatred of Israel, and perhaps the type of people that live there, and their hatred of America that they can't see the moral dimension of this conflict.
explanation: Sharply us-vs-them; alienates rather than persuades the unconvinced.

text: As Shakespeare once said, “Measuring the minds of others by his own.”, and in Willie Jackson’s case you don’t need a very long ruler to make that measurement. This Government is taking the situation much more seriously than Willie Jackson has taken anything in his entire life.
explanation: A crowd-pleasing put-down that alienates rather than persuades.

text: Has the Minister considered engaging a private detective to get to the bottom of this weighty matter—who did it, who took it off the YouTube channel, and how do we make sure it never happens again?
explanation: A partisan applause line aimed at deflating opponents, not persuading them.

text: today, I'm proud to stand here in this House and support legislation that says that the required number of homes will only be 1.4 million. We're not going to force on Aucklanders something that they did not want.
explanation: Confident appeal to localism, but pitched to his own side's framing of the issue.

text: It’s not about Labour or National or ACT or the Greens; whoever’s in power is going to have to grapple with this for all New Zealand.
explanation: Explicitly non-partisan framing inviting all parties to share the problem — consensus-building.

text: I can’t help but admire the passion that Cushla Tangaere-Manuel has for her province.
explanation: Builds a bridge by recognising shared regional passion before making his own case.

text: I see that there have been a couple of amendments made by the Finance and Expenditure Committee. That tells me that the committee has done a great job of returning the bill in a stronger position than it was actually received in. I'm happy to commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Positive and constructive about the cross-party committee, though ultimately a partisan endorsement.

text: New Zealanders deserve treatments not based on identity or politics or what box they have to tick.
explanation: Appeals to fairness, but framed as a swipe at 'identity' politics rather than bridge-building.

text: good luck explaining that to your constituents in Wellington Central. If that is your position, I think you may find that Wellington Central constituents don't like the idea that—
explanation: Us-vs-them debating jab, not consensus-building.

text: there is now actually a consensus across the sensible parties in the Parliament that this is a supply issue and that urban planning rules need to reflect that.
explanation: Claims consensus but qualifies it as 'sensible parties', implicitly excluding opponents rather than inviting them in.

text: I am yet to find someone who thinks that we shouldn't grow around City Rail Link stations.
explanation: Frames a point of broad agreement to bring the House along.

text: Parliament, last year, passed time of use pricing legislation unanimously, and I was really pleased by that, and I was really pleased to engage with the Opposition around finding a framework that we can all accept.
explanation: Credits cross-party engagement and shared acceptance — consensus-building.

text: My hope is that we could get to some degree of consensus around many of the recommendations.
explanation: Explicit reach for cross-party consensus on the infrastructure response.

text: This is not the National Party of Bill English... this is a National Party that came in and was just intent on rolling back anything because Labour had done it
explanation: Largely a partisan contrast, though the appeal to 'the National Party of Bill English' gestures at shared values.

text: We have GDP that is lower than it was two years ago. That will be a context for the delivery of this year's Budget. We have unemployment that is higher now than it was two years ago. We have business liquidations higher now than they were two years ago. We have the number of children in poverty higher now than it was two years ago. And our economic outlook from our credit agency, Fitch, has been downgraded under this Government.
explanation: Effective for her own side but framed as an indictment, not bridge-building.

text: the wellbeing approach to budgeting, for us looking at something broader than just the simple traditional economic measures, was work that had begun when Bill English was the Minister of Finance. This is the work that Treasury had begun as far back as 2011
explanation: Reframes a partisan dispute by crediting a National finance minister, an attempt to find cross-party common ground.

text: we think opening up that window and getting that information out there for a longer time is good for our democracy and we can support that.
explanation: Credits a specific measure in the Government's bill (longer PREFU window) despite opposing the bill overall — a fair-minded, bridging note.

text: genuine collaborations, genuine multipartisanship, whoever is in Government, is actually about coming together to form enduring plans that can cross Governments, that can endure
explanation: Explicitly inclusive, cross-government framing aimed at durable consensus.

text: So I talked about this when I was campaigning in 2023. I put a member’s bill in the ballot in 2024: the KiwiSaver (First Home for Farmland and Service Tenancy Tenants) Amendment Bill.
explanation: Position held consistently from 2023 campaign through a 2024 bill to the Government bill announced — words match a sustained record.

text: We’re very proud of the changes we’ve made with Pharmac and actually changing that organisation to make sure it’s delivering for New Zealanders who need important medicines.
explanation: Aligns ACT's stated medicines focus with named recent Pharmac announcements — some consistency shown.

text: I wish to correct a statement that I made during the second reading of the Anzac commemoration bill.
explanation: Voluntarily correcting her own prior statement on the record shows words-and-actions consistency.

text: I lived through the 1990s National Party “mother of all Budgets” welfare reform, and I don’t think any of us have got an appetite to be doing major reform on the welfare system, just carte blanche cutting benefits.
explanation: A current National MP distancing herself from her own party’s historic welfare-cutting record; a candid, self-aware stance rather than defending the prior position.

text: I was very much there in 2017, when we talked about, as the last National Government, the Hawke’s Bay Expressway. It was almost all but there. Then what happened? We didn’t get in to Government that time. It got cancelled, and there goes another six years of that project.
explanation: Claims a consistent personal advocacy for the corridor since 2017, supporting words-match-record — but self-asserted.

text: 47 years of oppression of its own people, 30,000 Iranians who happened to wish to protest their Government murdered in January this year, and there's not a peep from the human rights proponents on the other side.
explanation: Specific figures (30,000 killed in January) are contested and not independently established from the text.

text: we had a situation, that we inherited, of massive inflation, up to over 7 percent. Debt—just the interest rates alone that the Minister of Finance is having to find money for—of $11 billion a year extra every single year; basically, borrowed money paying for borrowed money.
explanation: Inflation peaking above 7% is broadly accurate; the '$11 billion a year extra' debt-servicing figure is asserted without sourcing.

text: We have not received any request to contribute to the US and Israel's military action. New Zealand is not central to the issues in the Middle East. Any decision would be one for joint Ministers or Cabinet.
explanation: Factual claim about no request having been received; plausible but unverifiable from the text.

text: With over 3,000 New Zealanders already registered in the region and potentially thousands more unregistered, the ability to move many people quickly to safety relies on having aircraft like the C130J and skilled personnel ready to deploy.
explanation: Registration figure plausible from MFAT records but not verifiable here; the 'thousands more unregistered' is an estimate.

text: We finally got the second frigate on the water a week ago. We haven't had two frigates on the water since 2019.
explanation: Specific, checkable claim about frigate availability; plausible and consistent with NZDF capacity issues.

text: We estimate that if you gave your party vote to ACT in the last election, you actually saved $57,000 for the taxpayer.
explanation: A self-serving derived figure (savings divided by votes) presented as fact; methodology is dubious and unverifiable.

text: Can the Prime Minister confirm that the importer margin, which has been misnamed as the profit margin, fell dramatically in the early days of the Iran war, but has subsequently ceased to be reported because the data had become so erratic it might not be reliable; and wouldn't it be easier to invent that than make up conspiracies?
explanation: Asserts a specific reason the margin reporting stopped; plausible framing but unverified and self-serving.

text: I saw him pointing out that, in recent days, attendance has been as high as 91 percent of students at school... there is always the temptation for people to take an event like somebody not showing up and to try and view it through the lens of a perceived crisis and then catastrophise it into a moral panic.
explanation: Cites a 91% attendance figure; plausible but a 'as high as' best-case framing.

text: We've seen the time taken to consent an overseas investment application drop by 60 percent, from 71 days down to 28.
explanation: Concrete, internally consistent processing-time claim; plausible but not independently verified here.

text: a natural monopoly is a service that has constantly increasing returns to scale, so one provider is the most efficient way to provide. And, as it happens, roads and sewer networks and water pipes and public transport networks and a whole lot of things that cities rely on are natural monopolies. That's why you can't have a competitive market, and that is the public policy case for zoning
explanation: Accurate economics: the natural-monopoly characterisation of network infrastructure is sound.

text: when we came into Government, only 75 percent of Kiwis could access their GP. That's now gone up to 79.5 percent. Things are trending in the right direction.
explanation: Specific percentages presented without a defined measure or source; directional claim plausible but not verifiable here.

text: Eighty-three percent of people are being seen within one week for primary mental health and addiction support; nearly 82 percent are being seen within three weeks for specialist support—both exceeding the target of 80 percent.
explanation: Cited as latest quarterly data; precise and plausible though unverified here.

text: The latest quarterly data shows we’ve exceeded our target for training 500 mental health and addiction workers a year, with 514 in training over the past year, up from 457 in the previous year... we’ve grown the front-line workforce by over 11 percent since coming to office.
explanation: Quantified claims attributed to quarterly data; plausible and internally consistent.

text: I'm advised that, of 22 February 2026, there's been 70,754 funded consultations, for 56,498 individual users, provided by the online GP service.
explanation: Precise official figures attributed to advice; plausible and not contradicted, but unverifiable here.

text: 83 percent of Kiwis are now accessing primary mental health support within one week; 82 percent of Kiwis are now accessing specialist mental health support within three weeks.
explanation: Specific performance figures presented as fact; plausible but unverified from the text.

text: The long-term claims pool represents around 25,000 New Zealanders who have been on ACC for more than 12 months. Since 2017, this pool has grown dramatically; in fact, it has doubled, with growth exceeding 14 percent... Under this Government, that trend has been turned around, and, as of this week, growth has been reduced to below 1 percent.
explanation: Specific figures presented as fact; the juxtaposition of a long-run doubling with a single recent week's sub-1% growth risks overstating a turnaround.

text: Does she agree that 246 tamariki and rangatahi in care spending over 4,000 nights in motels, with the longest stay being nearly a year, is inconsistent with motels being used as a last resort?
explanation: Cites concrete figures: 246 children, over 4,000 nights, longest stay nearly a year.

text: Would you like me to find some stealth bombers? I don't have any of those. How about an aircraft carrier? We don't have any of those... but we do have some very well-qualified people involved in demining. That might be at the right time, at the right place, and at the right request—who knows.
explanation: Names a concrete capability (demining) but qualifies it heavily ('who knows', 'depends').

text: I am very excited about the million dollars over four years into the Game On initiative, with industry partners matching this funding, and I know this will mean the starting careers for these young people are between $65,000 and $80,000 to start.
explanation: Names the $1m-over-four-years funding and a $65k–$80k starting salary range.

text: With over 3,000 New Zealanders already registered in the region and potentially thousands more unregistered, the ability to move many people quickly to safety relies on having aircraft like the C130J and skilled personnel ready to deploy.
explanation: Gives a registration figure (over 3,000) and links it to a specific capability requirement.

text: I give you, then, international law on the law of the sea and the rights for this country and other countries to be able to have commercial shipping, and we call on Iran to comply with the United Nations Security Council Resolution 2817.
explanation: Names a specific legal basis (law of the sea) and a specific Security Council resolution.

text: Overnight, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I agreed to pre-deploy New Zealand consular staff and two C130Js to the region to be ready, when conditions allow, for any civilian evacuations.
explanation: Concrete action: pre-deploying consular staff and two named aircraft (C130J) to the region for evacuations.

text: It’s got to be a good deal, and it’s free to vote. It’s the sale of the century, actually!
explanation: Rhetorical sales-pitch flourish with no content.

text: we set a $2.4 billion a year operating allowance and then we keep to it, because we’ve seen the alternative—a Minister of Finance who set an operating allowance of, if I remember, $3.5 billion, but not only was it bigger, he couldn’t keep to it... fiscally incontinent.
explanation: Cites specific operating-allowance figures ($2.4b vs $3.5b).

text: The number one factor is that we need to ensure that Government behaviour does not add to inflation... we wanted to help people who are in the greatest need so we said that this is for people who are on the lower end of the income scale and who have children and who work... and we linked it to petrol prices so that if petrol prices come back down, we stop spending the money.
explanation: Describes the targeting criteria and the petrol-price linkage mechanism, though without amounts.

text: Tomorrow, legislation will come into force that will allow most overseas investments to be consented in just 15 days by introducing a new two-track system that puts the emphasis on risky investment
explanation: Names a timeframe (tomorrow), a target (15 days) and a mechanism (two-track system).

text: We've seen the time taken to consent an overseas investment application drop by 60 percent, from 71 days down to 28.
explanation: Precise before/after figures (71 days to 28) and a percentage.

text: For the first time, the Government’s target of 25 percent of the ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding has been invested in prevention and early intervention.
explanation: Names a 25% ring-fenced funding target for prevention, though without dollar amounts.

text: Eighty-three percent of people are being seen within one week for primary mental health and addiction support; nearly 82 percent are being seen within three weeks for specialist support—both exceeding the target of 80 percent.
explanation: Precise percentages against named wait-time targets.

text: 83 percent of Kiwis are now accessing primary mental health support within one week; 82 percent of Kiwis are now accessing specialist mental health support within three weeks.
explanation: Precise percentages tied to defined access windows.

text: this Government committed $24 million directly to fund 800 more counsellors on Gumboot Friday to deliver to 15,000 young people more access and support.
explanation: Dollar figure, counsellor count, and beneficiary count all named.

text: I'm advised that, of 22 February 2026, there's been 70,754 funded consultations, for 56,498 individual users, provided by the online GP service.
explanation: Exact counts (70,754 consultations; 56,498 users) and a date.

text: The long-term claims pool represents around 25,000 New Zealanders who have been on ACC for more than 12 months. Since 2017, this pool has grown dramatically; in fact, it has doubled, with growth exceeding 14 percent... Under this Government, that trend has been turned around, and, as of this week, growth has been reduced to below 1 percent.
explanation: Gives pool size (~25,000), historical growth (doubled, >14%) and current growth (below 1%).

text: In the recent letter of expectation sent to ACC, I set out three priorities: (1) putting clients first by providing care that supports lasting recovery; (2) helping New Zealanders return to work and independence... and (3) resetting ACC by getting the organisation back to basics, with a clear focus on delivery and outcomes.
explanation: Lists three named priorities, though they remain fairly high-level objectives without metrics.

text: I’ve written to the Commerce Commission to clearly set my expectation that it closely monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices, as well as importer margins, to ensure motorists continue to receive a fair deal at the pump.
explanation: Names a concrete action (letter to the Commission) and what it covers, though no thresholds.

text: this Government should have a greater focus on jobs—and the Labour Party absolutely will—because when people are in jobs, not only is their income better but their mental health is better, their social connectedness is better, their self-esteem is better.
explanation: States a focus on jobs but no policy, target, or measure.

text: That's why we think three free GP visits is a good idea: because we know how to measure wellbeing.
explanation: Names a concrete policy (three free GP visits) though without cost or timing detail.

text: an admin data-first approach has a bias towards people who are administered—that is to say, if you have a connection with the health system, Inland Revenue, the Ministry of Social Development, or any other Government agency, you're going to be touching the system and you'll be recorded. Whereas there is a cohort of people... who aren't touched by the State in the same way. They live on the edges
explanation: Names concrete agencies and the specific bias mechanism, though without quantification.

text: The statement, which was clearly hurriedly put together, is itself internally inconsistent. We see in its last paragraph that it talks about upholding the principles of international law and freedom of navigation, but in the immediately preceding paragraph it says... "We express our readiness to contribute to appropriate efforts to ensure safe passage through the Strait [of Hormuz]".
explanation: Cites the exact paragraphs and wording of the statement under debate.

text: Standing Order 46 is very clear that the House on a Thursday rises at 6 p.m. except when Standing Order 53 applies when you may interrupt the business up to five minutes before to avoid interrupting a speaker. To allow the speeches to continue now would be to not be consistent with Standing Orders.
explanation: Cites exact Standing Orders, the day, the time, and the precise procedural condition.

text: I'm really excited about the future ahead with the changes that we're going to be making under this bill... When quality data is collected more regularly, essentially what it means is that we can provide better outcomes with more knowledge.
explanation: General enthusiasm and a vague 'better outcomes with more knowledge'; no mechanisms, figures, or concrete detail.

text: Sometimes, some decisions that we have to make are very hard decisions to make, but that doesn't mean they shouldn't be made.
explanation: General reflection with no policy detail.

text: there's a situation where in two groups of people, one group is being treated more generously than the other. Is that fair? When they want to talk about fairness... what about those that are not being treated as generously as the other group?
explanation: Frames the two-cohort comparison without figures or mechanism.

text: On Sunday 1 March, I received a text message from the chair of TVNZ asking for a call. We spoke about a range of matters including TVNZ financials and board appointments, and he observed, as I recall, that TVNZ had been in the news that week over a law and order story and that he was taking an interest in it... I didn't engage further in the discussion on that matter.
explanation: Asked on what dates he discussed TVNZ news coverage with the board/chair; he gives specific dates and an account of the calls and what was said.

text: I may possibly have grunted, but I'm not sure.
explanation: Asked what he said when crime-numbers coverage was raised by the chair; a candid if flippant answer that conveys he gave no substantive response.

text: What we grumbled about was the fact that on the day that we had announced that there were 49,000 fewer victims of crime in this country, there was a story that ignored that entirely and talked about something else. We weren't happy about it—that's life.
explanation: Asked whether Mitchell raised the coverage with him; he confirms it and candidly explains the grievance.

text: He probably shouldn't have, but it's certainly not a major issue.
explanation: Asked whether it was appropriate for the chair to raise One News coverage with him; he gives a candid concession that the chair probably shouldn't have.

text: My experience of the Minister is that he always keeps his promises. He’s a very a decent human being, and frankly, I only wish that everyone would recognise that instead of asking such stupidly loaded questions.
explanation: Asked about beef mince up 23% and bread up 57%, she addresses neither figure.

text: there was the same issue prior to this Government, except that it was worse because, under the extensive and overdone lockdowns in Auckland, the home of most Pasifika people in New Zealand, many young people were denied their education... attendance rates were a mere 17 percent.
explanation: Asked about 21% of young Pasifika not in employment/education/training now, she deflects to past lockdowns.

text: I’m sorry, but that doesn’t concur with the figures I have been given by Stats NZ, which show there are now 7,000 more people of Pasifika ethnicity who are employed in Auckland, from December 2024 to December 2025.
explanation: Disputes the questioner's figure but answers with an employment-gain stat rather than the unemployment figure asked about.

text: Would you like me to find some stealth bombers? I don't have any of those. How about an aircraft carrier? We don't have any of those... but we do have some very well-qualified people involved in demining. That might be at the right time, at the right place, and at the right request—who knows.
explanation: Sarcastic in tone but does substantively address what NZ realistically could contribute (demining), while hedging on whether it will.

text: I’m advised by Stats NZ that the number of unemployed Pacific people in New Zealand rose by 13,000 people compared with December 2023, but the positive news is that from December 2024 to December 2025, in Auckland alone, Pasifika employment rose by 7,000 people.
explanation: Directly concedes the 13,000 rise in unemployment asked about before adding context.

text: I'm advised that, of 22 February 2026, there's been 70,754 funded consultations, for 56,498 individual users, provided by the online GP service.
explanation: Verrall asked how many had a consult since launch; he gives precise figures directly.

text: It was never meant to be a silver bullet. It was to complement our primary care services. We announced it six months ago, and we're looking to scale it up.
explanation: Asked how the usage compares to the original 1-million-a-year claim, he reframes the service's purpose rather than addressing the gap to that target.

text: I refute that question. It was never—promised. This was a service that was always about complementing GP practices.
explanation: Verrall asked whether the service would be at a tenth of promised volumes; he rejects the premise that anything was promised rather than engaging the volume comparison.

text: 83 percent of Kiwis are now accessing primary mental health support within one week; 82 percent of Kiwis are now accessing specialist mental health support within three weeks.
explanation: Leary asked about unaffordable counselling costs and six-month waits; he answers with access stats, prompting a point of order that he didn't address costs.

text: Eighty-three percent of people are being seen within one week for primary mental health and addiction support; nearly 82 percent are being seen within three weeks for specialist support—both exceeding the target of 80 percent.
explanation: Directly answers the progress question with figures.

text: Since this Government came into office, over 7,000 net new social houses have been delivered. Of those, 308 were funded in Budgets 2024 and 2025, and, of course, we've funded lots more social and affordable homes that are under way.
explanation: Directly confirms the 7,000 figure and gives the specific subset (308) funded in those Budgets as asked.

text: Eligibility for the social housing register is unchanged from the previous Government to today, which allows for comparisons. Is the measure perfect? No, it is not... Is the register going down? Yes, it is.
explanation: Directly answers whether eligibility changed (no) and acknowledges the measure's imperfections while affirming his core point.

text: Yesterday, the Minister of Finance and the Minister for Energy and I announced the number of electric vehicle public chargers will more than double thanks to $52.7 million in zero-interest loans from ChargeNet and Meridian. Half the chargers will be spread across Auckland, Hamilton, Tauranga, Wellington, Christchurch, and Dunedin—
explanation: Directly answers Butterick's question about EV charger announcements.

text: Instead, we have taken an approach of concessionary loans to bring forward private investment by lowering the cost of capital. This is essentially akin to the Ultra-fast Broadband model that rolled out between 2008 and 2016. It is much better value for money for the taxpayer; it provides a long-term pipeline of EV chargers rather than one-off dollops of grant funding being invested.
explanation: Directly answers why concessionary loans were chosen over grants.

text: In the recent letter of expectation sent to ACC, I set out three priorities: (1) putting clients first by providing care that supports lasting recovery; (2) helping New Zealanders return to work and independence... and (3) resetting ACC by getting the organisation back to basics, with a clear focus on delivery and outcomes.
explanation: Asked what direction he gave ACC; he enumerates the three priorities directly.
