text: I’ve written to the Commerce Commission to clearly set my expectation that it closely monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices, as well as importer margins, to ensure motorists continue to receive a fair deal at the pump.
explanation: Directly answers what actions he has taken on fuel markets.

text: Does she agree that 246 tamariki and rangatahi in care spending over 4,000 nights in motels, with the longest stay being nearly a year, is inconsistent with motels being used as a last resort?
explanation: Uses the long-stay data to challenge the 'last resort' characterisation; a reasonable evidence-based contradiction, though it sets aside the median-stay context.

text: I've often made the observation that a politician complaining about the media is like a farmer complaining about the weather: you may be right, but it makes no difference, and so you've got to figure out how to succeed in any respect.
explanation: Rests on an appeal to analogy (farmer/weather) rather than a substantive argument.

text: How can he expect to house the growing number of homeless when the pipeline of houses contracted or under construction has dropped from 8,863 in 2023 to just 1,513 today, a drop of 83 percent in just two years?
explanation: Uses concrete pipeline data to challenge the Government's housing delivery; evidence-based, though it focuses on one metric.

text: when you have just agreed with the point of order made by Chris Hipkins that the assertion that the previous Government closed Marsden Point is incorrect, and he then turns around and ignores that and says it anyway, we are going to express concern about that.
explanation: Clearly articulates the inconsistency between a conceded point and the Minister's repeated claim.

text: this Government wants to see no evil—and it's certainly evil that it's doing as it undermines social cohesion, the health of New Zealanders, the equity of New Zealanders, and really what's going on in New Zealand.
explanation: Sweeping accusation across multiple domains with no evidence offered.

text: this Government should have a greater focus on jobs—and the Labour Party absolutely will—because when people are in jobs, not only is their income better but their mental health is better, their social connectedness is better, their self-esteem is better.
explanation: The link between employment and improved mental health, connectedness and self-esteem is broadly evidence-supported, though stated without citation.

text: for someone who arrived at six and who is now 39, that is a 501 situation—the 501 situation that we have vilified our Australian cousins for, and I’m not sure we’d want to put ourselves in the same situation of then reducing appeal rights.
explanation: Reasons from a worked example (arrived at 6, deportable at 39) to a consistency argument against Australia's 501 regime NZ has criticised.

text: The statement, which was clearly hurriedly put together, is itself internally inconsistent. We see in its last paragraph that it talks about upholding the principles of international law and freedom of navigation, but in the immediately preceding paragraph it says... "We express our readiness to contribute to appropriate efforts to ensure safe passage through the Strait [of Hormuz]".
explanation: Builds a specific textual argument quoting adjacent paragraphs to show an internal tension.

text: there is a risk, on one analysis, that you can do sweeping reforms. It's clearly not intended... particularly those first three—could look like a reform programme. But we know that that's not what revision bills actually are about.
explanation: Carefully reasoned concern about scope creep from the removal of 'minor', grounded in the specific subsections.

text: The reason why we don't have enough gas today is the previous Government banned oil and gas, and that's why our energy prices are high. Thank you, Labour.
explanation: Sarcastic 'Thank you, Labour' is a partisan jab, though aimed at a policy decision rather than a person.

text: The challenge is that the last Government stopped gas exploration and, as a result, we have no gas. So we are looking to import that.
explanation: Criticism of a prior policy decision, not a personal attack.

text: We don't have a policy to tax people's homes. We don't have a policy to tax people's farms or their baches—which I appreciate the member is keen to do all that, or a 66 percent tax rate, which seems to be on the agenda; we're not doing any of that.
explanation: Misrepresents Russell's position ('keen to do all that', '66 percent... on the agenda') when she raised 66% only as historical context; a strawman attributing intentions she did not state.

text: Nicola Willis tells people it’s bad luck, basically, if they lose their job—“Oh, well.”
explanation: Caricatures the Finance Minister's position with a mocking paraphrase ('Oh, well') rather than engaging her actual stance.

text: this is a finance Minister who has borrowed more we did when we were in Government, and the only strategy that she seems to have is hope, and that has been no more evident than what we've seen over the last three or four weeks as New Zealand has navigated a cost of living crisis.
explanation: 'Only strategy is hope' is a sharp characterisation but aimed at strategy, not person.

text: Well, by Shane Jones' logic, Oji Fibre Solutions, Smithfield meatworks, Winstone Pulp, Carter Holt Harvey, Heinz Wattie's, and McCain Foods have all been allowed to be shut down by this Government.
explanation: Combative but engages the logic of the opponent's argument.

text: Now, Labour is opposing this bill, because I’ll come to the changes that are being made that mean we can’t vote for it—but it doesn’t mean that there aren’t some things in this bill that we do think are good, and are positive changes.
explanation: Respectful, concedes the opposing side's good provisions while explaining the basis for opposition; no personal attack.

text: Will the Government under any phase of the National Fuel Plan offer a financial underwrite or guarantee to fuel companies, as Australia is doing?
explanation: Neutral, substance-focused question with no personal edge.

text: I can tell those members on the other side who has to fight those fights; it's actually our Defence Force. Frankly, I'm not putting them forward if we don't have to do something, because it's their lives while people on the other side are talking from their very, very excited position of holier than thou.
explanation: Substantive concern undercut by the 'holier than thou' characterisation of opponents.

text: My experience of the Minister is that he always keeps his promises. He’s a very a decent human being, and frankly, I only wish that everyone would recognise that instead of asking such stupidly loaded questions.
explanation: Dismisses the question as 'stupidly loaded' — disparaging the questioner rather than the substance.

text: when she doesn't even pronounce Mark Rutte's name correctly. For goodness' sake, get these things right. If you're going to start quoting the secretary-general of NATO, for goodness' sake, give the man his name.
explanation: Belittles an opponent over pronunciation, though softened by prior praise of her; more cheap shot than substance.

text: 47 years of oppression of its own people, 30,000 Iranians who happened to wish to protest their Government murdered in January this year, and there's not a peep from the human rights proponents on the other side.
explanation: Legitimate point about the regime, but the 'not a peep from the human rights proponents' jab targets opponents' motives.

text: I think it is important to have some semblance of respect in this House towards each other. Every member is supposed to be an honourable member.
explanation: An explicit call for mutual respect and decorum in debate.

text: The fact that Nicola Willis and her peers can't open a Budget and say, "This funding ends in 2023 or 2024 or 2025." is a reflection not on the budgeting of the Labour Government but on the innumeracy of the National Party.
explanation: Direct personal attack ('innumeracy') on Nicola Willis and the National Party rather than the policy.

text: You can sit down—I've got a full 12 seconds; I wouldn't want you to get worn out standing up.
explanation: Sarcastic, mocking aside aimed at another member rather than the debate.

text: Now, I agree with much of what has been said on the other side: the Iranian regime is a despicable regime that has an atrocious human rights record. We rightly recognise the people of Iran, both resident in Iran and the communities in New Zealand and around the world.
explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the other side's case.

text: there is a risk, on one analysis, that you can do sweeping reforms. It's clearly not intended... particularly those first three—could look like a reform programme. But we know that that's not what revision bills actually are about.
explanation: Pointed but engages substance; invites the Minister to clarify rather than attacking.

text: I know that in his inimitable way, Mr Xu-Nan is going very methodically through the legislation
explanation: Gracious and respectful.

text: I've often made the observation that a politician complaining about the media is like a farmer complaining about the weather: you may be right, but it makes no difference, and so you've got to figure out how to succeed in any respect.
explanation: Disarming, self-deprecating turn of phrase that deflects tension, though it does not build cross-party consensus.

text: We agree that fiscal responsibility is important. We agree that transparency is important, but that's the fringes of this bill. The centre of this bill is the gutting of the most innovative economic measures that have been seen not only in New Zealand but around the world.
explanation: Opens by conceding shared ground on fiscal responsibility and transparency before pivoting to disagreement — a partial bridge-building move.

text: Now, I agree with much of what has been said on the other side: the Iranian regime is a despicable regime that has an atrocious human rights record. We rightly recognise the people of Iran, both resident in Iran and the communities in New Zealand and around the world.
explanation: Explicitly concedes valid points from opponents and finds common ground before pressing his own argument.

text: I know that in his inimitable way, Mr Xu-Nan is going very methodically through the legislation
explanation: Warm, good-humoured acknowledgement of a colleague's contribution.

text: We’re not opposed to any change, but we do think that real care is needed to be taken.
explanation: Measured, non-oppositional framing that signals openness to the bill while flagging concerns.

text: We're not going to agree on everything all the time, but I do think, on something as important as statistics and how we approach the census question, it's really good that we try to get as much agreement as we can.
explanation: Explicitly seeks cross-party common ground and acknowledges shared importance of the issue — consensus-building.

text: Overnight, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I agreed to pre-deploy New Zealand consular staff and two C130Js to the region to be ready, when conditions allow, for any civilian evacuations.
explanation: Describes a concrete decision being acted on, though it is a pre-deployment readiness measure rather than a completed evacuation.

text: We finally got the second frigate on the water a week ago. We haven't had two frigates on the water since 2019.
explanation: Claims a delivered capability (second frigate operational) as her government's doing, though follow-through detail is thin.

text: We've seen the time taken to consent an overseas investment application drop by 60 percent, from 71 days down to 28.
explanation: Claims a delivered, measurable change in consent timeframes attributable to the Government.

text: Tomorrow, legislation will come into force that will allow most overseas investments to be consented in just 15 days by introducing a new two-track system that puts the emphasis on risky investment
explanation: Legislation imminently in force represents follow-through, though the operational outcome is yet to be delivered.

text: Brooke van Velden’s leading one of the most significant and most needed legislative reform programmes of any Government in over two decades, including the repeal of the widely loathed Holidays Act 2003. The Holidays Act has been so needlessly complex that even Government departments with all their resources have struggled to pay their employees correctly, racking up hundreds of millions of dollars in liabilities along the way.
explanation: Bill introduced this week—committed and progressing, not yet enacted.

text: Speaking as the leader of the ACT Party, I’m immensely proud of the savings and the improvements that we’ve managed to drive: Karen Chhour, in youth crime; the attendance that I’ve been responsible for; the improvements in medicine funding
explanation: Claims credit for specific delivered areas (attendance, medicine funding, youth crime), though delivery extent is asserted not demonstrated.

text: we campaigned and won an agreement to remove that three by three storey house rule, and it will be gone.
explanation: A campaign commitment now being delivered through the bill before the House — concrete follow-through, though final passage is pending.

text: The long-term claims pool represents around 25,000 New Zealanders who have been on ACC for more than 12 months. Since 2017, this pool has grown dramatically; in fact, it has doubled, with growth exceeding 14 percent... Under this Government, that trend has been turned around, and, as of this week, growth has been reduced to below 1 percent.
explanation: Claims a delivered improvement (growth reduced) attributable to his direction, but it is an early/partial trend rather than a settled result.

explanation: A concrete step taken, but it is setting expectations rather than a delivered outcome.

text: I refute that question. It was never—promised. This was a service that was always about complementing GP practices.
explanation: Denies a target was ever promised, which sits in tension with the original publicly stated 1-million-a-year ambition Verrall is quoting.

text: I'd just like to say I admire the thought and consideration of all parties on this bill. It's a shame that we were not able to reach consensus.
explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of all parties' contributions.

text: I’ll start off by saying that the Commerce Commission do a very good job.
explanation: Respectful, generous acknowledgement of an institution before critiquing the reform.

text: like the previous Labour Government’s long, largescale asset purchasing programme, COVID spending, half of which was helicopter money creating inflation, debt, and asset hikes, with real house prices having left the room.
explanation: Critiques the previous government's programme rather than attacking individuals.

text: I rise on behalf of the Green Party in total opposition to this bill, a bill that will just cause more harm coming from a Government that clearly does not care about the most vulnerable in our society. This bill is absolutely a disgrace.
explanation: Attributes bad faith ('clearly does not care') and uses charged language ('disgrace').

text: The problem I have with the Green Party is that when you're outraged about everything, you're really outraged about nothing.
explanation: Dismissive ad hominem about a party's temperament rather than its argument.

text: Virtue signalling over wellbeing doesn’t help pay the bills.
explanation: Dismisses the wellbeing framework as 'virtue signalling' — a belittling characterisation, though aimed at the policy approach.

text: next time someone from the Government gets up and tells us that they care about workers, I urge the public to think, "How much do they care about workers in this country? How much do they care about people?—full stop."

text: How absolutely 1984 can we get? ... a statement that was made by George Orwell ... which was that "Some animals are more equal than others."
explanation: Hyperbolic Orwell framing of the Government, more rhetorical flourish than personal attack.

text: There is absolutely no way that I can do the job I want to do for my constituents and go through this in the thorough way that they deserve, when it is their neighbourhood that's being affected ... I do not accept that there is any reason why this has to happen so urgently.
explanation: Earnest objection to the urgency process focused on constituents' right to participate, not personal attack.

text: This piece of legislation might not be perfect. There probably are issues because there always will be such issues, but it's a damn sight better than what we've had.
explanation: Measured, balanced assessment that concedes imperfections rather than overselling; constructive tone.

text: I absolutely respect Dr Webb's fear and hesitancy and the note of this Parliament that there are risks with that that we go too far, that we open things too wide and there are risks in that... I think, as he says, the balance is right here, and it can be looked at again if things go astray.

text: for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn't be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what's lawful or not.

explanation: Slips in a cheap shot equating Green Party members with 'dry' rather than engaging their reasons for voting against.

text: The other side of the House had six years to do something about competition, so that they could bring grocery prices down. It didn’t happen in six years; at least on this side of the House, we’re moving.
explanation: A pointed but legitimate criticism of the opposition's record rather than a personal attack.

text: Some members of the House that had six years to do something about it didn't do something about it.
explanation: A jab at the previous Labour Government's record, but a fair line of attack on performance.

text: we were able to negotiate with the Government—and I thank the Government for their good-faith interactions with us in this respect—to have a short select committee process of around a week.
explanation: Credits opponents for good-faith dealing even while opposing the bill.

explanation: Measured, substance-focused questioning of the Minister.

text: We are putting more money into health, contrary to what we've just heard and the scaremongering that's going on.
explanation: Labels the opposition's case 'scaremongering' rather than rebutting its substance.

explanation: Relies on an appeal to authority ('take them at their word') despite contrary evidence raised in the debate.

text: the famous Thomas Sowell quote that in the 1920s in the US they taxed the rich people at 76 percent and wondered why they weren’t getting much income. When they reduced it to 24 percent, the income skyrocketed.
explanation: Appeal to authority (Sowell) and a contested historical anecdote presented as a general law of taxation; ignores confounders.

text: like the previous Labour Government’s long, largescale asset purchasing programme, COVID spending, half of which was helicopter money creating inflation, debt, and asset hikes, with real house prices having left the room.
explanation: Asserts a causal chain to inflation and asset hikes without supporting evidence.

explanation: Rhetorical dismissal with no engagement of the substantive claims.

text: this legislation is something we live and breathe, but it is extremely disempowering when you don't know what the law is. explanation: Acknowledges a genuine trade-off and risk in the bill rather than overselling it.

text: it’s a great opportunity to consider how partnering with iwi and honouring iwi, hapū, and whānau is a great and a wise investment for Parliament, no matter who is in Government.
explanation: Frames the case inclusively and explicitly across the partisan divide (‘no matter who is in Government’).

text: It's almost unsettling to hear the speeches opposite; I feel like they should be sitting on this side. I'm all for it—ka pai koutou; I'm really glad to hear that you are listening to the public of New Zealand.
explanation: Warmly acknowledges that opponents are listening to the public and finds common ground across the aisle rather than attacking.

text: Sometimes, some decisions that we have to make are very hard decisions to make, but that doesn't mean they shouldn't be made.
explanation: Acknowledges difficulty and the opponents' concern before defending the decision.

text: for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn't be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what's lawful or not.
explanation: Divisive partisan attack.

text: This bill can seem dry to the average listener—like the Green Party members that voted against it—but, in fact, it's actually transformative in the milieu of legislation. I am very happy to commend it to the House.
explanation: Mildly partisan quip at opponents' expense; does not seek common ground or persuade the unconvinced.

text: we were able to negotiate with the Government—and I thank the Government for their good-faith interactions with us in this respect—to have a short select committee process of around a week.
explanation: Acknowledges cross-party cooperation, modelling constructive engagement.

text: the bill mistakes measurement for improvement... No one disagrees with the fact that performance should be visible... but simply writing targets into law isn't going to do anything to create capacity.

text: Obviously, we are supporting this bill, and we enjoyed going through the process.
explanation: Constructive, cross-party tone supporting a Government bill and praising the process.

text: These were changes that were made by a previous National-Act Government in establishing Auckland Transport, but bringing these functions back now under elected members feels like the right thing to do. It strengthens, we believe, both voice and responsibility.
explanation: Endorses a current Government reform on its merits despite noting its origins, seeking common ground.

text: Labour agrees, though, that the closing of a double-dipping loophole in welfare is important, because we, like everyone, know that Kiwis must feel confident in our welfare system

text: I will be the first one to admit that some of these wellbeing objectives could have been implemented and reflected better in Government policies
explanation: Concedes a fault on his own side's preferred framework rather than defending it uncritically — a candid, self-consistent admission.

text: I heard from our colleagues that it's a targeted welfare system, no impacts on claimants, clients will not get less under this amendment, and we take them at their word.
explanation: Says NZ First want no claimant disadvantage yet accept assurances rather than test them, then vote for the bill.

text: New Zealand First do not want any undue hardship or material hardship as a result of these changes; however, we support this bill.
explanation: Tension: states a value against hardship while voting for the bill that submitters and the courts say causes that hardship.

text: I said no, I’m not writing another strategy, we’re forming an action plan with projects on it and we’re going to implement them, and we did.

text: the Labour Party started in a position of supporting this bill because of what it was told. It was just awake on the job. It found out what was going on. It found out that there was an injustice afoot and it wasn't prepared to tolerate it.
explanation: Openly acknowledges Labour's position change and frames it as evidence-driven rather than concealing the shift.

text: Yes, it's a very important issue. We have to, otherwise we will not be doing justice to those who are going to be affected, because, as days go by, there will be more and more people—those who will be affected.
explanation: Responds to the 'rushed process' criticism by justifying speed, but only partially addresses the substance of the complaint.

text: this bill will deepen hardship for survivors of abuse, for survivors of sexual violence and abuse, and for those who suffer most in all of Aotearoa.
explanation: Prediction of worsened hardship; directionally supported by the affected cohort data, magnitude uncertain.

explanation: Predicts everyone 'will get' their entitlements; contested by the harm evidence raised.

text: If we receive a request or if an international coalition was established in the future to safeguard commercial shipping, any possible contribution will be a matter for—guess who!—the Cabinet, first of all, to determine, based on careful consideration of New Zealand’s interests. text: in 2022, when the Marsden Point refinery was closed down, with the approval of the then Labour Government—

text: this Government has chosen to spend billions of dollars in tax cuts that have been funded by debt, which produces precisely zero jobs.

explanation: A logically structured consistency argument linking domestic mitigation cuts to a larger offshore bill, supported by cited cost estimates.

text: "In effect, this reduces the requirement from approximately 2 million dwellings to approximately 1.4 million dwellings." That's a quote from the legislation that the Minister introduced.
explanation: Anchors her argument directly in the bill's own explanatory text — strong, verifiable evidence.

explanation: Paragraph references and precise dates.

explanation: Exact days of cover by fuel type and the twice-weekly reporting cadence.

explanation: Multiple concrete figures: 960m litre option, 24m litres/day consumption, 700m litres of lost storage.

text: This Government says that they want to cut red tape—oh, but they mean it everywhere but the Epsom electorate.
explanation: Names the Epsom electorate as the exception.

text: That is precisely what we’re proposing in Green Party policies like ensuring that everybody has free access to GPs and to dentistry but also to early childhood education.

text: more than 200 New Zealanders, with the majority of them young New Zealanders, leave the country every single day.

text: we would be looking at a quantum anywhere between $3 billion and $24 billion in offshore mitigation.
explanation: Concrete dollar range tied to a named obligation.

explanation: Names the policy and quantifies the EV market-share change with years.

explanation: Names the exact measure, who it affects, and the 1 April commencement.

explanation: Describes the discretion's scope and the concrete qualifying conditions for overseas student-loan borrowers.

text: I want to acknowledge the families, the healthcare workers, the business owners, and the tens of thousands of Kiwis who gave evidence to the commission. This report exists because of them.

text: I want to acknowledge the families, the healthcare workers, the business owners, and the tens of thousands of Kiwis who gave evidence to the commission. This report exists because of them.
explanation: Respectful, dignified tone focused on those affected.

text: The Prime Minister, of course, is always right, and, ultimately, the tens of thousands of New Zealanders are using this service, and it will continue to grow, as people become more aware of the service.

explanation: Measured and policy-focused despite the charged questioning.

explanation: Belittles opponents' position as 'vacuous virtue signalling' rather than engaging it.

text: Could I ask the Minister: how many tens of thousands of 12- to 17-year-olds could have been adversely affected as a result of the Government of that time ignoring the advice of people who knew what they were talking about?
explanation: Pointed and accusatory of the former government, though aimed at a policy decision.

text: this was never going to be a painless exercise, but the fact is that the dogs are no longer going to be in pain.

explanation: Belittles the predecessor's work as 'doodling on the side of a Cabinet paper', a personal/dismissive jab.

explanation: Directly answers that he has not received recent legal advice, then addresses the underlying concern.

explanation: Good-humoured and non-adversarial.

text: To rework the bill in the way that I think he’s proposing would have taken more policy work and time. I think that’s possibly as far as you’ll get from me as an acknowledgment that he makes a very jolly good point and that’s maybe something that could be looked at further.

text: I always find the committee of the whole House stage with the particular Minister in the chair to be extremely enjoyable and engaging.
