explanation: Advocates inclusion of an under-served group in a constructive way.

text: if we were to say that it must be available as far as or much as possible, then that would inevitably be read in a way as to mean something along the lines of “reasonably possible” or “possible in the circumstances”. If the circumstances were that the first and second server were down and there was not a third then that would be a matter of impossibility as well as impracticability. So I take his point, but I’m not sure that we would justify our time and energy as a committee in debating it much further or indeed amending.
explanation: Plausible interpretive argument that 'possible' would be read as 'reasonably possible'; some assertion rather than authority cited.

text: in the absence of any particular consequence being outlined for non-compliance with the particular requirements of new section 68A in terms of how law is to be published, I wouldn’t have thought there was any different outcome to that which would currently be the case.
explanation: Reasonable inference from the bill's silence on consequences, though no external authority cited.

text: We have seen that ManageMyHealth, and also other health data that’s held by private companies, has been subject to malicious attacks. What reassurance can the public have that legislation—including regulations—that is held and is more available to the public and now more vulnerable to attack will be protected from being undermined?
explanation: Reasons by analogy from health-data breaches to a single-point-of-access legislation site; plausible but the analogy carries the argument.

text: thinking about either malicious attacks or just mistakes or just data being lost: can I be reassured that there is some way that there will be paper? I’m not requiring any stone tablets to be produced by this Government or any other.
explanation: Raises a legitimate redundancy/data-loss concern, but the case is made colourfully/rhetorically rather than with evidence.

text: I’m not convinced that that change would make a material difference. Of course, there are probably arguments that as soon as you’re accessing something online, through a device, you have actually downloaded that data, anyway, so there may well be some technical interpretation questions as to why you have “accessed… or downloaded” as being the option.
explanation: Plausible technical point that accessing online entails downloading, but somewhat asserted rather than established.

text: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
explanation: Reasoned point about reconciling cross-language interpretation, though asserted generally rather than evidenced.

text: the fact that the secondary legislation doesn't come into force until it's published kind of takes care of that. If the regulator wants the rule to be enforced or regulatable, they should publish it and bring it into force.
explanation: Reasoning is coherent: non-commencement-until-publication logically substitutes for a mandatory publication requirement.

text: the better way to look at what the intention of Parliament is when it passes a statute is to look at the words in the purpose in the context of the statute.
explanation: Sound statutory-interpretation principle offered to address Webb's and Xu-Nan's concern about reliance on Hansard.

text: If it was "must include", then, therefore, the report would be legally required to include recommendations on something that it might not have a recommendation on. A report has the option of including a recommendation, but it doesn't have to do it
explanation: Clean logical reasoning: a mandatory 'must include' would force reporting on a recommendation that may not exist.

text: The Greens think anything that makes legislation more accessible to the ordinary person is a good thing.
explanation: Broad value statement with no mechanism or measure.

text: As for the instrument of the Crown, I might benefit from some advice on that point and would look forward to coming back to him.
explanation: In response to Webb's direct question on what an 'instrument of the Crown' is, he honestly admits he cannot answer yet and defers.

text: I would say that cybersecurity and other considerations are of course important, but I think properly outside the remit of the legislation.
explanation: Engages Webb's security question but answers by deflecting it as out of the bill's scope rather than addressing sovereign-hosting risk substantively.

text: if we were to say that it must be available as far as or much as possible, then that would inevitably be read in a way as to mean something along the lines of “reasonably possible” or “possible in the circumstances”. If the circumstances were that the first and second server were down and there was not a third then that would be a matter of impossibility as well as impracticability. So I take his point, but I’m not sure that we would justify our time and energy as a committee in debating it much further or indeed amending.
explanation: Directly engages Webb's 'practicable vs possible' question and states a view.

text: in the absence of any particular consequence being outlined for non-compliance with the particular requirements of new section 68A in terms of how law is to be published, I wouldn’t have thought there was any different outcome to that which would currently be the case.
explanation: Gives a cautious but direct answer to Xu-Nan's question on consequences for non-compliance.

text: an “instrument of the Crown” is not a department but might otherwise describe—I’m trying not to use the word “entity”, because a Crown entity is different again. An example of the instrument of the Crown, I’m told, is PCO, the Parliamentary Counsel Office
explanation: Returns to Webb's earlier question and gives a direct, concrete answer with an example.

text: New Zealand law includes the Bill of Rights 1688, which is New Zealand law that predates New Zealand in terms of New Zealand
explanation: Accurate: the Bill of Rights 1688 is retained as part of New Zealand law (via the Imperial Laws Application Act 1988) and predates the modern NZ state.

text: We have seen that ManageMyHealth, and also other health data that’s held by private companies, has been subject to malicious attacks. What reassurance can the public have that legislation—including regulations—that is held and is more available to the public and now more vulnerable to attack will be protected from being undermined?
explanation: Health-data systems including ManageMyHealth have been subject to security incidents; broadly accurate though stated generally.

text: we are seeing, for example, in Canada, legislation is published in both English and French; and, for example, in Wales, legislation is published in both English and Welsh.
explanation: Accurate: Canadian federal legislation is bilingual (English/French) and Welsh legislation is published in English and Welsh.

text: even in British or English legislation, they currently still use Normandy French because Law French goes back to the courts in the 13 th century.
explanation: Law French is genuine and dates to the Norman period; 'currently still use' is accurate only for a few residual formulae (e.g. royal assent phrases), so partly overstated.

text: currently, our tax base does not cover certain revenue-generation methods when it comes to things like capital gains and additional assets like private jets, superyachts, etc.
explanation: Broadly accurate—New Zealand has no comprehensive capital gains tax; the high-asset examples are illustrative rhetoric but the core claim holds.

text: those who are uber-wealthy in Aotearoa New Zealand pay half the effective tax rate of a nurse.
explanation: Echoes the 2023 IRD high-wealth study finding that the wealthiest pay a much lower effective rate; directionally supported but the 'half a nurse's rate' framing is a simplification.

text: When we’re seeing the wealth gap increasing by more than ever before in the history of Aotearoa
explanation: Superlative claim ('more than ever before in the history') is hyperbolic and unsupported; inequality trends do not clearly establish an all-time record.

text: The Greens think anything that makes legislation more accessible to the ordinary person is a good thing.
explanation: Consistent with the Greens' stated accessibility/transparency positioning, but no action shown either way in the text.

text: Regulations made under the bill will set out what forms and formats legislation must be published in. We anticipate that this will require publication of secondary legislation in machine-readable formats, and so that means that people who are supported by screen readers will be able to use them to read published legislation. The new website will also aim to comply with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Level AA
explanation: Forecast that the regulations 'will require' machine-readable formats; plausible given the stated policy intent, but contingent on future regulations.

text: It is the case that if a piece of secondary legislation is needing to be published, which provides a consolidation of all secondary legislation that incorporates all of the amendments made by every amending instrument—if it doesn't meet the requirements of publication, it is all repealed. So I have to correct that: it is all repealed.
explanation: Self-correction shows consistency between his stated aim of clarity and his conduct.

text: I have been assured that no front-line firefighters or comms centre positions are proposed to be affected. However, on the other hand, I’m advised that savings will be reinvested in areas including those that support the safety of volunteers and paid firefighters, such as fleet, training and equipment.
explanation: Identifies which positions are unaffected and where savings are reinvested.

text: The previous Government set up the Holidays Act task force in 2018, but by the 2023 election, draft legislation still wasn’t complete and ready for introduction.
explanation: Anchored with specific years (2018, 2023).

text: It also means no more waiting for six months to access sick leave or 12 months to access annual leave.
explanation: Concrete timeframes (six months, 12 months) and a specific effect of the bill.

text: Fire and Emergency New Zealand is not making cuts of $50 million per year; they are looking for cost efficiencies, something I support. In fact, I’m advised that in this financial year alone, they are planning to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment
explanation: Names a precise investment figure ($84.7m) and what it funds.

text: In fact, 70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers expressed a preference for more significant change to the annual leave provisions.
explanation: Precise figures (70%, 67%) tied to named groups.

text: I have been assured that no front-line firefighters or comms centre positions are proposed to be affected. However, on the other hand, I’m advised that savings will be reinvested in areas including those that support the safety of volunteers and paid firefighters, such as fleet, training and equipment.
explanation: Relayed assurances ('I have been assured'/'I'm advised') presented honestly as second-hand.

text: It also means no more waiting for six months to access sick leave or 12 months to access annual leave.
explanation: Describes a stated effect of the bill; plausible but a one-sided summary of how accrual changes access.

text: Fire and Emergency New Zealand is not making cuts of $50 million per year; they are looking for cost efficiencies, something I support. In fact, I’m advised that in this financial year alone, they are planning to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment
explanation: Reframes 'cuts' as 'efficiencies' and cites a specific investment figure; the framing is contestable but the figure is concrete.

text: Fire and Emergency New Zealand has inherited decades of under-investment in old trucks with the amalgamation of multiple services into one. They have a plan, and have had a plan for a number of years, to invest in new fleet and equipment. This year alone, they have a plan to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment.
explanation: Concrete, checkable budget figure presented as fact.

text: The previous Government set up the Holidays Act task force in 2018, but by the 2023 election, draft legislation still wasn’t complete and ready for introduction.
explanation: Dates and the broad failure to complete Holidays Act reform are accurate to the public record.

text: The previous Government set up the Holidays Act task force in 2018, but by the 2023 election, draft legislation still wasn’t complete and ready for introduction.
explanation: Criticism of the previous government's delay, but focused on the policy record rather than personal attack.

text: As I said, if this question had actually been about the fuel plan, I would've been able to come to the House with those relevant pieces of information. … I've had the exact same question in writing for pretty much month on month on month on end, and it's very difficult to know where she's going to go with the technical aspects of the question.
explanation: Mildly dismissive of the persistent questioner without a personal attack.

text: Ah, she’s bit confused there, because the premise of the report was, actually, that for private counsellors, the cost was going up, resulting in delays for people going private, which is quite contrary to that question.
explanation: 'She's a bit confused' is a mild personal jab, though paired with a substantive point about the report's premise.

text: If the National Party had an off week last week, isn’t Labour having a terrible week this time? The emperor has no clothes.
explanation: Rhetorical jab at the opposing party rather than engagement with substance.

text: Don’t let them gaslight you that the National Party voted for and supported their more than $60 billion spend-up. Yes, we supported the core and immediate health and wage support response, but, no, we never supported the billions of dollars in subsequent wastage
explanation: 'Gaslight' frames opponents as deliberately deceptive, an accusatory move.

text: Thirty billion dollars of the $60 billion-plus was spent on non-core COVID spending—that is what these reports reveal... and it’s absolutely disgusting.
explanation: 'Absolutely disgusting' is heated, but directed at spending decisions rather than a person.

text: Other parties, as we have heard, opposed all savings—opposed all savings. They want to bring back expensive programmes and spend and borrow more.
explanation: Caricatures opponents' position rather than engaging specific objections.

text: We are legislating to make it harder to hide unfunded fiscal cliffs, and we remember them well... we remember having to find money for Pharmac, and we remember having to find money for the school lunch programme.
explanation: Partisan but framed around policy/funding decisions rather than personal attack.

text: I am proud of the significant progress made already, to have legislation ready and available for public feedback—a milestone that successive Ministers tried and failed to reach.
explanation: Claims progress, but the deliverable is legislation out for feedback, not yet enacted — intent with in-progress delivery.

text: this Government committed $24 million directly to fund 800 more counsellors on Gumboot Friday to deliver to 15,000 young people more access and support.
explanation: Points to a funded, concrete commitment with delivery targets.

text: Eighty-three percent of people are being seen within one week for primary mental health and addiction support; nearly 82 percent are being seen within three weeks for specialist support—both exceeding the target of 80 percent.
explanation: Reports targets being exceeded, evidencing delivery against a stated goal.

text: The latest quarterly data shows we’ve exceeded our target for training 500 mental health and addiction workers a year, with 514 in training over the past year, up from 457 in the previous year... we’ve grown the front-line workforce by over 11 percent since coming to office.
explanation: Demonstrates delivery against a workforce target with year-on-year improvement.

text: We’ve funded 74 clinical psychology interns, exceeding the 2025 target of 60... We’ve also seen a record uptake in psychiatry, with 48 first-year registrars entering training last year, up from 33 in 2024. That’s a 50 percent increase.
explanation: Shows targets met/exceeded on training intakes, evidencing follow-through.

text: For the first time, the Government’s target of 25 percent of the ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding has been invested in prevention and early intervention.
explanation: Claims a target met 'for the first time', suggesting actual delivery on a prevention commitment.

text: That sort of question would have been quite helpful to have in writing as the primary question. That sort of detail can be sourced through a written parliamentary question.
explanation: Asked how many days of operational diesel reserves Fire and Emergency holds, she declines to answer and redirects to written questions.

text: I haven’t done that.
explanation: A terse blanket denial to a loaded multi-part question that does not engage any of its specifics.

text: I have been assured that no front-line firefighters or comms centre positions are proposed to be affected. However, on the other hand, I’m advised that savings will be reinvested in areas including those that support the safety of volunteers and paid firefighters, such as fleet, training and equipment.
explanation: Engages the substance of the restructure question, noting decisions are not final.

text: I'm advised that Fire and Emergency is taking a coordinated set of actions to manage the current fuel prices and potential supply pressures. They have established a Fuel Planning Group … classified as a 'critical customer' … working closely with their sector partners, including New Zealand Police and St John.
explanation: Substantively answers what actions have been taken on fuel reserves and contingency.

text: Fire and Emergency New Zealand is not making cuts of $50 million per year; they are looking for cost efficiencies, something I support. In fact, I’m advised that in this financial year alone, they are planning to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment
explanation: Directly disputes the premise of the question and offers a counter-figure.

text: So I suggest that member look in the mirror.
explanation: Jackson asked whether she modelled the social/fiscal costs of hardship; she does not answer at all.

text: Our Government is very clear about the fact that what is happening in the Middle East is having an impact on many New Zealanders, with the fuel-price pressure that they are facing. We are also very clear that any response needs to be targeted, timely, and temporary, otherwise every single person in New Zealand would be affected by inflation going up again.
explanation: Asked whether $12 is enough for those in poverty; pivots to the 'targeted, timely, temporary' rationale without answering.

text: the policy that the member refers to is about lowering energy prices, but let me say this: our Government fully accepts that there are too many New Zealanders today who are finding it challenging... We will not resile from our single focus on the cost of living and growing the economy.
explanation: Asked about an LNG levy's effect on heating-vs-eating households; disputes the premise and pivots to growth rhetoric.

text: what we are seeing are green shoots in terms of economic recovery if you look at the latest filled jobs data, showing the strongest annual growth in the hospitality sector.
explanation: Affirms she stands by her statement and gives indicators, though not a date for reduction as asked.

text: Yes, it is $20, not $50.
explanation: A direct, concrete correction of the figure put to her.

text: As this House knows, we have been absolutely focused on enabling a number of fast-track Act projects throughout the country... nearly 25 of the 149 in Schedule 2 of that Act—are either Māori-partnered or -led.
explanation: Asked whether Māori unemployment will rise given factory closures, he pivots entirely to fast-track projects.

text: That comes from a very dark and dank place, that comment—very dingy. What we’re all about is making sure we’ve got the basics sorted, infrastructure in place, better energy prices... and all the necessary steps and phases to ensure that, actually, housing is affordable.
explanation: Asked what policies will permanently lower rents, he opens by attacking the question's tone and lists vague 'basics'.

text: I’d recommend, for a specific quarter in a specific town and a specific decline rate, that that matter is put through the written parliamentary questions process. But what I will say is this: the vast majority of people who seek some sort of housing assistance through the Ministry of Social Development get it.
explanation: Asked to confirm a 63% Auckland decline rate, he redirects to the written-question process and reverts to a general claim.

text: We have seen nearly 5,500 Māori come off the jobseeker benefit in the quarter ending September 2025. We continue with a serious housing programme alongside, with, and for Māori, particularly in places like Hopuhopu, alongside Waikato-Tainui and their $35 million we committed to... the hundred homes that are being built up in Kaikohekohe right now by Te Hau Ora o Ngāpuhi
explanation: Asked about funding cuts and rising Māori unemployment; answers with off-benefit and housing figures rather than the cuts.

text: the credible measures of rent price changes show that rents are flat. For instance, the stock measure, Stats New Zealand’s rent price index measure, shows rents up 1.2 percent in the year to January 2026—lower than inflation.
explanation: Directly answers whether rents rose 10% — 'no' — with supporting data.

text: In fact, 70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers expressed a preference for more significant change to the annual leave provisions.
explanation: Uses survey evidence to support the case for change rather than mere assertion.

text: It's sorry to hear that members opposite don't believe this group of New Zealanders should have an increase.
explanation: Builds a claim about opponents' beliefs on no stated evidence — a strawman.

text: at that point there were close to 190,000 people on jobseeker support. Those numbers have been steadily rising since 2022, which is before we took office. The COVID-19 royal commission inquiry has found the previous Government’s increased spending drove up debt, inflation, and interest rates, which leads to higher unemployment... As of December, the quarterly figures show 223,500 people on jobseeker support
explanation: Builds a causal argument (spending → debt/inflation → unemployment) citing an inquiry, but skips the link steps.

text: Yes. If you look at the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research report that came out in January this year, it shows that business confidence is at the highest it’s been since 2014.
explanation: Reasonable confidence→hiring chain, but relies on one indicator as proxy for recovery.

text: When you think about more than 50 percent of the Government’s spending during the years of COVID-19, having nothing to do with COVID-19... I am really proud that despite those challenges, 83,000 New Zealanders left welfare for a job, in the last year. That’s something worth celebrating.
explanation: Causal spending argument repeated; the 83,000 gross figure ignores net flows.

text: widespread, untargeted support, where the hose of money is spread around, leads to high inflation. Who does that hurt the most? According to the Governor of the Reserve Bank … high inflation hurts everyone, but it particularly hurts households with low incomes.
explanation: Cites the Reserve Bank Governor (appeal to authority) for a defensible economic point about inflation incidence.

text: what we are seeing are green shoots in terms of economic recovery if you look at the latest filled jobs data, showing the strongest annual growth in the hospitality sector.
explanation: Implies an emerging recovery; directionally supported by cited filled-jobs data but uncertain as a forecast.

text: Well, I remain optimistic that our economic plan is working, and, as I said, business confidence is the highest it’s been since 2014. Will we get the target or not? We’ll get close
explanation: Predicts getting 'close' to the jobseeker reduction target, against Treasury advice of a large miss; optimistic vs current evidence.

text: If the National Party had an off week last week, isn’t Labour having a terrible week this time? The emperor has no clothes.
explanation: An applause line for his own side; combative rather than consensus-building.

text: Other parties, as we have heard, opposed all savings—opposed all savings. They want to bring back expensive programmes and spend and borrow more.
explanation: Rallying his own side via a blanket characterisation of opponents.

text: Don’t let them gaslight you that the National Party voted for and supported their more than $60 billion spend-up. Yes, we supported the core and immediate health and wage support response, but, no, we never supported the billions of dollars in subsequent wastage
explanation: Defends the consistency of his party's voting record (backed core support, opposed later spending); plausible but unverified from the text.

text: Until you give our young people a reason to stay here, they will be on the next plane, even with the fuel charge, off to Australia, where they can feel they can get their first home, where they can get a job that pays them well, and where they can access the healthcare that they need.
explanation: Predicts continued youth emigration to Australia absent policy change; directionally consistent with current net-migration trends but conditional and unquantified.

text: When Labour takes over in November this year, that’s exactly the Government New Zealand will have.
explanation: Predicts Labour wins the November 2026 election; a verifiable forecast but uncertain and self-interested, no polling cited.

text: In 20 years, Māori will be over 25 percent of the population and the median age for Māori will be mid-30s, compared to early 40s for the rest of the population.
explanation: 20-year demographic projection consistent with StatsNZ population trends; demographic forecasts of this kind are relatively reliable.

text: The amendments proposed in this bill threaten that. They threaten kaitiakitanga, they threaten the value of consulting with kaitiaki and, therefore, the sustainability of our kāpata kai and, potentially, the sustainability of our commercial interests.
explanation: Predicts harm to sustainability of food sources and commercial interests if the bill proceeds — plausible but magnitude and timeframe uncertain.

text: by 2040, we’re going to hit 90 percent of debt-to-GDP, and by the 2060s, debt-to-GDP will balloon to 200 percent.
explanation: Long-range projection drawn from Treasury’s no-policy-change scenario; such scenarios are illustrative of trajectory, not forecasts, so high uncertainty over 15–40 years.

text: I say this because New Zealand has near on $200 billion of nominal debt and that has an interest attachment to that... Over the last few weeks that risk premium has gone up and we should expect it is going to make a difference to the Budget that is going to be announced in May.
explanation: Predicts the risk premium will affect the May Budget — plausible and near-term, though the size is unspecified.

text: the cost of living crisis is what’s biting people more than ever before. And that’s going to get worse under this Government.
explanation: Predicts worsening cost of living under the current government; partisan and unquantified, evidence mixed.

text: I’m confident that this bill will fulfil its promise and protect the legacy of Charles Rooking Carter and continue to serve the Carterton community for at least another 130 years.
explanation: A 130-year forecast of community benefit—rhetorical and effectively unfalsifiable over that horizon, plausible in direction only.

text: One of the very disappointing things for me about the last Government was that they had the mandate. They had an absolute majority, which was a rare thing in this Parliament under MMP, and yet they didn’t address the things that we’ve seen coming for decades.
explanation: Reasonable argument (majority + inaction) but asserts they ‘didn’t address’ long-term issues without specifics here.

text: you could see in the 1990s and late early 2000s there was actually a measurable impact and dip in life expectancy because of those [benefit cuts].
explanation: Cites a claimed measurable health impact to argue against benefit cuts, but the causal link is asserted, not evidenced.

text: When we came into Government, it was clear that the culture that had been inculcated through the Government Public Service was profligate, it was irresponsible, and it wasn’t even putting in basic, fundamental, profit-and-loss, balance-sheet sort of stuff that I’d expect as a governor.
explanation: Asserts profligacy by appeal to her own governance experience rather than evidence.

text: we cannot look at this bill without acknowledging that this was during a colonial era when a lot of Māori land was taken through unfair contract terms, unequal bargaining power, and pressure on Māori landowners.
explanation: Adds historical context with care, distinguishing the era’s injustices from the individual benefactor’s conduct.

text: Mr Carter himself was a man of great integrity and known in his community as being a really honourable person, but he did, through his endeavours, get tens of thousands of dollars and then left this really useful legacy... All of those things can be true at the same time.
explanation: Holds competing truths together without false dichotomy—nuanced reasoning about a complicated legacy.

text: Successive Governments have been woeful at doing that because we think about three years in advance—maybe we think about three months in advance. That is not good enough.
explanation: Reasonable point about short electoral horizons, asserted rather than evidenced.

text: growth, by and large, is not driven by births and deaths now; it is driven by migration.
explanation: Uses the fact to support his point that councils need a national migration/demographics strategy to plan.

text: the trust now has more than $200 million dollars in assets—$207 million, according to the annual report, but $173 million of that is essentially the ownership of the lines network that is there.
explanation: Distinguishes headline assets from the network’s book value to make a sound point about ongoing maintenance obligations.

text: yes, the market can sort itself out, but we need to make sure that we send the right market signals. If growth is not paying for growth, then we are not sending the right market signals.
explanation: Coherent conditional argument linking accurate price signals to functioning markets.

text: We asked them that question: "What proportion of the costs of growth are paid for by that growth?" ... And they said, "Rough order of magnitude: 30 to 50 percent." That means that 50 to 70 percent is paid for by existing ratepayers, existing taxpayers, existing consumers. Growth is not paying for growth.
explanation: Evidence-based: cites the Infrastructure Commission's testimony and draws the arithmetic conclusion that follows.

text: It’s really important that we work together across the House to have a orderly pipeline for those investments that need to be made so that we can continue to do that for the future.
explanation: Direction (orderly investment pipeline) but no amounts, named projects, or timing.

text: National is strengthening and helping to shore up the future by increasing the default payments for KiwiSaver, for example—that’s one of the things that we will be doing.
explanation: Names a real mechanism (KiwiSaver default payments) but no rate, amount, or date.

text: if there are new changes to the immigration instructions that happen while somebody is having their application for residence looked at that would be beneficial to them, then that is automatically applied to their application. I think that that is a very sensible change, and I commend the bill to the House.
explanation: Identifies a precise mechanism (beneficial instruction changes auto-applied to pending residence applications).

text: We’d be interested to explore if there’s any scope for the trust to support local residences, businesses, and groups with energy independence, for example, through initiatives such as solar power.
explanation: Names a concrete idea (solar power, energy independence) but only as something to ‘explore’, no commitment or detail.

text: they’ve got $1 million that they’re putting into solar on schools, marae, and council buildings.
explanation: Concrete figure ($1m) and named recipients (schools, marae, council buildings).

text: What we should be doing is working with local government, helping local government where it needs to be helped, to design cities in the way that makes the most possible sense.
explanation: States a direction but no mechanism for how the working-together would operate.

text: As of 2023, there was something like 545,000 houses in Auckland.
explanation: Gives a dated, concrete figure used to contextualise the capacity numbers.

text: the Infrastructure Commission has been very clear that growth is not paying for growth. At best, it’s paying for 50 percent of growth; at worst, 30 percent. The rest of that is falling on the taxpayer, the ratepayer, and whoever else it might be.
explanation: Cites a source and concrete percentage range.

text: We asked them that question: "What proportion of the costs of growth are paid for by that growth?" ... And they said, "Rough order of magnitude: 30 to 50 percent." That means that 50 to 70 percent is paid for by existing ratepayers, existing taxpayers, existing consumers. Growth is not paying for growth.
explanation: Gives concrete percentage ranges and the source of the figures.

text: the trust now has more than $200 million dollars in assets—$207 million, according to the annual report, but $173 million of that is essentially the ownership of the lines network that is there.
explanation: Exact dollar figures and breakdown of the asset base.

text: This is something that has been a failure of all sides of this House—it’s not one party or the other.
explanation: Accepts shared blame across parties rather than scoring points; builds common ground.

text: It’s really important that we work together across the House to have a orderly pipeline for those investments that need to be made so that we can continue to do that for the future.
explanation: Explicit cross-party, consensus-seeking call for a bipartisan infrastructure pipeline.

text: The reality is that National has no plan, and that’s why they’re just yelling a lot, because they think that if they yell a lot, New Zealanders won’t notice that they absolutely have no plan at all.
explanation: Combative rallying of her own side; no attempt to persuade across the aisle.

text: In a time when partisanship can often overshadow progress, it’s great to see a sense of unity and a shared commitment to Carterton’s future by supporting this bill.
explanation: Explicitly welcomes cross-party unity and shared purpose.

text: National is committed to constructive change. We believe that if the bill, however, does not undergo real, meaningful improvements during the select committee stage, we will not be able to support it beyond that point.
explanation: Constructive, conditional framing that signals openness rather than combativeness.

text: We must work together to protect our marine resources for future generations.
explanation: Unifying call to common purpose.

text: Mr Carter himself was a man of great integrity and known in his community as being a really honourable person, but he did, through his endeavours, get tens of thousands of dollars and then left this really useful legacy... All of those things can be true at the same time.
explanation: Bridges perspectives, inviting a shared, nuanced view across the House.

text: We’d be interested to explore if there’s any scope for the trust to support local residences, businesses, and groups with energy independence, for example, through initiatives such as solar power.
explanation: Constructive, collaborative suggestion aimed at the select-committee process.

text: This is something that has been a failure of all sides of this House—it’s not one party or the other.
explanation: Non-partisan framing, no personal attack, focuses on collective policy failure.

text: One of the very disappointing things for me about the last Government was that they had the mandate. They had an absolute majority, which was a rare thing in this Parliament under MMP, and yet they didn’t address the things that we’ve seen coming for decades.
explanation: Pointed criticism of the previous government’s record but aimed at inaction on policy, not personal attack.

text: When we came into Government, it was clear that the culture that had been inculcated through the Government Public Service was profligate, it was irresponsible, and it wasn’t even putting in basic, fundamental, profit-and-loss, balance-sheet sort of stuff that I’d expect as a governor.
explanation: Sweeping pejorative characterisation (‘profligate’, ‘irresponsible’) of the public service rather than a specific, substantiated critique.

text: I lived through the 1990s National Party “mother of all Budgets” welfare reform, and I don’t think any of us have got an appetite to be doing major reform on the welfare system, just carte blanche cutting benefits.
explanation: Acknowledges the human cost of past cuts without attacking opponents.

text: if there are new changes to the immigration instructions that happen while somebody is having their application for residence looked at that would be beneficial to them, then that is automatically applied to their application. I think that that is a very sensible change, and I commend the bill to the House.
explanation: Calm, substance-focused endorsement with no attack.

text: The quality of the debt is also important: about infrastructure, economic growth, things that power our economy out, not pet projects like the other side did when they were in Government.
explanation: ‘Pet projects’ is a dismissive jab at the opposition’s spending rather than a specified, substantiated critique.

text: it couldn’t get any more vivid as a picture to be cancelling a national resilience fund and handing out buckets of KFC. I mean, how short term can you get it?
explanation: Sensationalist ‘buckets of KFC’ mockery used as a cheap shot rather than engaging the policy substance.

text: National’s answers are property speculation. They are to sell off our assets; to look at overseas investments; and also mentioned is to promise roads that aren’t funded and don’t have a source of income; and offer things like $2.9 billion of tax cuts and additional millions of dollars for tobacco companies.
explanation: Largely attacks the opponent’s agenda; ‘additional millions for tobacco companies’ is a loaded characterisation, though most items target policy not person.

text: The reality is that National has no plan, and that’s why they’re just yelling a lot, because they think that if they yell a lot, New Zealanders won’t notice that they absolutely have no plan at all.
explanation: Dismissive characterisation (‘just yelling’, ‘no plan at all’) rather than engagement with the government’s stated approach.

text: Is it a sign of growth when 17,000 people attend a jobs fair in Auckland, when only 100 employers were looking for workers?
explanation: Pointed rhetorical question aimed at the economic record.

text: In a time when partisanship can often overshadow progress, it’s great to see a sense of unity and a shared commitment to Carterton’s future by supporting this bill.
explanation: Gracious, collaborative tone with no attacks.

text: Mr Carter himself was a man of great integrity and known in his community as being a really honourable person, but he did, through his endeavours, get tens of thousands of dollars and then left this really useful legacy... All of those things can be true at the same time.
explanation: Balanced and respectful, acknowledging both merit and historical context.

text: one big mistake the Government made was killing off the community energy fund. Now we’re looking to the sector to provide that, and Horizon Trust is looking to do just that.
explanation: Direct criticism of a specific government decision (scrapping the community energy fund), focused on policy not person.

text: National is strengthening and helping to shore up the future by increasing the default payments for KiwiSaver, for example—that’s one of the things that we will be doing.
explanation: Claims a concrete policy (raising KiwiSaver default contributions) but framed as ‘will be doing’—intent/in-progress rather than demonstrated delivery.

text: Michael Cullen in KiwiSaver is a big promise in terms of how we deliver on that, and KiwiSaver has been a critical part of how we do that. I’m incredibly proud that that was delivered by a previous Labour Government.
explanation: Claims credit for KiwiSaver, a concrete policy that was actually designed and implemented under the previous Labour government—delivered, not just promised.

text: we cannot look at this bill without acknowledging that this was during a colonial era when a lot of Māori land was taken through unfair contract terms, unequal bargaining power, and pressure on Māori landowners.
explanation: Accurate historical characterisation of 19th-century Māori land alienation in the Wairarapa era.

text: one big mistake the Government made was killing off the community energy fund. Now we’re looking to the sector to provide that, and Horizon Trust is looking to do just that.
explanation: References a real policy change; the ‘mistake’ judgement is opinion but the factual basis is plausible.

text: Two million, 1.6 million, 1.4 million—these are theoretical houses. They are the houses that conceivably could be built under a set of planning rules, but they are not the houses that will be built.
explanation: Accurately characterises the disputed numbers as theoretical capacity figures.

text: there’s only so far that you can push costs down before builders say, “Actually, it’s not worth it. I can’t make a dollar out of it.”, and they won’t build… in the COVID situation, we saw prices ramp up very, very fast; we saw development ramp up very, very fast; and then the market turned… development dropped down as the prices dropped down.
explanation: Accurately describes the boom-then-slowdown in construction activity following the pandemic price cycle.

text: We asked them that question: "What proportion of the costs of growth are paid for by that growth?" ... And they said, "Rough order of magnitude: 30 to 50 percent." That means that 50 to 70 percent is paid for by existing ratepayers, existing taxpayers, existing consumers. Growth is not paying for growth.
explanation: Reports the Commission's figures and the implication accurately as presented.

text: growth, by and large, is not driven by births and deaths now; it is driven by migration.
explanation: Accurate — net migration is the dominant driver of NZ population growth in recent years.

text: That growth is no longer being delivered by births being greater than deaths, because we know, actually, that we’re now at less than replacement level. It’s being delivered by migration.
explanation: NZ's fertility rate is below replacement and population growth is migration-driven—both accurate.

text: Michael Cullen in KiwiSaver is a big promise in terms of how we deliver on that, and KiwiSaver has been a critical part of how we do that. I’m incredibly proud that that was delivered by a previous Labour Government.
explanation: Long-term-savings advocacy backed by Labour’s actual record of establishing KiwiSaver and the Super Fund; words match deeds.

text: The New Zealand Superannuation Fund is another excellent investment that we see. Sadly, it was paused under a previous National Government—they paused those Government contributions—and they were restarted again by the previous Labour Government.
explanation: Cites Labour’s record of restarting Super Fund contributions to back its long-term-planning claims—consistent words and deeds.

text: I want to say, first off, that the contributions from my colleagues Duncan Webb and Vanushi Walters, I thought, were first grade. Both of these members participated in the select committee process and all the prior stages of the bill going through the House, and they were thoroughly across the detail of the bill.
explanation: Respectful praise grounded in his colleagues' substantive engagement with the bill; no personal attack.

text: It's sad that other than the opening contribution by the Minister James Meager reading the notes prepared by officials, we haven't had a single other substantive contribution in this debate from the Government benches.
explanation: Legitimate criticism of the Government's lack of debate engagement, but carries a mild jab ('reading the notes prepared by officials') at the Minister's effort.

text: The principle is this: don't say anything that might attract a late night tweet from the White House. New Zealand's once proud, independent foreign policy has under this Government... been reduced to abject servility to the Trump White House.
explanation: Mocking characterisation ('abject servility') aimed at impugning the government rather than its policy reasoning.

text: Speaking in the debate on the first reading of the Immigration (Enhanced Risk Management) Amendment Bill, I incorrectly asserted that Erica Stanford had attended a five countries immigration ministers meeting. I withdraw that statement.
explanation: Retracts a false claim about an opponent respectfully and without spin.

text: ordinary people are waking up to the fact that this Government is acting in the interests of its rich mates and some ideologs—and, in the case of New Zealand First, some conspiracy theory "cookers"—in not acting in the interests of all New Zealanders, the long-term interests, making sure the firefighters get the equipment they need to work. They're doing this because they don't understand, or they're beholden to donors.
explanation: Heavy personal/name-calling ('rich mates', 'ideologs', 'cookers', 'beholden to donors') rather than engaging the substance.

text: so far, it’s pretty obvious that for a lot of people on the Government benches, you know, math is not their strong point; I’m being very diplomatic here. Not everybody is, you know, mathematically inclined in their reasoning, and it’s obvious that the members in the Government are not mathematically inclined.
explanation: Personal attack on opponents' competence/intelligence rather than their policy; the 'being diplomatic' aside underlines the jab.

text: Yeah. It’s been out for years. What are you talking about? It’s like, update your negs, man. God, you’re so out of date.
explanation: Dismissive personal jab at an interjector rather than substantive engagement.

text: That is what is meant by fossil fools: fossil fools love fossil fuels. The people who believe that we can’t take action on change climate or that we shouldn’t take action on climate change are the biggest threat to the future of humanity.
explanation: Name-calling ('fossil fools') and labelling opponents the 'biggest threat to humanity' — personal and inflammatory.

text: this Government needs to grapple with the reality that the Roads of National Significance it campaigned on are unfundable and not the best use of money.
explanation: Sharp but policy-focused criticism of a named programme rather than a personal attack.

text: the Green Party, who, if you look at their social media posts, would be quite happy for Kiwis to live in the dark, drive nothing, and maybe actually go back to a time when New Zealand was poor
explanation: A caricature of the Greens' positions amounting to a strawman attack.

text: what you Sim City obsessed planning nerds believe should be the right number of houses, Tamatha Paul
explanation: Direct name-calling (“planning nerds”) aimed at a named member.

text: They can choose to live out a SimCity planner’s unicorn world where there’s a 10-kilometre radius around the CBD and not a single house should ever be built outside it, or they can choose to listen to Aucklanders.
explanation: Mocking framing of opponents' position rather than engaging it.

text: So the member Tamatha Paul makes a good point: the Resource Management Act is broken.
explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opposing member's argument.

text: Now, Phil to some of us is a hero. I probably shouldn’t be admitting that as an ACT MP, but the National Policy Statement on Urban Development, Mr Twyford, actually set the scene for why it’s important to build up around these expensive investments in transport, like the City Rail Link
explanation: Respectful and gracious toward a political opponent.

text: I was fascinated to read that our secondary legislation is published by a plethora of different agencies—central government and local government—and that estimates range from around 7,500 to 20,000 current instruments published by around 120 Government, local government, and non-Government agencies.
explanation: Factual claim about the scale and dispersion of secondary legislation; consistent with the bill's background material and plausibly accurate, though cited as an estimated range.

text: remember that under Labour's Helen Clark, New Zealand stayed out of the United States and the UK and Australia's disastrous invasion of Iraq in 2003
explanation: Accurate: NZ did not join the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

text: I was fascinated to read that our secondary legislation is published by a plethora of different agencies—central government and local government—and that estimates range from around 7,500 to 20,000 current instruments published by around 120 Government, local government, and non-Government agencies.
explanation: Names concrete figures (7,500–20,000 instruments, ~120 agencies) and categories rather than speaking in generalities.

text: now this law is going to place an obligation on all of the publishing agencies—the 120 different agencies will be obliged to actually publish the secondary legislation that they are responsible for, a number of other obligations, as well, in the way that that information is kept and published, and then PCO simply will provide internet links to all of those off that main website.
explanation: Describes the concrete mechanism of the bill: distributed publishing obligations on 120 agencies plus PCO linking, rather than vague praise.

text: Will you rule out sending New Zealand personnel and New Zealand defence assets to the Strait of Hormuz?
explanation: Targets a concrete, answerable commitment (ruling out personnel/assets to a named location).

text: There is a way to clear the Strait of Hormuz and get the oil flowing again, and it's very simple. It's stop the war; stop the war.
explanation: 'Stop the war' is a slogan, not a mechanism NZ can deliver; no concrete steps offered.

text: now this law is going to place an obligation on all of the publishing agencies—the 120 different agencies will be obliged to actually publish the secondary legislation that they are responsible for, a number of other obligations, as well, in the way that that information is kept and published, and then PCO simply will provide internet links to all of those off that main website.
explanation: Reasoned contrast between the rejected centralised model (which would 'crush' PCO) and the adopted distributed model, with the conclusion following from the premises.

text: Will you rule out sending New Zealand personnel and New Zealand defence assets to the Strait of Hormuz?
explanation: A pointed question grounded in the specific wording of the joint statement he just quoted.

text: There is a way to clear the Strait of Hormuz and get the oil flowing again, and it's very simple. It's stop the war; stop the war.
explanation: Identifies the root cause but presents an oversimplified single solution as 'very simple'.

text: ordinary people are waking up to the fact that this Government is acting in the interests of its rich mates and some ideologs—and, in the case of New Zealand First, some conspiracy theory "cookers"—in not acting in the interests of all New Zealanders, the long-term interests, making sure the firefighters get the equipment they need to work. They're doing this because they don't understand, or they're beholden to donors.
explanation: Ad hominem and imputed motives ('beholden to donors', 'rich mates') asserted without evidence.

text: so far, it’s pretty obvious that for a lot of people on the Government benches, you know, math is not their strong point; I’m being very diplomatic here. Not everybody is, you know, mathematically inclined in their reasoning, and it’s obvious that the members in the Government are not mathematically inclined.
explanation: Ad hominem — attributes policy disagreement to opponents' supposed inability to do math rather than any argument.

text: Members opposite may claim to care about equality of opportunity, but unless they address the structural inequities in our economy through progressive taxation, then there is no equality of opportunity.
explanation: Coherent argument linking opportunity to structural inequity, but asserts progressive taxation as the sole route without supporting evidence.

text: All climate action is basically action on cost of living, particularly when we look at the rising cost of oil internationally, so it simply makes sense for New Zealand to become less reliant on imported fossil fuels for transport.
explanation: Plausible cost/import-reliance link but sweeping ('all climate action') and leans on 'it just makes sense'.

text: if you look at page 66 of this report, it shows that New Zealand, far from being a high-tax country, is a country where we’re collecting lower than the OECD average in terms of Government revenue as a percentage of GDP.
explanation: Grounds the claim in a documented source to rebut the 'high-tax' framing.

text: so far, it’s pretty obvious that for a lot of people on the Government benches, you know, math is not their strong point; I’m being very diplomatic here. Not everybody is, you know, mathematically inclined in their reasoning, and it’s obvious that the members in the Government are not mathematically inclined.
explanation: Belittling, us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades the people she's addressing.

text: ordinary people are waking up to the fact that this Government is acting in the interests of its rich mates and some ideologs—and, in the case of New Zealand First, some conspiracy theory "cookers"—in not acting in the interests of all New Zealanders, the long-term interests, making sure the firefighters get the equipment they need to work. They're doing this because they don't understand, or they're beholden to donors.
explanation: Pure us-vs-them framing that demonises opponents; alienating rather than consensus-building.

text: Yeah. It’s been out for years. What are you talking about? It’s like, update your negs, man. God, you’re so out of date.
explanation: Combative put-down that shuts down dialogue.

text: I look forward to changing the Government later this year, to one that cares about our people.
explanation: Implies the current Government does not care about people; partisan rather than unifying.

text: Members opposite may claim to care about equality of opportunity, but unless they address the structural inequities in our economy through progressive taxation, then there is no equality of opportunity.
explanation: Casts opponents' stated values as empty; appeals to her own side rather than seeking common ground.

text: But, luckily, we have an election later this year and we can choose something much more sensible and long term.
explanation: Predicts an election later in 2026 — verifiable and consistent with NZ's fixed parliamentary term; the partisan editorialising aside, the core forecast is reliable.

text: It is true that we do not have enough petrol and diesel, and we are probably going to run out of diesel in the next few weeks.
explanation: Forecasts a national diesel shortage within a few weeks; specific and falsifiable but a strong, uncertain claim hedged with 'probably'.

text: I look forward to changing the Government later this year, to one that cares about our people.
explanation: Asked via the point of order to withdraw and apologise for imputing improper motives, she pivots entirely to a partisan talking point rather than addressing it.

text: it was, I think, a 0.2 percent growth in GDP over the entire last year
explanation: Selectively cites one quarter's figure as the whole year; Nancy Lu notes a 0.9% September quarter, so this understates measured growth.

text: Twenty thousand New Zealanders are still alive, the lowest excess mortality rate in the world—businesses have survived; livelihoods that were protected. That’s what we have to show for it.
explanation: NZ did record among the lowest excess mortality globally, but 'lowest in the world' is likely overstated and the 20,000 figure is a contested modelled estimate.

text: We've actually got a fairly good income tax system. It's well-regarded worldwide; it's fairly clean; there are very few special rules in it giving special treatment to people.
explanation: Broadly accurate: NZ's income tax is internationally regarded as relatively clean with few concessions, though 'well-regarded worldwide' is a mild generalisation.

text: As of today, if you bought a rental property 20 years ago for $500,000 and you sold it today for maybe $1.2 million—because that's the kind of increases we've had in value over the last 20 years—that $700,000 gain would be untaxed. It would be completely free in the seller's hands.
explanation: Accurate description of NZ tax treatment of long-held rental capital gains (outside brightline), and the magnitude reflects real 20-year property appreciation.

text: Labour—and thank you, Sir Michael Cullen—is the party that set up the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, that sovereign wealth fund that will enable us to stay prosperous into the future.
explanation: The NZ Super Fund was established under the Cullen-era Labour government; accurate.

text: if you look at page 66 of this report, it shows that New Zealand, far from being a high-tax country, is a country where we’re collecting lower than the OECD average in terms of Government revenue as a percentage of GDP.
explanation: NZ's general-government revenue as a share of GDP is below the OECD average; consistent with the cited report.

text: All climate action is basically action on cost of living, particularly when we look at the rising cost of oil internationally, so it simply makes sense for New Zealand to become less reliant on imported fossil fuels for transport.
explanation: Reasonable directional claim about import exposure, but the universal framing overstates it.

text: I think 20 years ago, Sue Kedgley was announcing the Green Party policy of an ombudsman on supermarkets, and we saw some version of that finally get implemented.
explanation: Broadly accurate that the Greens long advocated supermarket oversight and a grocery commissioner was later created; the '20 years' and exact framing are approximate.

text: around COVID, the Labour Government spent $60 billion. Nearly half of that was not even related to the COVID pandemic—$60 billion was spent and not even half of that was related to the pandemic itself.
explanation: The 'nearly half unrelated' characterisation is a contested political framing of fiscal-package classification rather than an established fact.

text: In fact, many of those projects—50 percent of those projects—didn’t even start until two years after the funding was approved, so they can hardly be called shovel-ready.
explanation: A specific quantified claim about timing that is plausible given known delivery criticisms but not independently shown here.

text: the large asset programme, or the LSAP, as it’s more affectionately known, has shown losses of $10.5 billion as early as last year—$10.5 billion.
explanation: The Reserve Bank's LSAP has produced multi-billion realised/indemnified losses of roughly this scale; plausible.

text: The average hospital is 45 years old. Education: one-third of our school buildings are more than 50 years old and nearly half are between 20 and 15 years old, many with deferred maintenance.
explanation: Asset-age statistics consistent with infrastructure reporting, though the '20 and 15 years' phrasing is garbled.

text: As at 30 June 2024, the Crown held $571 billion in assets, or roughly $107,000 per person, and $380 billion in liabilities. This leaves a net worth of $191 billion
explanation: Reports Crown balance-sheet figures consistent with the investment statement being debated.

text: We have a plan for action on the cost of living. We have a plan for good jobs at home that pay enough to get ahead. We have a plan for healthcare that you can actually afford and for homes that do not take up all your income.
explanation: Repeated 'we have a plan' with no detail on mechanisms, figures, or timeframes — vague platitudes.

text: They need to consider being good Keynesians; in a downturn, the standard Keynesian rule is to spend in order to support the economy.
explanation: Names a clear economic principle but no specific spending proposals.

text: We know from people like the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and our own Treasury that New Zealand faces a structural deficit—that over time, the amount of Government expenditure is projected to exceed the amount of Government revenue by quite a significant margin.
explanation: Cites named institutions and defines the concept, but no figures for the margin.

text: the way to provide resilience in the energy sector—the way to ensure that we have enough generation—is to go much faster down the renewables route... that we get much more wind and solar power distributed on households, and then to use to some of our existing facilities—our hydro lakes down south, our geothermal power—as our firming.
explanation: Describes a concrete generation mix and the firming/peaking architecture, though without targets or timelines.

text: As of today, if you bought a rental property 20 years ago for $500,000 and you sold it today for maybe $1.2 million—because that's the kind of increases we've had in value over the last 20 years—that $700,000 gain would be untaxed. It would be completely free in the seller's hands.
explanation: Concrete worked example with figures and timeframe illustrating the untaxed-gain point.

text: We have enough—we have enough wealth and resources in Aotearoa to end child poverty. We could do that. It’s a political decision not to do that.
explanation: States a goal (end child poverty) but no mechanism, figures, or named policy for how.

text: We need to change our tax system so that we have options to broaden the revenue base in a progressive way. That means the wealthiest pay more than their fair share.
explanation: States a direction (progressive broadening, wealthy pay more) but no rates, thresholds, or instruments.

text: this Government needs to grapple with the reality that the Roads of National Significance it campaigned on are unfundable and not the best use of money.
explanation: Names a specific programme but asserts 'unfundable' without supporting figures here.

text: Let’s be honest about what this is about: this is about secrecy for the ultra-wealthy.
explanation: Names the actual policy at issue (trust disclosure secrecy) but frames it as a slogan rather than detailing the mechanism.

text: if you look at page 66 of this report, it shows that New Zealand, far from being a high-tax country, is a country where we’re collecting lower than the OECD average in terms of Government revenue as a percentage of GDP.
explanation: Cites a page reference and a specific comparative metric.

text: the residential solar power tweaks that we did was a sensible addition among many in this bill, which make practical changes to make this system more effective. They remove barriers that hold back investment and growth. With this bill, we're backing businesses, attracting investment, and creating the conditions for a stronger economy.
explanation: Opens with one concrete item (solar tweaks) then lapses into general slogans ('backing businesses', 'stronger economy').

text: around COVID, the Labour Government spent $60 billion. Nearly half of that was not even related to the COVID pandemic—$60 billion was spent and not even half of that was related to the pandemic itself.
explanation: Gives a total figure and a proportion.

text: the International Monetary Fund and the OECD estimated the discretionary fiscal response was approximately 20 percent of GDP for our COVID response, and this is among the largest COVID-19 responses globally.
explanation: Cites named sources, a percentage, and a global comparison.

text: The average hospital is 45 years old. Education: one-third of our school buildings are more than 50 years old and nearly half are between 20 and 15 years old, many with deferred maintenance.
explanation: Concrete ages and proportions for the asset base.

text: As at 30 June 2024, the Crown held $571 billion in assets, or roughly $107,000 per person, and $380 billion in liabilities. This leaves a net worth of $191 billion
explanation: Precise dated figures including a per-person breakdown.

text: We had a fast-track process; they repealed it... What was wrong with the fast-track process that we had in place? Nothing, except that Labour did it, and so they flipped it.
explanation: Attributes motive without evidence and dismisses the opposing rationale rather than rebutting it.

text: The more little special rules that are sitting there, the easier it is for people to circumvent the intent of the tax system.
explanation: Reasonable causal argument (more carve-outs leads to more avoidance opportunities), but asserted as a principle without supporting evidence.

text: Twenty thousand New Zealanders are still alive, the lowest excess mortality rate in the world—businesses have survived; livelihoods that were protected. That’s what we have to show for it.
explanation: Defends COVID spending with concrete evidence (mortality, surviving businesses) rather than pure assertion, though 'lowest in the world' leans on overstatement.

text: We know from people like the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and our own Treasury that New Zealand faces a structural deficit—that over time, the amount of Government expenditure is projected to exceed the amount of Government revenue by quite a significant margin.
explanation: Grounds the claim in authoritative sources and defines the deficit clearly.

text: We know that the Inland Revenue Department hasn't collected the data yet, because the income tax year hasn't ended, so there is no data available from the Inland Revenue Department. On what grounds can the Minister say that that policy is a success
explanation: Evidence-focused challenge: success claims require data, and she explains why no data can yet exist (tax year not ended).

text: In fact, many of those projects—50 percent of those projects—didn’t even start until two years after the funding was approved, so they can hardly be called shovel-ready.
explanation: Draws a labelled conclusion ('hardly shovel-ready') from a cited statistic about start times.

text: a bit more than half of that increase, $119 billion, was not new capability; it was re-evaluations driven by inflation; rising land and construction costs, especially for State highways, rail, and public buildings. This means our balance sheet looks stronger on paper without delivering more or better services.
explanation: Distinguishes paper revaluation from real capability — a sound analytical point with a figure attached.

text: Labour is the party that introduced KiwiSaver, that has enabled New Zealanders to build their own savings for retirement.
explanation: Claim of being a long-term-planning party is backed by an actual delivered policy on her own record — words match deeds.

text: It was deeply inconvenient to us as a Government at the time, but I'm looking at it now and thinking, actually, it's really worth looking at.
explanation: Candid admission that her own former government found the 2022 IR briefing inconvenient; self-aware rather than self-serving, a consistent-with-record acknowledgement.

text: We had KiwiSaver set up by a Labour Government and the New Zealand Super Fund set up by a Labour Government.
explanation: Backs the claim of long-term planning with two real, delivered institutions on Labour's record.

text: Labour is the party that introduced KiwiSaver, that has enabled New Zealanders to build their own savings for retirement.
explanation: Names a concrete policy Labour designed and implemented, not merely promised.

text: Labour—and thank you, Sir Michael Cullen—is the party that set up the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, that sovereign wealth fund that will enable us to stay prosperous into the future.
explanation: Credits Labour with a concrete, delivered institution still operating today.

text: We have promised a Future Fund for a future made in New Zealand.
explanation: A promise/announcement with no delivery demonstrated.

text: We had KiwiSaver set up by a Labour Government and the New Zealand Super Fund set up by a Labour Government.
explanation: Points to concrete, enduring policies actually delivered rather than promised.

text: We set up the national resilience plan, which then the National Party scrapped as one of their first decisions coming into Government in 2023.
explanation: Claims delivery of a plan, but undercut by its being scrapped — follow-through did not endure.

text: The Minister of Finance is a failure, and this Budget Policy Statement just reinforces that.
explanation: Blunt personal verdict ('is a failure') on the Minister rather than her policies.

text: That is the party that sold off State assets.
explanation: Pointed attack on opponents' record but addresses a policy action rather than personal character.

text: I think we need a little bit of humility from that side about what might or might not affect New Zealand.
explanation: Pointed but mild rebuke about consistency; aimed at conduct/argument, not personal abuse.

text: someone who sits on an asset and gets the value in it just out of it sitting there pays much less tax on their economic income than our cleaners, our baristas, our supermarket checkout clerks, and so on.
explanation: Makes a substantive equity point about workers vs asset-holders without personal attack.

text: The Minister asserted that we have a broad based – low rate tax, but I do not see how that can be consistent with his assertion that we should not have capital gains. If we're not taxing capital gains, it is not a broad-base system
explanation: Sharp but engages the Minister's actual claim on the substance; no personal attack.

text: none of this is actually logical; it is ideological.
explanation: Dismissive of the Government's motives but framed as a critique of reasoning rather than a personal insult.

text: what this bill does is reduce the supply of housing, or the potential supply of housing, in our largest city by 600,000 units—it's insane. It's bonkers.
explanation: 'Insane'/'bonkers' is hyperbolic but aimed at the policy outcome, not a person.

text: We are truly living in the Upside Down, where we have a Minister of the Government saying ... something that is so demonstrably untrue.
explanation: Accuses the Minister of stating something 'demonstrably untrue' — pointed, edging toward an integrity attack though tied to the bill text.

text: This Government says that they want to cut red tape—oh, but they mean it everywhere but the Epsom electorate.
explanation: Sarcastic accusation of selective hypocrisy directed at the Government.

text: some payments were made to people who were not intended to receive them, such as—wait for it, Sam Uffindell—people who were overseas; think French backpackers or, in some cases, deceased people.
explanation: Uses a vivid, slightly mocking example ('wait for it') though aimed at programme design rather than a person.

text: Do you know anything about transparency, Mr O’Connor?
explanation: A direct personal jibe at a named member rather than substantive debate.

text: In the 1960s, there were seven New Zealanders aged 15 to 64 for every New Zealander over the age of 65. Now, it is the case that it is one in four, and in 2065 it will be one in two.
explanation: The 2065 ratio is a long-range demographic forecast, well-grounded in current projections but inherently uncertain.

text: I think it’s a real problem, when you open this long-term fiscal statement, that you see that debt will reach 200 percent of GDP. At the moment, it’s in the low 40s.
explanation: A 40-year debt forecast; he himself notes it won't materialise, so it's a conditional projection of high uncertainty.

text: where there were, only a few decades ago, 15 taxpayers or working people for every retiree; there’s now only four. In a couple of decades, there will only be two people of working age—and that’s defined as 15 to 64—for every person over 65.
explanation: Projects a 2-to-1 ratio in two decades, consistent with demographic forecasts.

text: I think it is important to have some semblance of respect in this House towards each other. Every member is supposed to be an honourable member.
explanation: Appeals to shared norms across the House, though prompted by a personal grievance.

text: Some of them we can make together. For some of them, quite clearly our values won’t align.
explanation: Acknowledges scope for cross-party cooperation while being honest about differences — a measured, bridge-leaving tone.

text: I do want to acknowledge the Finance and Expenditure Committee's work on this. We had very constructive discussions around whether some of the measures went far enough... I do want to also acknowledge the 275 individuals and groups who submitted on this bill.

text: how does this temporary brief oversight for a few minutes compare with the over $52 million bribe through the Public Interest Journalism Fund?
explanation: Characterising the PIJF as a 'bribe' contingent on running 'a certain narrative' is a misleading mischaracterisation of the fund.

text: if you read the document in 2021 it is as plain as daylight they are being asked “What are the consequences if we make this decision? That's an approval of closure and we're not going to stand by here and turn a document of evidence into something that we can't use.
