text: if you're the architect of a plan to build 100,000 homes and you build less than 1,000, then you'd talk that sort of trash, wouldn't you?
explanation: KiwiBuild's 100,000 target was massively under-delivered, so directionally true; 'less than 1,000' likely understates the eventual count, so partly misleading.

text: This one we don’t quite understand, because, unlike Australia, New Zealand has not expressed explicit support for the US attacks on Iran. Instead, we acknowledged those US attacks and said we understood the reasons behind them, without ourselves endorsing them.
explanation: Draws a precise factual distinction between NZ's 'acknowledged/understood' framing and Australia's explicit support; presented carefully and plausibly accurate.

text: Over the weekend, New Zealand joined a statement with 21 other countries, emphasising the importance of getting ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz so that fuel and goods can be transported freely.
explanation: Specific factual claim about NZ joining a 22-country statement on the Strait of Hormuz; presented as fact, plausible.

text: They lament that the New Zealand Government does not currently place an emphasis on mindless moral posturing and vacuous virtue signalling. You get that? We will never do that. Our focus is on dealing with the world as it is, not as we would wish it to be, and on getting the best possible outcomes for New Zealanders.
explanation: 'Dealing with the world as it is' is a slogan with no concrete policy content.

text: I've got a transitional authority of experts, serious experts, who are going to find that out, but to take a stab in the dark, when you could be out by $10 million or more, would be irresponsible in the extreme.
explanation: Quantifies the potential error ($10 million or more) but provides no actual cost estimate.

text: If we receive a request or if an international coalition was established in the future to safeguard commercial shipping, any possible contribution will be a matter for—guess who!—the Cabinet, first of all, to determine, based on careful consideration of New Zealand’s interests. That’s what we intend to do.
explanation: Specifies the conditional and the decision process (Cabinet, on NZ's interests), though no concrete commitment.

text: This one we don’t quite understand, because, unlike Australia, New Zealand has not expressed explicit support for the US attacks on Iran. Instead, we acknowledged those US attacks and said we understood the reasons behind them, without ourselves endorsing them.
explanation: Specifies exactly what NZ did and did not say, contrasted with Australia.

text: Over the weekend, New Zealand joined a statement with 21 other countries, emphasising the importance of getting ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz so that fuel and goods can be transported freely.
explanation: Names the timeframe, the number of countries (21 others), and the subject of the statement.

text: That account is dedicated to a range of expenses, and if the member would like to write me a letter without squiggles, I shall provide a detailed answer.
explanation: Asked a precise figure (the levy account balance) and refuses to give one, deflecting with a quip.

text: Yes, the former Minster did leave some squiggles on a Cabinet paper. There was, however, no well-developed proposal and, I just want to remind the House, that it was September 2021 when the Labour Cabinet approved the closure of the refinery, and then it took until—
explanation: Asked about a $50m levy surplus for a diesel reserve; minimises ('squiggles') rather than addressing the funds.

text: Yes, I can confirm there was some doodling left on the side of a Cabinet paper by the former Minister. There was, however, no budget, no proposal that I could credibly take forward to my colleagues. Consequently, we’ve taken the option of putting the acid on the oil companies to secure 28 days.
explanation: Partly answers why he scrapped the buffer (no funded proposal) but wraps it in dismissive characterisation rather than engaging the cost evidence raised.

text: As night fell on the last Labour Government and as they fled from their Cabinet offices, there was a half-baked proposal—unfunded, incomplete—and in the interests of good constitutional Government, I couldn't take that forward in that incomplete state.
explanation: Does offer a reason for not proceeding, amid the rhetoric.

text: I have received advice from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) confirming that fuel supply remains healthy, with strong stock levels across New Zealand. MBIE is now reporting the fuel stock and fuel shipment data two times a week. I say again, echoing the Minister of Finance’s contribution in public engagements: we have 50 days of petrol, 45 days of diesel, and 44 days of jet fuel.
explanation: Directly answers Foster's question on what energy-security reports he has received.

text: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I would say to Billy Clemens: be very careful how people may use your quotes for political advantage in Parliament.
explanation: Entirely dodges the substantive freight-vulnerability concern, addressing the quoted person instead.

text: Just in the last few hours, it has announced that those who face the greatest and most acute challenges with the cost of living are going to get an extra $50 a week to help absorb the pressure of this crisis, and we’re doing it in a way that is targeted, that is temporary, and that is timely.
explanation: Pivots from Verrall's questions about home-care workers and prescription fees to the new package, partially addressing cost-of-living but not the specific points.

text: When the Opposition say, “Oh, we already had ferries arriving.”, maybe you did, but you didn’t know how to fit them through the channel that they had to pass through, you didn’t have the ports that they needed to load and unload, so you are pointing to a fantasy rather than a solution.
explanation: Partly addresses resilience by referencing the affordable rail-enabled pathway, but mainly relitigates the past plan.

text: I absolutely have confidence in the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries because he has listened to feedback and changed course. He’s listened to what people out there are saying and actually adapted his course to do the right thing.
explanation: Directly affirms confidence and gives a reason (the Minister changed course on the reforms).

text: The number one factor is that we need to ensure that Government behaviour does not add to inflation... we wanted to help people who are in the greatest need so we said that this is for people who are on the lower end of the income scale and who have children and who work... and we linked it to petrol prices so that if petrol prices come back down, we stop spending the money.
explanation: Directly answers what factors the Government weighed.

text: If we receive a request or if an international coalition was established in the future to safeguard commercial shipping, any possible contribution will be a matter for—guess who!—the Cabinet, first of all, to determine, based on careful consideration of New Zealand’s interests. That’s what we intend to do.
explanation: Directly addresses the central charge (that NZ is committing forces) by stating any contribution would require a future Cabinet decision.

text: I've got a transitional authority of experts, serious experts, who are going to find that out, but to take a stab in the dark, when you could be out by $10 million or more, would be irresponsible in the extreme.
explanation: Declines to give a figure but explains why (no reliable basis yet) and who will determine it — a reasoned non-answer.

text: Oh, well, in the interests of making democracy efficient, I apologise if I’ve upset the tender mercies of Taranaki.
explanation: Withdraws under pressure but the mocking tone undercuts the sincerity of the apology.

text: We have for decades stood up for freedom of navigation in the Middle East and through the Indo-Pacific.
explanation: Frames the current stance as consistent with a long-standing, bipartisan NZ position on freedom of navigation; broadly defensible.

text: The Government's intention has always been to support industry members as they transition away from greyhound racing. … The bill allows for support, and the transition agency has flexibility to provide for additional compensation, such as for lost income, should this be seen as necessary.
explanation: Claims consistency between stated intent and the bill's provisions, pointing to mechanisms already in the law.

text: this is a great bill, which I am very proud to be commending to the House.
explanation: Vague praise ('a great bill') with no substantive detail about what the bill does or why.

text: The Reserve Bank said, last October, that during the pandemic, aggressive fiscal and monetary support helped avert deeper harm, but that the combined responses ultimately contributed to an inflation outbreak.
explanation: Attributes the claim to a named body and timeframe.

text: Treasury’s long-term insights briefing, highlighted by the finance Minister last August, examined the way the Government finances were used during and after the COVID period and said that the responses wound up costing NZ$66 billion
explanation: Names the source, the figure, and the timing.

text: temporary, targeted, and timely support for 143,000 of the working families with children, to support them through this very tough time, through the in-work tax credit.
explanation: Names the mechanism (in-work tax credit), the cohort, and a figure (143,000).

text: the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, who mentioned only just one quarter of the growth—very, very selective in her speech, that she failed to mentioned the 0.9 percent growth in the September 2025 quarter, then followed by another positive-growth quarter of 0.2 percent in the December quarter. Together, that is 1.1 percent growth in the last half year
explanation: Exact quarterly growth figures with named quarters.

text: I want to acknowledge those that were involved in building the straight track at the Wanganui Racecourse for its positive impact on the health of greyhounds since that has been opened.
explanation: Asserts a positive welfare impact from the straight track; plausible and specific but offered without evidence and hard to verify.

text: I wanted to particularly thank all the members on the Finance and Expenditure Committee, including all the parties that have provided a lot of very valuable feedback, as well as the submitters who came before us and gave us real-life examples.
explanation: Wholly respectful acknowledgement of colleagues and contributors; no attack or sensationalism.

text: absolutely no to the spending, spending, spending on reckless projects like the last Government.
explanation: Critique of the previous government's fiscal approach; partisan and repetitive but policy-directed.

text: the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, who mentioned only just one quarter of the growth—very, very selective in her speech, that she failed to mentioned the 0.9 percent growth in the September 2025 quarter, then followed by another positive-growth quarter of 0.2 percent in the December quarter. Together, that is 1.1 percent growth in the last half year
explanation: Accuses an opponent of being 'very selective' but backs it with data rather than abuse.

text: I just want to take the opportunity to acknowledge the trainers, the industry players, and, particularly, those from Whanganui who are affected by the closure of this industry.
explanation: Respectful and considerate; focuses on affected people, no attacks or rancour.

text: I wanted to particularly thank all the members on the Finance and Expenditure Committee, including all the parties that have provided a lot of very valuable feedback, as well as the submitters who came before us and gave us real-life examples.
explanation: Inclusive and gracious, explicitly crediting all parties and submitters—consensus-building across the aisle.

text: discipline is not cruelty; discipline now in our Government spending is actually about protecting New Zealand, to give Government headroom to act when the next shock arrives.
explanation: Tries to reframe austerity sympathetically with a memorable line, but speaks to those already sympathetic rather than bridging.

text: I know that a number of people were very unsettled about the changes that Labour brought in around being able to do this and to be able to use this information for the development of policy, and so there were some suggestions that, OK, if people were that unsettled by it, then maybe we could put in some stronger guardrails around that in terms of how it can be used, and all those kinds of things, but that was not agreed to.
explanation: Consistently defends a policy Labour itself introduced, acknowledges the objections to it, and reports an offered compromise (stronger guardrails)—a coherent, principled position rather than a reversal.

text: The only difference is that in Government, when we saw something shutting down, as a Cabinet, we discussed it; we took a paper to Cabinet, and we said, “What are the implications for New Zealand? We need to put a plan in place to respond to that.” Have we seen this Government do that? No, we have not.
explanation: Claims a consistent process for her own former government; plausible but self-serving and unverified here.

text: we think opening up that window and getting that information out there for a longer time is good for our democracy and we can support that.
explanation: Supports a transparency measure on principle even though it comes from opponents, consistent with her stated value of transparency.

text: one of the things that we have been pushing for—which we have not been able to see in this bill—is the introduction of a tax-free threshold for lower-income earners, because, frankly, that’s what they do across the Ditch, in Australia.
explanation: Consistent with the Greens' established advocacy for tax reform and redistribution; 'we have been pushing for' aligns with the party's record.

text: The bill limits objections to those who live or work in the local council area or within 1 kilometre of the proposed licence... In one case, a venue spent $45,000 preparing for a hearing that the objector didn't even turn up for.
explanation: The anecdote is plausible but unverifiable from the text.

text: The ministerial video was mistakenly uploaded to the wrong site. When brought to my attention it was resolved within about 15 minutes, and an email to the sector was sent this morning with the correct link to the same video.
explanation: A specific account of events (wrong upload, 15-minute fix) — plausible, not independently verifiable here.

text: This work has been shaped by extensive sector engagement; more than 10,000 New Zealanders took part in consultation, alongside detailed input from a principal advisory group and sector experts.
explanation: A factual participation claim, plausible but unverifiable from the text.

text: There are currently 12 known refugee claims from people who have been convicted of serious offences in New Zealand, including for murder, accessory to murder, rape, indecent acts on a child, drug offences, and dangerous driving causing death.
explanation: A concrete, checkable statistic offered to justify the policy; plausible and presented as official.

text: This bill makes a series of changes which will free New Zealanders and businesses from the stranglehold of red tape and support economic growth.

text: The bill limits objections to those who live or work in the local council area or within 1 kilometre of the proposed licence... In one case, a venue spent $45,000 preparing for a hearing that the objector didn't even turn up for.
explanation: Concrete mechanism (1 km / same council area) plus a dollar figure example.

text: They also strengthen safeguards around rapid alcohol delivery to protect against sales to minors and intoxicated people. In short, these reforms cut red tape, back local decision-making, and take practical steps towards keeping our communities safe.
explanation: Names a concrete safeguard area (rapid delivery to minors/intoxicated) alongside more general claims.

text: If you come to New Zealand and you comply with our laws and contribute, you are welcome here. But if you are convicted of criminal offending or provide false or fraudulent information, you should be expected to be required to leave.
explanation: States the principle and the trigger conditions but not the operational detail.

text: This work has been shaped by extensive sector engagement; more than 10,000 New Zealanders took part in consultation, alongside detailed input from a principal advisory group and sector experts.
explanation: Quantifies consultation (10,000+ participants) and names advisory structures.

text: The reports will provide a snapshot of school performance across 14 areas including literacy and numeracy, school achievement, attendance, equity, and provision for learners with additional needs.
explanation: Quantifies the scope (14 areas) and names several concrete categories.

text: As we speak, 86 writing groups of writers and subject experts schools across the country are creating a senior secondary curriculum in 175 subject areas. This national curriculum will be internationally benchmarked and will drive what is assessed in our new national qualification.
explanation: Cites concrete figures: 86 writing groups and 175 subject areas.

text: There are currently 12 known refugee claims from people who have been convicted of serious offences in New Zealand, including for murder, accessory to murder, rape, indecent acts on a child, drug offences, and dangerous driving causing death.
explanation: A precise count (12) and an itemised list of offence types.

text: I know that the member is very excited about her very first question as education spokesperson and would love a great conspiracy, but unfortunately there is not one here. But I look forward to her next question abut something that is relevant to achievement.
explanation: Condescending personal framing of the questioner ('excited', 'would love a conspiracy').

text: Genuine consultation is about making sure you take time to get the detail right... Perhaps if this good process had been followed the last time NCEA was refreshed, it wouldn’t have been such an unmitigated disaster—take note.
explanation: Pointed dig at the previous refresh as an 'unmitigated disaster'; criticises a process but with a barbed 'take note'.

text: I know that the member is very excited about her very first question as education spokesperson and would love a great conspiracy, but unfortunately there is not one here. But I look forward to her next question abut something that is relevant to achievement.
explanation: Dodges the 'pattern of behaviour' question by dismissing it.

text: It was human error. Of course, I take responsibility for all of the things that happen in my office, as you would expect.
explanation: Addresses the responsibility question, though leaves the 'who authorised' specifics unanswered.

text: As we speak, 86 writing groups of writers and subject experts schools across the country are creating a senior secondary curriculum in 175 subject areas. This national curriculum will be internationally benchmarked and will drive what is assessed in our new national qualification.
explanation: Addresses how curriculum drives assessment, though somewhat at the level of process.

text: The ministerial video was mistakenly uploaded to the wrong site. When brought to my attention it was resolved within about 15 minutes, and an email to the sector was sent this morning with the correct link to the same video.
explanation: Directly explains the error and the remedy in response to the question.

text: Today, I announced the first major step in rebuilding New Zealand’s senior secondary qualification, with Cabinet agreeing to major structural decisions to replace NCEA with a new system... The new qualification across years 12 and 13, and the stand-alone foundational award in literacy and numeracy, will be phased from 2028 with a foundational award; 2029 for the year 12 qualification; and 2030 for year 13.
explanation: Directly answers what she announced with concrete detail.

text: The bill limits objections to those who live or work in the local council area or within 1 kilometre of the proposed licence... In one case, a venue spent $45,000 preparing for a hearing that the objector didn't even turn up for.
explanation: Relies on a single anecdote ($45,000 case) to justify a general rule.

text: This bill makes a series of changes which will free New Zealanders and businesses from the stranglehold of red tape and support economic growth.
explanation: Introduction of a bill is action-in-progress, not delivered reform.

text: From term 2 this year, parents will have access to clearer, more useful information about how their child's school is performing... The new ERO reports will focus on student achievement, progress, and engagement, with clear measures, visual summaries, as well as more detail in the back end.
explanation: An announced overhaul not yet implemented — intent with delivery pending.

text: Today, I announced the first major step in rebuilding New Zealand’s senior secondary qualification, with Cabinet agreeing to major structural decisions to replace NCEA with a new system... The new qualification across years 12 and 13, and the stand-alone foundational award in literacy and numeracy, will be phased from 2028 with a foundational award; 2029 for the year 12 qualification; and 2030 for year 13.
explanation: An announcement of Cabinet decisions with future rollout; structural decision taken but delivery years away, not yet implemented.

text: The Government has progressed the Immigration (Enhanced Risk Management) Amendment Bill to improve the integrity of our immigration system and strengthen the consequences for serious offending. … This bill delivers practical, targeted changes to improve compliance and enforcement, increase the maximum penalty for migrant exploitation, and ensure there are immigration consequences for criminal offending.
explanation: A bill progressed (introduced/advancing), showing follow-through, though not yet enacted.

text: Well, I have raised expectations with the Director-General of Health that advice is made sufficiently clear to both Ministers and the public. Equally, I understand that as a Minister, I’m obligated to question advice as it is presented to me... It is critically important that we have transparency about the information we have in this regard.
explanation: Describes actions taken (raising expectations with the DG) but they are process commitments, not delivered outcomes.

text: Health New Zealand will invest an additional $25 million to prepare our healthcare system for higher demand over the busy winter months... This important investment in preparation for winter will deliver up to 378 additional front-line staff, 71 extra winter hospital beds, and up to 567 short-stay beds in aged residential care to free up hospital capacity.
explanation: A newly announced investment with 'up to' targets; commitment stated, delivery still prospective.

text: The sector has been calling out for this change since 2022. We heard their calls, and we have delivered.
explanation: Claims delivery on a long-standing sector ask, though the change takes effect 'next year'.

text: the latest quarterly results for October to December 2025 showing 74.2 percent of patients being admitted, discharged, or transferred within 6 hours, up from 72.1 percent at the same time the year before.
explanation: Points to a measured improvement against a reinstated target, evidencing some delivery.

text: 62.2 percent of patients are now receiving their first specialist assessment within four months, up from 60.6 percent the same time the year before; while 64.5 percent of patients are receiving their elective treatment within four months, up from 59.2 percent the same time the year before... 179,816 first specialist assessments carried out in this quarter, up by more than 11,000 compared to the same time the year before; and 51,513 elective treatments, up by more than 4,500 compared to the same time the year before.
explanation: Claims credit for measurable improvements actually being delivered.

text: It was human error. Of course, I take responsibility for all of the things that happen in my office, as you would expect.
explanation: Owns the mistake rather than deflecting; words align with accepting accountability.

text: instead what we'd see are New Zealand – trained graduate nurses getting on the plane with the tens of thousands of other young New Zealanders who are leaving the country because they do not see a future here. We are in danger of becoming a training ground for Australia when it comes to our medical professionals.
explanation: Predicts continued emigration of NZ-trained nurses; directionally consistent with current outflow trends but magnitude uncertain.

text: I want to, first of all, acknowledge the Iranian people... any family in a conflict zone is in a horrific place, but, of course, the brutal regime that they have had to survive under for some decades is terrible as well.
explanation: Respectful, measured tone that engages the humanitarian substance.

text: Words matter, and we need to dial it back a notch from some of the rhetoric that we've heard on the other side of the House.
explanation: Calls for restraint and lower temperature, though directed pointedly at 'the other side'.

text: thanks to this Trump-loving, MAGA hat - wearing, Aotearoa-hating, New Zealand First, ACT, and National coalition
explanation: String of personal/character insults ('Aotearoa-hating', 'MAGA hat-wearing') aimed at opponents, not policy.

text: It's emblematic of what this Government has done through the entire term: giving tax cuts to big landlords, big fossil, and big tobacco.
explanation: Rhetorical 'big landlords/fossil/tobacco' framing characterises motives rather than engaging specifics.

text: The so-called digital nomad tax exemption stems from some fantasy that this Government has that the way to create a modern, resilient, productive economy is to sell our country to foreign investors. It is selling to them our conservation land, allowing them to buy our houses, and now, apparently, exempting them from the tax regimes in this country.
explanation: Attributes a 'fantasy' motive to the government rather than engaging the policy's stated rationale.

text: This Government, like the French generals of World War II, are fighting the last war.
explanation: Pointed critique of approach via metaphor, not a personal attack.

text: Now, there is one good measure, and I want to front-foot it because I'm a positive guy. I like to start by saying positive things. One good measure that this bill does that we do support is the change to exempt income from selling electricity to the grid. That is a good change.
explanation: Constructive, acknowledges merit in an opponent's bill.

text: I give you, then, international law on the law of the sea and the rights for this country and other countries to be able to have commercial shipping, and we call on Iran to comply with the United Nations Security Council Resolution 2817.
explanation: Grounds the position in a concrete legal instrument rather than rhetoric.

text: I can tell those members on the other side who has to fight those fights; it's actually our Defence Force. Frankly, I'm not putting them forward if we don't have to do something, because it's their lives while people on the other side are talking from their very, very excited position of holier than thou.
explanation: Reasonable point that real personnel bear the risk, but leans on an emotive 'holier than thou' framing.

text: there was the same issue prior to this Government, except that it was worse because, under the extensive and overdone lockdowns in Auckland, the home of most Pasifika people in New Zealand, many young people were denied their education... attendance rates were a mere 17 percent.
explanation: Uses a single anecdotal 17% attendance figure from one principal in 2021 to characterise the prior era.

text: we had a situation, that we inherited, of massive inflation, up to over 7 percent. Debt—just the interest rates alone that the Minister of Finance is having to find money for—of $11 billion a year extra every single year; basically, borrowed money paying for borrowed money.
explanation: Blames the prior government for inherited conditions but doesn't connect this to the Pasifika outcomes asked about.

text: It's endorsed and cosigned by many countries that we would typically have strong and close partnerships with—the United Kingdom, France, Netherlands, Canada, Japan. They've all signed on because they also understand the importance of the international rules-based system.
explanation: Supports the case with the fact of broad co-signing, but partly an appeal to the company kept rather than the statement's merits.

text: thanks to this Trump-loving, MAGA hat - wearing, Aotearoa-hating, New Zealand First, ACT, and National coalition
explanation: Ad hominem with no evidence offered for the characterisations.

text: This Government, like the French generals of World War II, are fighting the last war.
explanation: Argument by historical analogy; rhetorically apt but does little to establish the claim on its own.

text: We know that 311 of the wealthiest families in Aotearoa already hold more wealth than the bottom 50 percent.
explanation: Uses a concrete statistic to support the inequality argument, though cited loosely.

text: The Budget Policy Statement does not mention the word “resilience” or the phrase “climate change” even once.
explanation: Uses a verifiable textual fact to support a point about the Government's priorities.

text: countries, like the United States, that are net exporters of oil are being affected by this crisis and are having their fuel prices increase as well, because fossil fuel is a global commodity in traded in global markets, whereas local renewable energy generation, such as this bill is encouraging through the renewable energy income tax exemption, is traded locally and means it’s exempt from the global oil shocks that we are seeing
explanation: Logically sound: uses the US net-exporter case to show domestic refining wouldn't insulate prices, since oil clears globally.

text: That is something that New Zealand has stood in strong support of over many, many years and in many parts of the world. That's why we sent a vessel up through the Taiwan Strait as well.
explanation: NZ did sail a vessel through the Taiwan Strait — substantially accurate.

text: They don't want to know how much racism there is in our community, because under Christopher Luxon it's got worse.
explanation: An unmeasurable and unsupported assertion that racism 'got worse' under a named leader.

text: child poverty has got worse under this Government as well. It got worse and is getting worse, because this is not a Government that cares.
explanation: Child poverty trends are contested across measures; the claim is asserted without the figures and bundled with a motive attribution.

text: this Government defunded—stopped building—3,500 social houses
explanation: Cites a specific figure on cancelled social housing; directionally consistent with reported cuts but the exact number is contestable.

text: the wellbeing Budget was a world-leading idea. It was well established. The OECD absolutely was watching what was going on in New Zealand because they wanted to know, how do you measure things that really count?
explanation: Accurate that NZ's wellbeing Budget drew international/OECD interest, though 'world-leading' is a favourable framing.

text: New Zealand has a proud history of accepting people who are from conflict zones or who are oppressed in their home country and giving them refuge here, including people who arrive and claim asylum
explanation: Broadly accurate characterisation of NZ's refugee/asylum history.

text: in Australia, one in five cars sold are electric; in China, one in two new cars sold are electric. The global average is one in four new cars sold are electric
explanation: Comparative international stats; China figure is plausible but the 'global average one in four' is likely overstated for the period.

explanation: Reasonable inference from concentration to weakened competition, consistent with the Commerce Commission's own findings.

text: at its heart, it’s not just a technical reform of the Commerce Commission; it’s a political choice. It’s a deliberate choice to weaken every watchdog that helps keep prices down for Kiwi families
explanation: Hyperbolic generalisation ('every watchdog') asserting deliberate intent to weaken oversight without evidence.

text: The war in Iran is already driving up oil prices, disrupting supply chains, and pushing inflationary pressures across the world.
explanation: Implicitly forecasts continued inflationary flow-through ('higher grocery bills are coming next'); directionally plausible but magnitude uncertain.

text: In fact, we’re not borrowing a cent to provide this relief at all.
explanation: Asserts the relief package is unborrowed; plausible as a framing of targeted relief but presented absolutely without supporting fiscal detail.

text: We know that a handful of supermarket giants dominate around 80 percent of the grocery market. We know that this level of concentration limits competition and keeps prices higher than they need to be
explanation: Accurate that two major chains dominate roughly 80%+ of NZ grocery sales.

text: The war in Iran is already driving up oil prices, disrupting supply chains, and pushing inflationary pressures across the world.
explanation: Consistent with the text's premise of a conflict-driven fuel crisis raising oil prices; specifics can't be fully verified from the text.

text: The other side of the House had six years to do something about competition, so that they could bring grocery prices down. It didn’t happen in six years; at least on this side of the House, we’re moving.
explanation: Labour was in government roughly six years and grocery competition remained concentrated; fair as far as it goes, though it elides the Grocery Commissioner Labour did create.

text: Some members of the House that had six years to do something about it didn't do something about it.
explanation: Labour governed roughly six years; the claim it 'did nothing' on housing is an overstatement but has some basis.

text: I think 20 years ago, Sue Kedgley was announcing the Green Party policy of an ombudsman on supermarkets, and we saw some version of that finally get implemented.
explanation: Claims a long-held, consistent party position on supermarket regulation, consistent with the Greens' record.

text: Obviously, we are supporting this bill, and we enjoyed going through the process.
explanation: Cooperative and respectful engagement on the substance of the bill.

text: These were changes that were made by a previous National-Act Government in establishing Auckland Transport, but bringing these functions back now under elected members feels like the right thing to do. It strengthens, we believe, both voice and responsibility.
explanation: Notes the policy history matter-of-factly without partisan point-scoring.

text: Submitters did also raise some concerns, though, that there was the potential that some of that decision making could become fragmented across, I think there’s 21, local boards. There will be some work needed in that sphere
explanation: Even-handed treatment of opposing concerns.

text: The Reserve Bank said, last October, that during the pandemic, aggressive fiscal and monetary support helped avert deeper harm, but that the combined responses ultimately contributed to an inflation outbreak.
explanation: A balanced, fairly stated paraphrase of the Reserve Bank's position acknowledging both benefit and inflationary cost.

text: Treasury’s long-term insights briefing, highlighted by the finance Minister last August, examined the way the Government finances were used during and after the COVID period and said that the responses wound up costing NZ$66 billion
explanation: Cites a Treasury figure, but '$66 billion costing' is a contestable headline number whose framing as pure 'cost' may overstate.

text: Fitch Ratings have now placed New Zealand’s AA+ long-term credit rating on a negative outlook.
explanation: A specific, checkable claim about a ratings action, corroborated by another speaker (Bidois).

text: the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, who mentioned only just one quarter of the growth—very, very selective in her speech, that she failed to mentioned the 0.9 percent growth in the September 2025 quarter, then followed by another positive-growth quarter of 0.2 percent in the December quarter. Together, that is 1.1 percent growth in the last half year
explanation: Cites specific Stats NZ quarterly figures; the figures look accurate, though summing two quarters to '1.1% in the last half year' is a slightly loose construction.

text: the Reserve Bank Governor also warned—just yesterday, actually—that the conflict in the Middle East now is likely to mean higher headline inflation pressure in the near term and will somewhat weaken the growth momentum that we have finally developed
explanation: Attributed to the Governor 'yesterday'; an accurate-sounding relay of an authoritative forecast.

text: a big part of that came about over the COVID period, when we borrowed $60 billion, $30 billion of which didn’t go to COVID expenses.
explanation: The borrowing figure is in the right range; the claim that '$30 billion didn’t go to COVID expenses' is a contestable partisan characterisation.

text: We’re paying $10 billion in interest now, and that’s in a year. That is the combined expenses of the New Zealand Police, the Department of Corrections, the Ministry of Justice, the Customs Service, and the New Zealand Defence Force.
explanation: The ~$10bn interest cost is plausible; the claimed equivalence to those five agencies' combined budgets is unverified.

text: our good reputation for our sovereign risk profile was trashed with the summary announcement of the oil and gas ban some years ago.
explanation: Strong causal claim that the oil-and-gas ban 'trashed' NZ's sovereign risk reputation; not supported by NZ's credit ratings over that period.

text: One entity that I know of was lining up an investment from money markets, and they were told, “No, we’re not going to give you that money any more.” It was all signed off and they cancelled it
explanation: Unverifiable second-hand account of an unnamed entity.

text: Education: an hour of reading, writing, and maths—fantastic. That’s the future that we’re investing in and we should focus on that, and the feedback from the schools and from parents is that that has been such a hit that children are making real progress in the confidence that they are growing
explanation: 'Children are making real progress' is an outcome claim supported only by anecdotal feedback.

text: The Reserve Bank said, last October, that during the pandemic, aggressive fiscal and monetary support helped avert deeper harm, but that the combined responses ultimately contributed to an inflation outbreak.
explanation: Cites a dated, authoritative source and represents both sides of its finding.

text: Treasury’s long-term insights briefing, highlighted by the finance Minister last August, examined the way the Government finances were used during and after the COVID period and said that the responses wound up costing NZ$66 billion
explanation: Sourced, but leans on a single dramatic number to carry a broad lesson.

text: the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, who mentioned only just one quarter of the growth—very, very selective in her speech, that she failed to mentioned the 0.9 percent growth in the September 2025 quarter, then followed by another positive-growth quarter of 0.2 percent in the December quarter. Together, that is 1.1 percent growth in the last half year
explanation: Rebuts a specific claim with the omitted quarter's figures and an arithmetic total.

text: discipline is not cruelty; discipline now in our Government spending is actually about protecting New Zealand, to give Government headroom to act when the next shock arrives.
explanation: Offers a coherent rationale (fiscal headroom for future shocks) for the discipline argument.

text: We’re paying $10 billion in interest now, and that’s in a year. That is the combined expenses of the New Zealand Police, the Department of Corrections, the Ministry of Justice, the Customs Service, and the New Zealand Defence Force.
explanation: Uses a comparison to convey scale; the equivalence is illustrative and the agency-budget sum is asserted.

text: our good reputation for our sovereign risk profile was trashed with the summary announcement of the oil and gas ban some years ago.
explanation: Sweeping causal attribution offered without evidence beyond assertion.

text: One entity that I know of was lining up an investment from money markets, and they were told, “No, we’re not going to give you that money any more.” It was all signed off and they cancelled it
explanation: Single unnamed anecdote used to support a broad claim about sovereign risk — appeal to anecdote.

text: a big part of that came about over the COVID period, when we borrowed $60 billion, $30 billion of which didn’t go to COVID expenses.
explanation: Concrete dollar figures and a breakdown.

text: We’re paying $10 billion in interest now, and that’s in a year. That is the combined expenses of the New Zealand Police, the Department of Corrections, the Ministry of Justice, the Customs Service, and the New Zealand Defence Force.
explanation: A precise figure with a vivid, concrete equivalence to named agencies' budgets.

text: Education: an hour of reading, writing, and maths—fantastic. That’s the future that we’re investing in and we should focus on that, and the feedback from the schools and from parents is that that has been such a hit that children are making real progress in the confidence that they are growing
explanation: Names the concrete policy but measures 'progress' only impressionistically.

text: For us, it is imperative that we do have a long-term plan, we do invest in our future, and we set up a reason for our young people to stay—not something we have seen from this Government.
explanation: Sweeping stated intent with no concrete commitment or delivery described.

text: If the Greens were in Government, this Budget Policy Statement would deliver relief for real people who need it the most, a payment to adults who are below the median income, and free universal public transport
explanation: Hypothetical commitments from opposition with no delivery possible or described.

text: I said no, I’m not writing another strategy, we’re forming an action plan with projects on it and we’re going to implement them, and we did.
explanation: Claims concrete follow-through ('and we did') on an action plan during his regional development role; delivery asserted but not detailed.

text: temporary, targeted, and timely support for 143,000 of the working families with children, to support them through this very tough time, through the in-work tax credit.
explanation: Describes an actual announced support measure, though it is just announced and its delivery is in progress.

text: Education: an hour of reading, writing, and maths—fantastic. That’s the future that we’re investing in and we should focus on that, and the feedback from the schools and from parents is that that has been such a hit that children are making real progress in the confidence that they are growing
explanation: Points to an implemented policy (the hour of core subjects) and claimed positive uptake, though outcomes are asserted from 'feedback'.

text: The Minister of Finance is a failure, and this Budget Policy Statement just reinforces that.
explanation: Combative closing aimed at her own side, not persuasion of the undecided.

text: By 2030, we could have saved 1.3 billion litres of petrol just from the Clean Car Discount and the feebate discounts alone.
explanation: Counterfactual projection to 2030; directionally plausible but the exact magnitude is uncertain and unverifiable.

text: the Reserve Bank Governor also warned—just yesterday, actually—that the conflict in the Middle East now is likely to mean higher headline inflation pressure in the near term and will somewhat weaken the growth momentum that we have finally developed
explanation: Relays a near-term forecast of higher inflation and weaker growth that is plausible given an oil shock, though uncertain in magnitude.

text: The Minister of Finance has said today, “Look, actually, on balance, the net impact on the balance sheet is not going to be positive.” For most New Zealanders... the Government is not making money out of this crisis.
explanation: Acknowledges a negative fiscal impact rather than spinning it, consistent with the Government's stated fiscal-prudence line.

text: Submitters did also raise some concerns, though, that there was the potential that some of that decision making could become fragmented across, I think there’s 21, local boards. There will be some work needed in that sphere
explanation: Candidly concedes a downside of a bill her party supports, rather than only its merits.

text: Based on the most recent figures published by Stats New Zealand, 48 percent of all children in material hardship—around 81,000—are in working households. Not all of these children will be in households eligible for the in-work tax credit, as some families in material hardship have incomes above the Working for Families threshold.
explanation: Proactively corrects an inaccurate answer she gave earlier on the Minister's behalf.

text: So far, all I've got is nonsensical comments from the Leader of the Opposition, on what is actually really important to people.
explanation: Dismisses the opposition's questions as 'nonsensical' rather than engaging them.

text: It does set a problematic precedent if there's an expectation that, when an industry has fallen out of favour with the public and has moved beyond being acceptable, in terms of social licence, they will be compensated if the Government does what is appropriate and brings an end to that industry.
explanation: Engages the substance of the opposing amendment respectfully.

text: in the last two years, I'm extremely proud, as a country, of how, in fact, we didn't wait for Mr Jerry Mateparae's report to come back to us after Cyclone Gabrielle; the whole of our emergency management system had already responded … We've never been in a stronger position to be able to respond to these events.
explanation: 'Never been in a stronger position' is an unverifiable self-assessment.

text: It does set a problematic precedent if there's an expectation that, when an industry has fallen out of favour with the public and has moved beyond being acceptable, in terms of social licence, they will be compensated if the Government does what is appropriate and brings an end to that industry.
explanation: Articulates a clear principled objection about precedent, with the conclusion following the premise.

text: I have a proposed amendment to Mr. Luxton's Amendment Paper 567 … at new clause 35: '(2) The purpose of the review is to—(a) assess the extent of transitional challenges for any affected person … and (b) recommend the establishment of a scheme that seeks to support retraining for those affected persons.' It very specifically narrows the scope just to support and retraining.
explanation: Offers a concrete, reasoned alternative that addresses the worker-transition concern while avoiding the compensation precedent.

text: how much monetary cost does he think is about to be imposed on the participants of the industry? How much … in a compensation regime … How much would an independent reviewer say, 'This is lost capital investment which has been made valueless after the closing of this industry.'? How much retraining cost?
explanation: Structures the inquiry logically, though largely rhetorical and repetitive in pressing the Minister.

text: I have a proposed amendment to Mr. Luxton's Amendment Paper 567 … at new clause 35: '(2) The purpose of the review is to—(a) assess the extent of transitional challenges for any affected person … and (b) recommend the establishment of a scheme that seeks to support retraining for those affected persons.' It very specifically narrows the scope just to support and retraining.
explanation: Quotes precise amendment text and explains exactly how it narrows the scope.

text: how much monetary cost does he think is about to be imposed on the participants of the industry? How much … in a compensation regime … How much would an independent reviewer say, 'This is lost capital investment which has been made valueless after the closing of this industry.'? How much retraining cost?
explanation: Breaks the cost question into distinct components (lost earnings, lost capital, retraining).

text: in the last two years, I'm extremely proud, as a country, of how, in fact, we didn't wait for Mr Jerry Mateparae's report to come back to us after Cyclone Gabrielle; the whole of our emergency management system had already responded … We've never been in a stronger position to be able to respond to these events.
explanation: Asked for assurances that emergency vehicles will have guaranteed diesel access, he pivots to the Cyclone Gabrielle response and a general boast.

text: I have a proposed amendment to Mr. Luxton's Amendment Paper 567 … at new clause 35: '(2) The purpose of the review is to—(a) assess the extent of transitional challenges for any affected person … and (b) recommend the establishment of a scheme that seeks to support retraining for those affected persons.' It very specifically narrows the scope just to support and retraining.
explanation: Seeks middle ground that recognises the Minister's intent and the workers' needs.

text: this was never going to be a painless exercise, but the fact is that the dogs are no longer going to be in pain.
explanation: A neat rhetorical close that reframes the cost in terms of animal welfare, appealing chiefly to supporters of the ban.

text: the development of future storage capacity is under way as we work through a proposal. This proposal will happen not over three or four years but in a matter of months.
explanation: Describes work under way but it is a proposal in progress, not delivered capacity.

text: in the last two years, I'm extremely proud, as a country, of how, in fact, we didn't wait for Mr Jerry Mateparae's report to come back to us after Cyclone Gabrielle; the whole of our emergency management system had already responded … We've never been in a stronger position to be able to respond to these events.
explanation: Claims a strong emergency-management response record but does not address the diesel-supply guarantee asked about.

text: the development of future storage capacity is under way as we work through a proposal. This proposal will happen not over three or four years but in a matter of months.
explanation: Predicts new storage capacity within months rather than years — an optimistic, falsifiable timeframe given infrastructure realities.

text: There is scope to rapidly develop the capacity for 90 million litres worth of storage in a matter of months. I suspect the person who made that stupid remark in the media was reading the Māori calendar or something like that.
explanation: Predicts 90 million litres of storage developed within months — a specific, falsifiable but optimistic claim.

text: Is tomorrow's minimum wage increase of just 2 percent, or 45c, enough for working families to keep on top of the bills when inflation was over 3 percent in the last year and is likely to be even higher this year—especially when we know beneficiaries and other low earners typically face worse inflation than others?
explanation: Predicts inflation 'likely to be even higher this year' — directionally plausible but uncertain.

text: Successive Governments have been woeful at doing that because we think about three years in advance—maybe we think about three months in advance. That is not good enough.
explanation: Pointed criticism aimed at institutions and the short-termism of governments generally, not personal attack.

text: I think there’s an element to which there’s a bit of faux outrage on this.
explanation: “Faux outrage” is a mild jab at opponents' sincerity but restrained and not a personal attack.

text: We actually did a damn good job, and you were trying to wreck the place. ... Yeah, absolutely, you were trying to wreck the place, Tamatha Paul.
explanation: Direct accusatory exchange naming a member ('you were trying to wreck the place, Tamatha Paul').

text: This Government is leaving too many people behind for us to get behind any of this.
explanation: A critical stance toward the Government's record, directed at policy outcomes rather than at individuals.

text: Auckland Council has resisted growth for decades, through nonsensical planning decisions like denying the ability for a new seven-storey residential building on K Road, what’s now a car park, for heritage reasons.
explanation: A concrete, checkable example of a refused development; the broad “resisted growth for decades” is editorialised.

text: ACT was the only party to oppose it. It didn’t account for infrastructure when we have artists like Gretchen Albrecht… ACT said at the time this is not sustainable—… ACT has been consistent about that.
explanation: ACT's lone opposition to the bipartisan MDRS is accurate.

text: Watercare in Auckland, while delivering a fantastic central interceptor project, has underspent their capital expenditure budget by $100 million to $200 million a year for the past decade. That’s a $1 billion to $2 billion infrastructure deficit
explanation: Presents a specific underspend claim; broadly directionally plausible but the precise multi-year figures are not independently verifiable from the text.

text: it’s about rich, wealthy people in Epsom who don’t want the poor people coming and living next door to them.
explanation: Us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades.

text: there are more of us in this generation that deserve to live close to the places where we work our asses off than the people who sit there, have no job, own multiple properties, and do nothing to earn their wealth.
explanation: Strongly divisive “us vs them” rhetoric that rallies one side and demonises the other.

text: When you are planning for more housing, there is a collective responsibility for everybody to share the load, which is exactly what Mr Twyford was talking about.
explanation: Reaches across to Labour's Twyford to find common ground on shared responsibility, though within a largely combative speech.

text: if Auckland Council say, “We actually don’t want that minimum; we want to go further than that.”, isn’t that up to Auckland Council to decide that?… If there’s any council that’s big enough and grown up enough to make those decisions, it’s Auckland Council, and we should be allowing them to do that.
explanation: Respectful, trust-the-council tone, though appealing within his own devolution stance.

text: All those things should be the sorts of thing that Governments—whether red, blue, or whatever colour they are—should be looking at focusing on.
explanation: Deliberately non-partisan framing inviting all parties into a shared long-term project.

text: Penny Simmonds, when she was speaking in the first reading, said that “major investments”—I think I’m quoting her roughly accurately—“like CRL only achieve their full value when you get, essentially, full development around them.” That’s exactly right.
explanation: Approvingly cites a National MP's point, building cross-party agreement.

text: What we should be doing is working with local government, helping local government where it needs to be helped, to design cities in the way that makes the most possible sense.
explanation: Collaborative, partnership framing toward councils.

text: We actually did a damn good job, and you were trying to wreck the place. ... Yeah, absolutely, you were trying to wreck the place, Tamatha Paul.
explanation: Combative, alienating rather than persuasive.

text: I’ve fought against those same powerbrokers—those same old powerbrokers that live in the leafy suburbs—and guess what! I won my seat, over and over again, actually, with historic margins on that
explanation: Claims a consistent record of fighting the powerbrokers she criticises, aligning her words with her electoral track record.

text: ACT was the only party to oppose it. It didn’t account for infrastructure when we have artists like Gretchen Albrecht… ACT said at the time this is not sustainable—… ACT has been consistent about that.
explanation: Asserts ACT's consistent opposition to MDRS over time; ACT did indeed vote against the MDRS, so words match the party's record.

text: Successive Governments have been woeful at doing that because we think about three years in advance—maybe we think about three months in advance. That is not good enough.
explanation: Includes his own side (“we”) in the criticism rather than only blaming opponents, a self-consistent stance.

text: when the Medium Density Residential Standards (MDRS) were proposed—at the time, I was the mayor of Wellington—I said, “The first thing you’ve done is you have killed any chance that we’ve got of intensifying development around a key public transport corridor, because you’re treating everywhere, effectively, as being the same.”
explanation: Cites his own consistent position from his time as Wellington mayor, matching his current argument against blanket MDRS.

text: I’ve fought against those same powerbrokers—those same old powerbrokers that live in the leafy suburbs—and guess what! I won my seat, over and over again, actually, with historic margins on that
explanation: Points to a delivered outcome (winning her seat) rather than mere aspiration, though it is a personal electoral claim not a policy delivery.

text: in a few short months, when Minister Chris Bishop and I passed the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill, Aucklanders and everyone in New Zealand are going to have a whole lot more options about where they develop
explanation: Claims credit for delivery that has not yet happened—commitment with follow-through still pending.

text: in a few short months, when Minister Chris Bishop and I passed the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill, Aucklanders and everyone in New Zealand are going to have a whole lot more options about where they develop
explanation: Predicts imminent passage of two bills and resulting outcomes; plausible given government majority but timing and effect are uncertain.

text: There will be plenty of capacity, and there will be plenty of choice there, regardless of what the number is.
explanation: Predicts ample housing capacity and choice under any of the proposed targets; plausible given the figures dwarf existing stock, but contingent on actual build-out.

text: National backs recreational fishers, and I'm proud to say I'm one of them.
explanation: Confident identification with constituents, but appeals to her own side rather than seeking cross-party consensus.

text: We have a vision on this side of the House for a sustainable oceans and fisheries sector, and I don't think that that's too far apart from what I've heard in the speeches on the other side.
explanation: Explicitly reaches for common ground, acknowledging opponents share the goal of a sustainable fisheries sector.

text: We only have to look to the Northcote housing development. Under both Governments—both a National and a Labour Government—that is what good practice looks like. It has the right houses. It has the right mix of houses. It has the recreational centres to build strong communities. It has the water infrastructure required.
explanation: Credits both National and Labour for a successful development — cross-party, consensus-minded.

text: I question why we're having to do this now. Why wasn't this work done before this bill was brought to the House? It seems a very mucky way of doing this.
explanation: Criticism of process ('mucky') — pointed but legitimate, aimed at how the bill was handled, not at a person.

text: We've seen the shambolic way that this bill has been shepherded in the short time that it's been released so far... It is a very embarrassing situation when a bill just gets tabled and then already we're starting to see a back-down, and that was on the size limit clause.
explanation: 'Shambolic' and 'embarrassing' are harsh, but the criticism targets the Government's process and conduct rather than personal character.

text: the ability to challenge fishery decisions with the 20-day limit on judicial review and changes to allow for multi-year catch limits without adequate data to support such decisions—they're just stupidity in the bill.
explanation: Labelling provisions 'stupidity' is dismissive rather than engaging the substance respectfully.

text: We have a vision on this side of the House for a sustainable oceans and fisheries sector, and I don't think that that's too far apart from what I've heard in the speeches on the other side.
explanation: Respectful, finds shared values across the House.

text: in the last term, National came to Labour with a bipartisan proposal of that mixed-density standard, and they said, "Yes, we want to do this together." Then there was a sniff of unhappiness from some of its Auckland-based MPs, and they reneged on that bipartisanship after it had been passed into law.
explanation: Charge of reneging is legitimate criticism of conduct rather than a personal slur.

text: Why is it that Ministers go to Cabinet meetings and Ministers pluck numbers out the air, and then change legislation that they've already changed in a very poor process... because they cannot make up their minds
explanation: 'Pluck numbers out the air' and 'cannot make up their minds' are derisive characterisations of the Government's conduct.

text: the Government is using urgency today to bypass the very democratic process it claims to champion. Ramming through a bill that rewrites Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland's housing future.
explanation: 'Ramming through' is charged, but the criticism is of the urgency process, not a personal attack.

text: Nicola Willis, Megan Woods, stand up on a podium back in 2022 and say, "We are going to solve the housing crisis together. We are going to work in a bipartisan way." Low and behold, in 2023, National backtracked
explanation: Legitimate criticism of an opponent's reversal of commitment, not a personal slur.

text: here we are again, under a National Government: weak, weak, weak. Nothing. It does not serve Aucklanders.
explanation: Repetitive rhetorical attack ('weak, weak, weak') with no substantive content.

text: The Labour Party is completely out of touch.
explanation: Dismissive blanket characterisation of opponents with no substantive content.

text: This bill seeks to overhaul the 1996 Act to modernise management and increase commercial efficiency, including changing the rules on landing, discarding of fish, and increasing ministerial powers over sustainability measures.
explanation: Accurate, even-handed description of what the bill does.

text: Last week, the Prime Minister, the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon, stepped in to ask that amendments removing commercial minimum legal sizes for nine fish species be dropped.
explanation: Specific factual claim consistent with the U-turn referenced throughout the debate.

text: in the last term, National came to Labour with a bipartisan proposal of that mixed-density standard, and they said, "Yes, we want to do this together." Then there was a sniff of unhappiness from some of its Auckland-based MPs, and they reneged on that bipartisanship after it had been passed into law.
explanation: Accurate account of the 2022 cross-party MDRS agreement and National's 2023 reversal.

text: the number in the regulatory impact statement—is it 1.4 million capacity for houses? No, I think you'll see that the headline number there is 1.6 million
explanation: Consistent with the RIS and with Bishop's own 1.6m figure; she correctly flags the discrepancy with the bill's 1.4m.

text: Nicola Willis, Megan Woods, stand up on a podium back in 2022 and say, "We are going to solve the housing crisis together. We are going to work in a bipartisan way." Low and behold, in 2023, National backtracked
explanation: Accurate account of the 2022 bipartisan MDRS announcement and National's 2023 reversal.

text: Minister Bishop deflected today. He talked about the rents in Auckland and said that they were coming down ... they don't think their rent has come down. They haven't seen any decreases there. So I don't know what he's talking about.
explanation: Partly mischaracterises Bishop, who argued rents are lower than they otherwise would be (a counterfactual), not that rents are falling; the constituent observation is anecdotal.

text: I question why we're having to do this now. Why wasn't this work done before this bill was brought to the House? It seems a very mucky way of doing this.
explanation: Reasonable procedural critique: if changes were needed they should have preceded introduction, though stated more as complaint than argued case.

text: We've seen the shambolic way that this bill has been shepherded in the short time that it's been released so far... It is a very embarrassing situation when a bill just gets tabled and then already we're starting to see a back-down, and that was on the size limit clause.
explanation: Points to an actual back-down as evidence of poor process, though leans on charged framing.

text: the ability to challenge fishery decisions with the 20-day limit on judicial review and changes to allow for multi-year catch limits without adequate data to support such decisions—they're just stupidity in the bill.
explanation: Identifies a real concern (catch limits without adequate data) but the conclusion is asserted as 'stupidity' rather than argued.

text: the number in the regulatory impact statement—is it 1.4 million capacity for houses? No, I think you'll see that the headline number there is 1.6 million
explanation: Cites the just-tabled RIS document as evidence for the inconsistency she alleges.

text: Why is it that Ministers go to Cabinet meetings and Ministers pluck numbers out the air, and then change legislation that they've already changed in a very poor process... because they cannot make up their minds
explanation: Underlying point about shifting figures has some basis, but is delivered as rhetorical accusation.

text: the Government is using urgency today to bypass the very democratic process it claims to champion. Ramming through a bill that rewrites Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland's housing future.
explanation: Reasonable procedural objection that all-stages urgency limits scrutiny, though framed rhetorically.

text: We only have to look to the Northcote housing development. Under both Governments—both a National and a Labour Government—that is what good practice looks like. It has the right houses. It has the right mix of houses. It has the recreational centres to build strong communities. It has the water infrastructure required.
explanation: Uses a real-world case to illustrate what good intensification looks like.

text: Minister Bishop deflected today. He talked about the rents in Auckland and said that they were coming down ... they don't think their rent has come down. They haven't seen any decreases there. So I don't know what he's talking about.
explanation: Rebuts a counterfactual claim with anecdote and slightly reframes what was said.

text: the ability to challenge fishery decisions with the 20-day limit on judicial review and changes to allow for multi-year catch limits without adequate data to support such decisions—they're just stupidity in the bill.
explanation: Identifies specific clauses (20-day judicial-review limit, multi-year catch limits) rather than vague objection.

text: This bill seeks to overhaul the 1996 Act to modernise management and increase commercial efficiency, including changing the rules on landing, discarding of fish, and increasing ministerial powers over sustainability measures.
explanation: Names the Act amended and the concrete areas of change (landing, discarding, ministerial powers).

text: Last week, the Prime Minister, the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon, stepped in to ask that amendments removing commercial minimum legal sizes for nine fish species be dropped.
explanation: Gives the actor, timing ('last week') and a precise figure (nine fish species).

text: National is committed to constructive change. We believe that if the bill, however, does not undergo real, meaningful improvements during the select committee stage, we will not be able to support it beyond that point.
explanation: Sets a condition (meaningful improvements) but does not define what those improvements are.

text: We must work together to protect our marine resources for future generations.
explanation: Platitude with no mechanism, measure, or timeframe.

text: in the last term, National came to Labour with a bipartisan proposal of that mixed-density standard, and they said, "Yes, we want to do this together." Then there was a sniff of unhappiness from some of its Auckland-based MPs, and they reneged on that bipartisanship after it had been passed into law.
explanation: Identifies the parties, the policy, and the sequence of events.

text: the number in the regulatory impact statement—is it 1.4 million capacity for houses? No, I think you'll see that the headline number there is 1.6 million
explanation: Pins the argument to specific competing figures.

text: Nicola Willis, Megan Woods, stand up on a podium back in 2022 and say, "We are going to solve the housing crisis together. We are going to work in a bipartisan way." Low and behold, in 2023, National backtracked
explanation: Names the politicians, the year, and the nature of the backtrack.

text: here we are again, under a National Government: weak, weak, weak. Nothing. It does not serve Aucklanders.
explanation: Vague pejorative; commits to nothing concrete.

text: We only have to look to the Northcote housing development. Under both Governments—both a National and a Labour Government—that is what good practice looks like. It has the right houses. It has the right mix of houses. It has the recreational centres to build strong communities. It has the water infrastructure required.
explanation: Names a concrete example and lists its features (mix of housing, amenities, water infrastructure).

text: the bill will pass its first reading, but be assured that our position is crystal clear; we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits.
explanation: Predicts the bill will pass first reading — confirmed by the party vote (National 49, ACT 11, NZ First 8) recorded immediately after.

text: I've been working closely with the Balmoral Residents Association, and the residents are particularly concerned that enabling large-scale development, often without confirming the infrastructure capacity, could lead to isolated and out-of-scale development.
explanation: Predicts that development without confirmed infrastructure 'could lead to' isolated, out-of-scale outcomes — plausible, conditional, uncertain.

text: National is committed to constructive change. We believe that if the bill, however, does not undergo real, meaningful improvements during the select committee stage, we will not be able to support it beyond that point.
explanation: A conditional commitment with follow-through dependent on the select committee outcome — intent stated, delivery unproven.

text: the capacity that will be unlocked as a result of this will be, roughly, around 1.6 million homes. That is a substantial advance on the status quo, which is in the Auckland Unitary Plan—which hasn't been updated for years—which is around 1.2 million homes.
explanation: Framing the bill as 'unlocking' more housing is in tension with the bill's own text reducing the required capacity from ~2m to 1.4m, which opponents quote against him.
